q: A tenant sued a city in a state trial court of general jurisdiction, alleging that city officials evicted her without a hearing in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment. Her only claim was under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, a federal statute that says nothing about which courts may hear such claims. The city moved to dismiss, arguing that a claim created by federal law may be heard only in a federal court. How should the court rule on the motion?
o: Deny it, because state courts may hear federal claims unless Congress has made federal jurisdiction exclusive.
Grant it, because a claim that arises under federal law falls within the federal courts' original jurisdiction.
Deny it, because the city waived any objection to the forum by appearing and filing a motion.
Grant it, because a state court may not enforce the Fourteenth Amendment against a municipality.
oe: Concurrent jurisdiction is the default. State trial courts have general jurisdiction, and nothing makes § 1983 claims exclusively federal. The city's remedy, if it wants a federal forum, is removal under § 1441, not dismissal.
Section 1331 gives federal district courts jurisdiction over such claims. It does not take jurisdiction away from state courts. Only an exclusivity provision does that.
Right result, wrong reason. There is nothing to waive: the state court has power over the claim whether or not the city objects.
State courts routinely decide federal constitutional claims, and state judges are bound by the Supremacy Clause to apply federal law.
topic: Wk 1 · Courts, sources of law & the life of a lawsuit — Concurrent jurisdiction

q: Variation: Same facts, except that instead of moving to dismiss, the city filed a timely notice of removal in the federal district court for the district where the state action was pending. The tenant moved to remand, arguing that she chose the state forum and that the city could not override her choice. How should the federal court rule?
o: Deny remand, because the action could have been filed in federal court originally.
Grant remand, because the plaintiff is the master of her complaint and chose the state forum.
Grant remand, because a federal court may not hear a case first filed in a state court.
Deny remand, but only if the tenant fails to object within 30 days of the notice of removal.
oe: Concurrency means the plaintiff chooses first, but a defendant may remove any civil action within the district courts' original jurisdiction. A § 1983 claim arises under federal law, so § 1441(a) removal was proper.
Being master of the complaint lets the plaintiff decide which claims to plead. Once she pleads a federal claim, she cannot prevent the defendant from removing it.
Removal exists precisely to move cases filed in state court into federal court when they are within original federal jurisdiction.
The 30-day limit in § 1447(c) applies to procedural defects. Here there is no defect at all, so removal stands regardless of timing.
topic: Wk 1 · Courts, sources of law & the life of a lawsuit — Removal instead of dismissal
pre: A tenant sued a city in a state trial court of general jurisdiction, alleging that city officials evicted her without a hearing in violation of the Fourteenth Amendment. Her only claim was under 42 U.S.C. § 1983, a federal statute that says nothing about which courts may hear such claims. The city moved to dismiss, arguing that a claim created by federal law may be heard only in a federal court. How should the court rule on the motion?

q: An inventor sued a competitor in a state court, alleging that the competitor's product infringed her patent and seeking damages under the federal Patent Act. The competitor answered on the merits and never raised any jurisdictional objection. Six months later, the state judge noticed that federal law gives the federal district courts exclusive jurisdiction over claims arising under the patent laws. What should the state court do?
o: Dismiss the action, because the state court has no subject-matter jurisdiction over the claim.
Proceed to judgment, because the competitor waived the objection by answering on the merits.
Proceed to judgment, because state courts have concurrent jurisdiction over federal claims.
Transfer the action to the federal district court for the district in which the state court sits.
oe: Section 1338(a) makes federal jurisdiction over patent-infringement claims exclusive. Subject-matter limits cannot be waived by answering on the merits, and a court may raise them on its own at any time.
Only personal-jurisdiction and similar defenses are waivable. A court's lack of power over the type of case cannot be cured by the parties' conduct.
Concurrency is only the default. Congress has displaced it for patent claims by making federal jurisdiction exclusive.
A state court has no power to transfer a case into the federal system. Only the defendant can move a case from state to federal court, by removal.
topic: Wk 1 · Courts, sources of law & the life of a lawsuit — Exclusive federal jurisdiction

q: A state's highest court affirmed a defamation judgment against a newspaper, rejecting the newspaper's argument that the First Amendment barred liability. State law gives the newspaper no further review in the state system. What is the newspaper's proper avenue for further review of the First Amendment ruling?
o: A petition for a writ of certiorari to the United States Supreme Court.
A notice of removal to the federal district court, because the case now turns on a federal question.
An appeal to the federal court of appeals for the circuit that includes the state.
A new action in federal district court asking it to review the state judgment for error.
oe: When a state case turns on federal law, the Supreme Court is the court of last resort for both systems, which keeps federal law uniform. Its review is usually discretionary, by certiorari.
Removal is available only to a defendant, within 30 days of receiving the complaint, and only for a case within original federal jurisdiction. A federal defense never supports removal.
The courts of appeals review federal district courts. They have no appellate power over state courts.
Federal district courts have original, not appellate, jurisdiction. They cannot sit in review of state-court judgments.
topic: Wk 1 · Courts, sources of law & the life of a lawsuit — Supreme Court review of state courts

q: Congress enacted a statute giving the federal district courts jurisdiction over "any action between citizens of the same State concerning title to land worth more than $1,000,000." Two citizens of the same state who are quarreling over a valuable ranch, and who raise no issue of federal law, filed suit in federal court under the statute. Does the federal court have subject-matter jurisdiction?
o: No, because the dispute falls within no category of the judicial power in Article III.
Yes, because Congress has the power to ordain and establish the lower federal courts.
Yes, because the Necessary and Proper Clause lets Congress implement the judicial power.
No, because disputes over title to land are reserved exclusively to state courts.
oe: Federal jurisdiction requires both an Article III category and a statutory grant. A dispute between citizens of the same state on state-law issues fits no Article III category, and Congress cannot enlarge Article III by statute.
That power lets Congress create lower courts and decide how much of the Article III judicial power to give them. It does not let Congress go beyond Article III.
The clause lets Congress carry out powers the Constitution grants. It cannot create jurisdiction the Constitution withholds.
Right result, wrong reason. Federal courts decide land-title disputes all the time when there is diversity or a federal question. The problem here is the parties' shared citizenship.
topic: Wk 1 · Courts, sources of law & the life of a lawsuit — Article III limit on Congress

q: A citizen of Ohio sued a citizen of Kentucky in federal court for $60,000 in damages for breach of a state-law contract. The defendant moved to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. The plaintiff argued that Article III extends the judicial power to controversies "between Citizens of different States" without any dollar minimum. How should the court rule?
o: Grant the motion, because no statute confers jurisdiction over this case on the district court.
Deny the motion, because the case is within Article III's grant of jurisdiction over diversity cases.
Grant the motion, because Article III requires that a controversy exceed $75,000.
Deny the motion, because the defendant waived the objection by not raising it in a state court first.
oe: Article III is necessary but not sufficient. The lower federal courts have only the jurisdiction Congress gives them, and § 1332(a) grants diversity jurisdiction only when the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000.
That satisfies only the first of the two requirements. Without a statutory grant, the district court cannot hear the case.
Article III contains no amount-in-controversy requirement. The $75,000 floor comes from the statute.
Subject-matter jurisdiction can never be waived, and there was no earlier state proceeding in which to raise it.
topic: Wk 1 · Courts, sources of law & the life of a lawsuit — Statutory grant needed too

q: A federal district court adopted a local rule requiring every defendant to serve an answer within 10 days after being served with the summons and complaint. A defendant was personally served and did not waive service. It served its answer 18 days after service. The plaintiff moved for entry of default, relying on the local rule. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because a local rule must be consistent with the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure.
Grant the motion, because a district court's local rules govern its own docket management.
Grant the motion, because a specific local rule controls over the general time limit in Rule 12.
Deny the motion, because an answer is timely if served within 30 days of service of process.
oe: Rule 83 lets district courts adopt local rules only if they are consistent with federal statutes and the Federal Rules. Rule 12(a) gives a served defendant 21 days to answer, so the 18-day answer was timely and the conflicting local rule cannot shorten it.
Local rules do govern many housekeeping matters, but they sit below the Federal Rules in the hierarchy and cannot contradict them.
Specificity does not change the hierarchy. A lower source of procedural law must be consistent with every higher one.
Right result, wrong rule. Rule 12(a)(1)(A)(i) gives a defendant 21 days after service, not 30.
topic: Wk 1 · Courts, sources of law & the life of a lawsuit — Local rules must yield

q: A federal statute creating a cause of action provides that suit must be "commenced" within two years after the claim accrues and says nothing more about commencement. A plaintiff's claim under the statute accrued on March 1, Year 1. She filed her complaint in federal district court on February 20, Year 3, and served the defendant on March 15, Year 3. The defendant moved to dismiss as untimely. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because the action was commenced when the complaint was filed.
Grant the motion, because an action is not commenced until the defendant is served.
Grant the motion, because the defendant did not receive notice of the suit within two years.
Deny the motion, because statutes of limitations are affirmative defenses that cannot be raised by motion.
oe: Rule 3 provides that a civil action is commenced by filing a complaint with the court. For a federal claim with no contrary statutory rule, filing on February 20 was within the two-year period.
That is the rule in some state systems, but in federal court Rule 3 makes filing the commencing act. Service is governed separately by Rule 4(m)'s 90-day limit.
The limitations period asks when the action was commenced, not when the defendant learned of it.
Limitations is an affirmative defense under Rule 8(c), but a defendant may raise it by a Rule 12(b)(6) motion when the defect appears on the face of the complaint.
topic: Wk 1 · Courts, sources of law & the life of a lawsuit — Commencement under Rule 3

q: A homeowner filed a single complaint in federal court against a neighbor, asking for $90,000 in damages for past flooding caused by the neighbor's drainage ditch and for an injunction requiring the neighbor to fill in the ditch. The neighbor moved to dismiss, arguing that the homeowner improperly combined a claim at law and a claim in equity in one action. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because the Rules provide for only one form of action, the civil action.
Grant the motion, because legal and equitable relief must be sought in separate counts or actions.
Deny the motion, but require the homeowner to elect between damages and the injunction before trial.
Grant the motion only as to the injunction, because federal courts sitting in diversity cannot grant equitable relief.
oe: Rule 2 abolished the old separation of law and equity. A plaintiff may seek damages and an injunction in a single civil action, and Rule 8(a)(3) expressly allows a demand for different types of relief.
Separate counts are required only for claims founded on separate transactions, and only when that would promote clarity (Rule 10(b)). The merger of law and equity means one action suffices.
No election is required. Rule 8(a)(3) permits a demand for relief in the alternative or of different types.
Federal courts grant injunctions in diversity cases regularly. Nothing in the Rules limits a diversity plaintiff to damages.
topic: Wk 1 · Courts, sources of law & the life of a lawsuit — One form of action

q: A defendant filed a motion raising four objections to a complaint filed in federal court. Assuming each objection is valid, which defect is least likely to be cured by amendment or by new service?
o: The complaint was filed after the applicable statute of limitations had already expired.
The process server left the summons and complaint with the defendant's 12-year-old nephew.
The complaint failed to allege that the plaintiff suffered any damages from the breach.
The summons served on the defendant did not bear the clerk's signature or the court's seal.
oe: A claim filed after the limitations period ran is an incurable defect. No amendment changes the date on which the claim accrued or the date the complaint was filed.
Defective service is curable. The plaintiff can serve again properly within the Rule 4(m) period or any extension.
An omitted element is the classic curable defect. Rule 15(a) permits amendment, and leave should be freely given.
A defect in the summons is insufficient process under Rule 12(b)(4). The plaintiff can have a proper summons issued and serve again.
topic: Wk 1 · Courts, sources of law & the life of a lawsuit — Curable and incurable defects

q: On May 1, a defendant served a Rule 12(b)(6) motion arguing that the plaintiff's breach-of-contract complaint failed to allege damages. On May 18, without the defendant's consent or leave of court, the plaintiff filed an amended complaint adding the damages allegations. The plaintiff had not amended before. The defendant moved to strike the amended complaint. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because the plaintiff amended within 21 days after service of the Rule 12(b) motion.
Grant the motion, because once a Rule 12(b) motion is served, the plaintiff must obtain leave to amend.
Grant the motion, because a complaint that omits an element must be dismissed with prejudice.
Deny the motion, because a plaintiff may amend as a matter of course at any time before trial.
oe: Rule 15(a)(1)(B) lets a party amend once as a matter of course within 21 days after service of a Rule 12(b) motion. May 18 is within that window, so no consent or leave was needed.
The rule is the opposite: service of a 12(b) motion opens a 21-day window to amend without leave.
Omitting an element is a curable defect. Courts ordinarily allow amendment rather than dismissing with prejudice.
Right result, wrong reason. The as-of-course right exists only within the 21-day windows of Rule 15(a)(1).
topic: Wk 1 · Courts, sources of law & the life of a lawsuit — Amendment as of course

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the plaintiff filed the amended complaint on June 15 without consent or leave. The defendant moved to strike it, and the plaintiff then asked for leave to amend. There is no evidence of bad faith, undue delay, or prejudice to the defendant. How should the court rule on the request for leave?
o: Grant leave, because the court should freely give leave when justice so requires.
Deny leave, because the time to amend as a matter of course has expired.
Deny leave, because a plaintiff may amend only once in the life of a case.
Grant leave, but only if the defendant consents in writing to the amendment.
oe: June 15 is outside the 21-day window, so the plaintiff needs consent or leave under Rule 15(a)(2). Leave should be freely given absent reasons like bad faith, undue delay, prejudice, or futility, and none appears here.
The expiration of the as-of-course window only shifts the plaintiff to Rule 15(a)(2). It does not bar amendment.
The once-only limit applies to amendment as a matter of course. With leave or consent, a party may amend again.
Written consent is an alternative to leave, not a precondition for it. The court may grant leave over the defendant's objection.
topic: Wk 1 · Courts, sources of law & the life of a lawsuit — Leave to amend
pre: On May 1, a defendant served a Rule 12(b)(6) motion arguing that the plaintiff's breach-of-contract complaint failed to allege damages. On May 18, without the defendant's consent or leave of court, the plaintiff filed an amended complaint adding the damages allegations. The plaintiff had not amended before. The defendant moved to strike the amended complaint. How should the court rule?

q: A buyer sued a seller in a state court for breach of warranty. After a full trial, the jury returned a verdict for the seller, and judgment was entered on the merits. The buyer did not appeal. A year later, the buyer sued the seller in federal court, asserting the same warranty claim arising from the same sale. Which doctrine most clearly bars the second action?
o: Claim preclusion, because the same claim between the same parties went to a final judgment on the merits.
Issue preclusion, because the jury necessarily decided the warranty issue in the seller's favor.
The well-pleaded complaint rule, because the second complaint relies on a prior state judgment.
Lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, because a federal court may not hear a claim already tried in state court.
oe: A claim decided on the merits in a final judgment cannot be relitigated between the same parties. That is claim preclusion, or res judicata.
Issue preclusion bars relitigating a particular issue actually decided. It may also apply, but when the identical claim is refiled, claim preclusion is the doctrine that bars the whole action.
That rule decides whether a case arises under federal law. It has nothing to do with relitigating a decided claim.
A federal court may have jurisdiction over the claim. The bar comes from the preclusive effect of the earlier judgment, which is an affirmative defense under Rule 8(c).
topic: Wk 1 · Courts, sources of law & the life of a lawsuit — Claim preclusion

q: In a federal breach-of-contract suit seeking $80,000, the plaintiff served a request for production of every email sent or received by any of the defendant's 4,000 employees during the past 20 years. Collecting and reviewing the emails would cost the defendant about $2 million. The defendant objected. On what ground is the court most likely to sustain the objection?
o: The request is not proportional to the needs of the case.
Emails are not documents subject to a request for production.
Discovery may be had only of matter that would be admissible in evidence at trial.
A party may not seek discovery until the court has ruled on a motion for summary judgment.
oe: Rule 26(b)(1) allows discovery of nonprivileged matter relevant to a claim or defense and proportional to the needs of the case. A $2 million burden in an $80,000 case is grossly disproportionate.
Electronically stored information is discoverable through requests for production.
Information within the scope of discovery need not be admissible in evidence to be discoverable.
Discovery ordinarily precedes summary judgment. Rule 56 motions are usually decided on the discovery record.
topic: Wk 1 · Courts, sources of law & the life of a lawsuit — Scope of discovery

q: After discovery in a federal negligence action, the defendant moved for summary judgment, submitting an affidavit from its driver stating that the light was green. The plaintiff submitted deposition testimony from a bystander stating that the light was red. The judge found the driver more believable. What should the judge do?
o: Deny the motion, because there is a genuine dispute as to a material fact.
Grant the motion, because the judge may resolve credibility questions on a written record.
Grant the motion, because the defendant's affidavit came from a witness with personal knowledge.
Deny the motion, because summary judgment is unavailable in negligence cases.
oe: Rule 56 permits summary judgment only when there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact. Conflicting sworn accounts of the light's color create one, and the judge may not weigh credibility at this stage.
Credibility determinations belong to the fact-finder at trial. On summary judgment the court views the evidence in the light most favorable to the non-movant.
Personal knowledge makes an affidavit usable, but the opposing deposition is equally competent, so the dispute remains.
Right result, wrong reason. Summary judgment is available in any kind of case when its standard is met.
topic: Wk 1 · Courts, sources of law & the life of a lawsuit — Summary judgment standard

q: A Georgia trucking company was sued in a Montana state court by a Montana rancher over a highway collision in Montana. The trucking company's lawyer advised it to remove the case to federal court. Which reason for removal best reflects the traditional justification for diversity jurisdiction?
o: Federal court may offer protection against bias in favor of local litigants.
Federal judges have greater expertise in applying Montana tort law.
Federal court will apply a uniform federal common law of negligence.
The federal government has a direct interest in suits involving interstate carriers.
oe: Diversity jurisdiction exists mainly to protect out-of-state parties from local prejudice. The lawyer's advice rests on exactly that concern about home cooking.
Federal expertise justifies federal-question jurisdiction over federal law. In a diversity case the federal court applies state law, often with less familiarity than a state judge.
There is no federal general common law. Under Erie the federal court must apply Montana's negligence law.
A direct federal interest supports jurisdiction over cases involving the United States or federal law, not ordinary state tort claims between private parties.
topic: Wk 1 · Courts, sources of law & the life of a lawsuit — Why diversity jurisdiction exists

q: A defendant lost a jury trial in the trial court of a state whose court system follows the typical three-tier structure. The defendant believes the trial judge wrongly admitted hearsay evidence, a question of state law. Which statement most accurately describes the defendant's appellate options?
o: It may appeal as of right to the intermediate court, then seek discretionary high-court review.
It may appeal directly to the United States Supreme Court, because a jury verdict is a final judgment.
It must seek discretionary review in the intermediate appellate court before any appeal as of right.
It may appeal to the federal court of appeals, because the trial raised an evidentiary question.
oe: In the typical state system the first appeal, to the intermediate appellate court, is usually available as of right, and further review in the high court is usually discretionary.
The Supreme Court reviews state judgments only on federal questions and only after the highest available state court rules. This is a state-law evidence issue.
This reverses the usual structure. Review as of right normally comes first, at the intermediate level.
Federal courts of appeals have no appellate jurisdiction over state trial courts.
topic: Wk 1 · Courts, sources of law & the life of a lawsuit — State appellate structure

q: A plaintiff sued a corporation in federal court. The corporation moved to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(1) for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction and, in the same motion, under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to state a claim. The judge believes the complaint plainly fails to state a claim and is uncertain about jurisdiction. Which issue should the court ordinarily resolve first?
o: Whether the court has subject-matter jurisdiction, because without it the court has no power to reach the merits.
Whether the complaint states a claim, because a merits dismissal is simpler and conserves judicial resources.
Whichever issue the defendant listed first, because the movant controls the order of decision.
Whether venue is proper, because venue must be decided before either jurisdiction or the merits.
oe: Jurisdiction is a threshold question. A court that lacks subject-matter jurisdiction cannot decide the merits, so a 12(b)(6) dismissal without first confirming jurisdiction would be a ruling the court had no power to make.
Efficiency does not let a court assume jurisdiction in order to reach the merits. Jurisdiction comes first.
The order is set by the court's need for power to act, not by how the motion is drafted.
Venue is itself a threshold issue, but it comes after subject-matter and personal jurisdiction in the usual order, and neither party raised it.
topic: Wk 1 · Courts, sources of law & the life of a lawsuit — Jurisdiction before merits

q: A customer stopped payment on a check for a defective pair of jeans. The store's manager then filed a bad-check criminal charge against her, and she was acquitted. She sued the store in federal court for malicious prosecution, alleging that the store's employees knew she had stopped payment because the goods were defective, knew she had committed no crime, and acted maliciously. The district court dismissed because the complaint did not allege specific "facts" showing a lack of probable cause and alleged malice only in general terms. Under the notice-pleading standard applied at the time, how should the court of appeals rule?
o: Reverse, because the complaint gave fair notice of the claim and malice may be alleged generally.
Affirm, because malicious prosecution sounds in fraud and must be pleaded with particularity.
Affirm, because a complaint must plead the evidence showing that each element is probable.
Reverse, because a complaint may be dismissed only after the defendant files an answer.
oe: In Rannels the Third Circuit reversed on these facts. The complaint gave fair notice of the claim and its grounds, Rule 9(b) allows malice to be alleged generally, and the Rules abolished code pleading's distinctions among facts, evidence, and conclusions.
Malicious prosecution is not fraud. Rule 9(b)'s particularity requirement applies only to fraud and mistake.
No pleading standard, even plausibility, requires pleading evidence or showing that success is probable.
A Rule 12(b)(6) motion is made before the answer. The dismissal was wrong because the complaint was sufficient, not because of timing.
topic: Wk 1 · Courts, sources of law & the life of a lawsuit — Notice pleading at its most generous

q: A state's long-arm statute authorizes jurisdiction over a nonresident only if the nonresident (1) transacts business within the state or (2) commits a tortious act within the state. The state's courts have held that a tortious act is committed "within the state" only if the defendant is physically present there when acting. From her office in Ohio, an Ohio consultant emailed a defamatory report about a forum-state engineer to the engineer's forum-state clients. The engineer sued the consultant in federal court in the forum state on the basis of diversity jurisdiction. The consultant has never been to the forum state or done business there, and she moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. Assume that exercising jurisdiction would satisfy due process. How should the court rule?
o: Grant the motion, because the long-arm statute does not reach the consultant's conduct.
Deny the motion, because exercising jurisdiction would be consistent with due process.
Deny the motion, because a long-arm statute reaches as far as due process permits.
Grant the motion, because an email sent from another state is not a contact with the forum.
oe: Personal jurisdiction requires both statutory authority and due process. In federal court, Rule 4(k)(1)(A) borrows the forum state's long-arm statute. As in Bensusan, an enumerated-acts statute read to require physical presence is narrower than due process, so the analysis ends at the statutory step.
Due process is a ceiling, not a grant. A court may exercise only the jurisdiction a statute or rule authorizes, and this statute does not authorize it here.
Some states' statutes do, but enumerated-acts statutes like this one can be narrower, and state courts control their meaning.
Right result, wrong reason. Emails deliberately aimed at the forum can be contacts for due process purposes. The obstacle here is the statute.
topic: Wk 2 · PJ framework & the territorial era — Enumerated-acts long-arm statute

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the forum state's long-arm statute authorizes jurisdiction "on any basis not inconsistent with the Constitution of this State or of the United States." How should the court rule on the motion?
o: Deny the motion, because the statutory inquiry merges into the due process inquiry, which is satisfied.
Grant the motion, because the consultant never entered the forum state.
Grant the motion, because a federal court in a diversity case must apply the Fifth Amendment national-contacts test.
Deny the motion, because a federal court is not bound by a state long-arm statute.
oe: When a long-arm statute reaches to the constitutional limit, as California's does, the two-step analysis collapses into a single due process question. The facts assume due process is met.
Physical entry is not required under the minimum-contacts test, and this statute has no physical-presence requirement.
In a diversity case the federal court borrows the state's reach under Rule 4(k)(1)(A), and the Fourteenth Amendment, which looks to contacts with the forum state, governs.
Right result, wrong reason. Under Rule 4(k)(1)(A), a federal court's reach in an ordinary case is the same as the forum state's courts.
topic: Wk 2 · PJ framework & the territorial era — Long-arm to the constitutional limit
pre: A state's long-arm statute authorizes jurisdiction over a nonresident only if the nonresident (1) transacts business within the state or (2) commits a tortious act within the state. The state's courts have held that a tortious act is committed "within the state" only if the defendant is physically present there when acting. From her office in Ohio, an Ohio consultant emailed a defamatory report about a forum-state engineer to the engineer's forum-state clients. The engineer sued the consultant in federal court in the forum state on the basis of diversity jurisdiction. The consultant has never been to the forum state or done business there, and she moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. Assume that exercising jurisdiction would satisfy due process. How should the court rule?

q: A Texas buyer sued a Maine seller in federal district court in Texas, invoking diversity jurisdiction, for breach of a contract to sell lobster traps. The seller has substantial business throughout New England but no contacts with Texas. Texas's long-arm statute reaches as far as due process permits. The buyer argued that because the case is in federal court, the seller's contacts with the United States as a whole are what matter. How should the court rule on the seller's motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction?
o: Grant the motion, because the federal court may reach only defendants a Texas state court could reach.
Deny the motion, because the Fifth Amendment governs actions in a federal court.
Deny the motion, because the seller has continuous and systematic contacts with the United States.
Grant the motion, because a federal court may reach only defendants found within the forum state.
oe: Rule 4(k)(1)(A) is the default rule: a federal court reaches whoever is subject to the jurisdiction of a state court of general jurisdiction where it sits. A Texas court would have to find Texas contacts under the Fourteenth Amendment, and there are none.
The Fifth Amendment national-contacts test applies only where a federal statute or Rule 4(k)(2) supplies nationwide reach. Neither applies to a diversity contract claim.
National contacts matter only under a federal statute authorizing nationwide service or Rule 4(k)(2), which is limited to federal-law claims.
Right result, wrong reason. Federal courts reach out-of-state defendants through long-arm statutes, the 100-mile bulge, and federal statutes.
topic: Wk 2 · PJ framework & the territorial era — Rule 4(k)(1)(A) and state-contacts analysis

q: A New York shipper sued a Connecticut trucking company in federal court in Manhattan, invoking diversity jurisdiction, over cargo damaged in Connecticut. The trucking company impleaded a New Jersey repair shop under Rule 14, alleging that the shop's faulty brake work caused the accident. The shop operates only in New Jersey and has no contacts with New York. It was served at its shop in Newark, New Jersey, about 10 miles from the courthouse. New York's long-arm statute would not reach the shop. Does the court have personal jurisdiction over the repair shop?
o: Yes, because the bulge rule reaches Rule 14 parties served within 100 miles.
No, because the shop has no contacts with New York and the long-arm statute does not reach it.
Yes, because the shop has minimum contacts with the United States as a whole.
No, because the 100-mile bulge applies only to defendants named in the original complaint.
oe: Rule 4(k)(1)(B), the 100-mile bulge, gives the court jurisdiction over a party joined under Rule 14 or 19 and served within the United States not more than 100 miles from where the summons issued. Newark is about 10 miles away.
That would end the analysis under Rule 4(k)(1)(A), but the bulge rule is an independent basis for impleaded parties.
National contacts are the test under Rule 4(k)(2) and federal statutes. The bulge rule turns on where the shop was served, not on national contacts.
The rule is the reverse. The bulge reaches only parties added under Rules 14 and 19, not original defendants.
topic: Wk 2 · PJ framework & the territorial era — The 100-mile bulge

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the repair shop is located in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, more than 300 miles from Manhattan, and was served there. Does the court have personal jurisdiction over the repair shop?
o: No, because the shop was served outside the 100-mile bulge and no other basis applies.
Yes, because the trucking company's claim against the shop arises out of the same accident.
Yes, because a third-party defendant may be served anywhere in the United States.
No, because a third-party defendant must reside in the state where the court sits.
oe: The bulge covers only service within 100 miles. With no New York contacts and no long-arm reach, Rule 4(k)(1)(A) fails too.
Relatedness of the claims may support supplemental subject-matter jurisdiction, but it does nothing for personal jurisdiction over the shop.
Nationwide reach exists only under a federal statute or Rule 4(k)(2). The bulge is limited to 100 miles.
Third-party defendants from other states are joined regularly when a basis for jurisdiction exists, such as the bulge or the long-arm statute.
topic: Wk 2 · PJ framework & the territorial era — Outside the bulge
pre: A New York shipper sued a Connecticut trucking company in federal court in Manhattan, invoking diversity jurisdiction, over cargo damaged in Connecticut. The trucking company impleaded a New Jersey repair shop under Rule 14, alleging that the shop's faulty brake work caused the accident. The shop operates only in New Jersey and has no contacts with New York. It was served at its shop in Newark, New Jersey, about 10 miles from the courthouse. New York's long-arm statute would not reach the shop. Does the court have personal jurisdiction over the repair shop?

q: A Delaware company sued an Italian manufacturer in federal court in Illinois for trademark infringement under the federal Lanham Act. The manufacturer sells the allegedly infringing handbags through its own website and distributors to customers in 30 states, but its sales in any single state, including Illinois, are too small to support jurisdiction in that state's courts. The manufacturer concedes that it is not subject to jurisdiction in any state's courts of general jurisdiction. No federal statute authorizes nationwide service for the claim. Does the court have personal jurisdiction over the manufacturer?
o: Yes, if the exercise is consistent with its contacts with the nation as a whole.
No, because Illinois's long-arm statute does not reach the manufacturer.
No, because Rule 4(k)(2) is available only when a federal statute authorizes nationwide service.
Yes, because a foreign defendant may be sued in any federal district under the venue statute.
oe: Rule 4(k)(2) covers a claim arising under federal law against a defendant not subject to jurisdiction in any state's courts, if exercising jurisdiction is consistent with the Constitution. The Fifth Amendment test looks to national contacts, and sales in 30 states are strong evidence.
That defeats jurisdiction under Rule 4(k)(1)(A), but Rule 4(k)(2) supplies a separate basis for federal claims.
That describes Rule 4(k)(1)(C). Rule 4(k)(2) fills the gap when no statute authorizes service.
Section 1391(c)(3) makes venue proper anywhere for a non-U.S. resident, but venue does not create personal jurisdiction.
topic: Wk 2 · PJ framework & the territorial era — Rule 4(k)(2)

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the Delaware company sued only for unfair competition under Illinois common law, invoking alienage jurisdiction. Does the court have personal jurisdiction over the manufacturer?
o: No, because Rule 4(k)(2) applies only to claims arising under federal law.
Yes, because an alien defendant may be reached through its contacts with the United States as a whole.
Yes, because alienage jurisdiction is a form of federal-question jurisdiction.
No, because a federal court may not hear a state-law claim against a foreign defendant.
oe: The national-contacts gap-filler is limited to federal claims. For a state-law claim, the court is limited to Rule 4(k)(1)(A), and the manufacturer concedes no state could reach it.
Alien status does not trigger national contacts. Only a federal claim under Rule 4(k)(2), or a federal statute, does.
Alienage jurisdiction is part of § 1332, not § 1331. The claim remains a state-law claim.
Section 1332(a)(2) permits exactly that, subject to the jurisdictional amount. The problem is personal, not subject-matter, jurisdiction.
topic: Wk 2 · PJ framework & the territorial era — State-law claim under 4(k)(2)
pre: A Delaware company sued an Italian manufacturer in federal court in Illinois for trademark infringement under the federal Lanham Act. The manufacturer sells the allegedly infringing handbags through its own website and distributors to customers in 30 states, but its sales in any single state, including Illinois, are too small to support jurisdiction in that state's courts. The manufacturer concedes that it is not subject to jurisdiction in any state's courts of general jurisdiction. No federal statute authorizes nationwide service for the claim. Does the court have personal jurisdiction over the manufacturer?

q: An investor sued a California promoter in federal court in New York under a federal securities statute. The statute provides that process in such actions "may be served in any district of which the defendant is an inhabitant or wherever the defendant may be found." The promoter was served at his home in California. He has never been to New York and has no New York contacts, and New York's long-arm statute would not reach him. Does the court have personal jurisdiction over the promoter?
o: Yes, because a federal statute authorizes nationwide service of process.
No, because the promoter has never been to New York and lacks minimum contacts with it.
No, because Rule 4(k)(2) applies only to defendants not subject to jurisdiction in any state.
Yes, because New York's long-arm statute reaches any defendant who violates federal law.
oe: Rule 4(k)(1)(C) recognizes jurisdiction when a federal statute authorizes service. Due process is then measured under the Fifth Amendment, by the defendant's contacts with the nation, which a California resident has.
State-specific contacts matter when the court borrows state reach under Rule 4(k)(1)(A). A federal statute authorizing nationwide service changes the relevant sovereign to the United States.
That is a correct statement of Rule 4(k)(2), but the court does not need it. The securities statute supplies jurisdiction through Rule 4(k)(1)(C).
The facts state the long-arm statute would not reach him. The statutory basis here is federal.
topic: Wk 2 · PJ framework & the territorial era — Federal statute authorizing nationwide service

q: An Oregon software company with no other connection to Delaware sued a Delaware customer in a Delaware state court for unpaid license fees. The customer filed a counterclaim against the software company for breach of warranty arising from the same license. The software company moved to dismiss the counterclaim for lack of personal jurisdiction, arguing that it has no contacts with Delaware. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because by suing in Delaware the company consented to jurisdiction there.
Grant the motion, because personal jurisdiction must be established separately for each party based on its contacts.
Grant the motion, because the software company's suit was about license fees, not warranties.
Deny the motion, because the software company waived its objection by failing to raise it in its complaint.
oe: A plaintiff that invokes a court's power submits to that court's jurisdiction on counterclaims (Adam v. Saenger). Choosing the forum is a form of consent.
Contacts are one route to jurisdiction, but consent is another. A plaintiff's choice of forum supplies consent for the counterclaim.
The counterclaim arises from the same license, and in any event the plaintiff's consent is not limited to the precise claim it filed.
Right result, wrong reason. A plaintiff does not raise defenses in its complaint. Its submission comes from choosing the forum.
topic: Wk 2 · PJ framework & the territorial era — Plaintiff consents by suing

q: A Texas resident signed a franchise agreement with a Michigan franchisor. The agreement provided that the franchisee "irrevocably consents to the personal jurisdiction of the state and federal courts located in Michigan for any dispute arising under this Agreement." The franchisee operated only in Texas, negotiated entirely by phone from Texas, and never visited Michigan. When the franchisee stopped paying royalties, the franchisor sued him in federal court in Michigan. The franchisee moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because the franchisee consented to jurisdiction in Michigan.
Grant the motion, because the franchisee never set foot in Michigan.
Grant the motion, because parties cannot confer jurisdiction on a court by agreement.
Deny the motion, because a contract with a forum resident establishes minimum contacts.
oe: Personal jurisdiction protects the defendant and can be waived or consented to, including by a contractual forum-selection or consent clause. A freely negotiated commercial clause like this one is enforceable.
Physical presence is not required for any basis of jurisdiction other than tag jurisdiction, and consent requires no contacts at all.
That principle applies to subject-matter jurisdiction. Personal jurisdiction is a waivable personal right.
Right result, wrong reason. A contract with a forum resident is not automatically enough for minimum contacts. Here consent makes the contacts analysis unnecessary.
topic: Wk 2 · PJ framework & the territorial era — Consent by contract

q: A Florida homeowner sued an Oregon roofing contractor in federal court in Florida, invoking diversity jurisdiction, for negligent work the contractor performed on the homeowner's vacation house in Oregon. A process server personally handed the summons and complaint to the contractor at his Oregon home. The contractor has never done business in Florida, advertised there, or visited the state. He moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. How should the court rule?
o: Grant the motion, because valid service cannot substitute for contacts with Florida.
Deny the motion, because the contractor was personally served in compliance with Rule 4.
Deny the motion, because the court has diversity jurisdiction over the action.
Grant the motion, because a defendant must be served within the forum state.
oe: Service, notice, and personal jurisdiction are separate requirements. Personal delivery under Rule 4(e)(2)(A) is valid service, but without contacts with Florida there is no basis for jurisdiction.
Compliance with Rule 4 satisfies the service requirement only. It does not answer whether the court has power over the defendant.
Subject-matter jurisdiction and personal jurisdiction are separate. A court can have one without the other.
Right result, wrong reason. Service outside the forum is common and valid. The problem is the lack of Florida contacts.
topic: Wk 2 · PJ framework & the territorial era — Service does not create jurisdiction

q: In 1875, a creditor sued a nonresident debtor in a state court for an unpaid debt. The debtor owned land in the state but was not present there. The creditor served the debtor only by publishing notice in a local newspaper, and the court did not attach the land. The debtor never appeared, and the court entered a personal judgment against him. After judgment, the sheriff seized and sold the land to satisfy the judgment. The debtor later sued the purchaser to recover the land. Under the rules announced in Pennoyer v. Neff, who should prevail?
o: The debtor, because the judgment was void for lack of jurisdiction over him or his property.
The purchaser, because the debtor owned property in the state and therefore was subject to its courts.
The purchaser, because publication is a reasonable method of notifying an absent defendant.
The debtor, but only if he can show that he never actually saw the published notice.
oe: There was no in-state personal service or voluntary appearance, so there was no in personam jurisdiction. The land was not attached at the outset, so there was no quasi in rem jurisdiction either. A judgment entered without jurisdiction violates due process and is void.
Owning property gives a state power over that property only if it is attached at the outset of the suit. It does not subject the owner to a personal judgment.
Under Pennoyer, publication cannot support a personal judgment against a nonresident. Notice is not a substitute for territorial power.
Whether he saw the notice is irrelevant. The defect is jurisdictional, not a failure of actual notice.
topic: Wk 2 · PJ framework & the territorial era — Pennoyer: publication against a nonresident

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the creditor had the sheriff attach the debtor's land when the suit was filed, before publication, and the debt claim was unrelated to the land. The court entered judgment for $5,000, and the land sold for $3,000. Under Pennoyer, what was the effect of the state court's judgment?
o: It was valid quasi in rem, enforceable only against the attached land, up to its value.
It was a valid personal judgment for $5,000, enforceable in other states through full faith and credit.
It was void, because a suit on a debt cannot be brought quasi in rem.
It was valid in rem, binding on everyone in the world as to title to the land.
oe: Attachment at the outset gave the court quasi in rem jurisdiction over the land. Without personal service or appearance, the judgment could be satisfied only from the property seized, not as a personal judgment for the remaining $2,000.
Attachment supports jurisdiction over the property, not the person. Only in personam judgments are enforceable against the defendant personally elsewhere.
Under Pennoyer, a creditor could seize a nonresident's in-state property to satisfy an unrelated claim if the property was attached at the outset.
In rem jurisdiction adjudicates rights in the property against everyone. This suit sought to collect a debt, which is quasi in rem.
topic: Wk 2 · PJ framework & the territorial era — Attachment at the outset
pre: In 1875, a creditor sued a nonresident debtor in a state court for an unpaid debt. The debtor owned land in the state but was not present there. The creditor served the debtor only by publishing notice in a local newspaper, and the court did not attach the land. The debtor never appeared, and the court entered a personal judgment against him. After judgment, the sheriff seized and sold the land to satisfy the judgment. The debtor later sued the purchaser to recover the land. Under the rules announced in Pennoyer v. Neff, who should prevail?

q: In 1880, a resident of State A was injured in State A by a carriage driven by a resident of State B. Months later, the State B resident traveled to State A for one day to attend a horse auction. While he was there, a sheriff handed him a summons in the injured resident's negligence suit. He returned home and never appeared, and the State A court entered a default judgment against him. Under Pennoyer, was the judgment valid?
o: Yes, because he was personally served while physically present within State A.
No, because he was in State A for only one day and did not intend to remain.
No, because he never voluntarily appeared in the action.
Yes, because he caused an injury in State A, which gave State A specific jurisdiction.
oe: Under Pennoyer, a state has power over persons within its borders, so personal service in the state supports in personam jurisdiction regardless of how brief the visit.
The duration of presence was irrelevant under Pennoyer. Presence at the moment of service was enough.
Voluntary appearance was an alternative basis. In-state personal service was sufficient on its own.
Right result, wrong reason. Specific jurisdiction based on in-state conduct is a post-International Shoe concept. Under Pennoyer, presence at service was the basis.
topic: Wk 2 · PJ framework & the territorial era — Pennoyer: in-state service

q: A state's statute provides that shares of stock in any corporation incorporated in the state are located in the state. A shareholder sued an Oregon resident who is an officer of a corporation incorporated in the state, alleging that the officer mismanaged the company's Oregon operations. The officer has never been to the state and has no contacts with it. The court sequestered the officer's shares in the corporation at the outset of the suit. The officer appeared specially to object to jurisdiction. Should the court sustain the objection?
o: Yes, because unrelated property cannot alone support jurisdiction over the officer.
No, because the shares were sequestered at the outset of the suit, before any judgment.
No, because the state has a strong interest in supervising the managers of its own corporations.
Yes, because Shaffer abolished quasi in rem jurisdiction in state courts.
oe: Shaffer v. Heitner held that all assertions of state-court jurisdiction, including quasi in rem, must satisfy International Shoe. Property in the state is one contact, but unrelated property cannot supply jurisdiction on its own.
Attachment at the outset satisfied Pennoyer. After Shaffer, it is no longer enough when the property is unrelated to the claim.
A state's interest is a fairness factor. It cannot substitute for the defendant's own contacts with the forum.
Right result, wrong reason. Shaffer did not abolish quasi in rem jurisdiction. It subjected it to the minimum-contacts test, which property related to the claim can satisfy.
topic: Wk 2 · PJ framework & the territorial era — Property after Shaffer

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the dispute concerns which of two claimants owns a lakefront cottage located in the state. One claimant, an Oregon resident with no other connection to the state, objects to jurisdiction. Should the court sustain the objection?
o: No, because the property in the state is itself the subject of the dispute.
Yes, because the Oregon resident has no minimum contacts with the state apart from the cottage.
Yes, because a court may adjudicate title to land only in the owner's state of domicile.
No, because the Oregon resident appeared to object and thereby consented to jurisdiction.
oe: Shaffer kept the rule that a state may adjudicate claims to property located there. When the suit is about the property itself, the property supplies the needed contact.
Owning the cottage is the contact, and the claim is about the cottage. Nothing more is required.
The rule is close to the opposite. The state where land is located has a strong interest in, and power over, title to it.
Appearing to object to jurisdiction is not consent. A timely jurisdictional objection is preserved.
topic: Wk 2 · PJ framework & the territorial era — Property related to the claim
pre: A state's statute provides that shares of stock in any corporation incorporated in the state are located in the state. A shareholder sued an Oregon resident who is an officer of a corporation incorporated in the state, alleging that the officer mismanaged the company's Oregon operations. The officer has never been to the state and has no contacts with it. The court sequestered the officer's shares in the corporation at the outset of the suit. The officer appeared specially to object to jurisdiction. Should the court sustain the objection?

q: A state statute provides that a nonresident's operation of a motor vehicle on the state's highways appoints the state's registrar of motor vehicles as the nonresident's agent for service in any action arising from an accident there, and requires that a copy of the process be mailed to the defendant. A driver from another state caused a collision on one of the state's highways. The injured resident served the registrar, mailed a copy to the driver, and sued in the state's courts. Under modern doctrine, what is the best justification for personal jurisdiction over the driver?
o: Specific jurisdiction, based on his in-state driving that gave rise to the claim.
Implied consent, because the driver is deemed to have appointed the registrar as his agent.
General jurisdiction, because using the state's highways makes the driver at home there.
Transient jurisdiction, because the registrar was personally served within the state.
oe: Hess v. Pawloski upheld such statutes on an implied-consent fiction. International Shoe replaced those fictions with a functional test, under which driving into the state and causing an accident there is purposeful availment with a related claim.
That was Hess's rationale, but it was a fiction that stretched Pennoyer. Modern doctrine rests the result on minimum contacts.
An individual is at home only in his state of domicile. One trip does not make a visitor at home.
Tag jurisdiction requires in-state service on the defendant himself. Serving a state official as a statutory agent is not the same thing.
topic: Wk 2 · PJ framework & the territorial era — Nonresident motorist statutes today

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the statute required only that process be left with the registrar and did not require that the driver be notified in any way. The driver did not learn of the suit until after a default judgment was entered against him. Is the judgment valid?
o: No, because the statute did not provide notice reasonably calculated to reach the driver.
Yes, because the driver impliedly consented to service on the registrar by driving in the state.
Yes, because the driver's in-state accident gives the state specific jurisdiction over him.
No, because a nonresident may be served only by personal delivery.
oe: Hess upheld the statute because it required mailing to the defendant. Due process requires notice reasonably calculated to apprise him of the action and give him a chance to be heard. Leaving papers with an official, and nothing more, fails that standard.
Even a valid basis for jurisdiction does not excuse the separate due process requirement of adequate notice.
Jurisdiction and notice are independent requirements. The state may have jurisdiction, but a judgment entered without constitutionally adequate notice is still invalid.
Many methods other than personal delivery satisfy due process, including mail. The defect is the absence of any notice to the driver.
topic: Wk 2 · PJ framework & the territorial era — No notice to the driver
pre: A state statute provides that a nonresident's operation of a motor vehicle on the state's highways appoints the state's registrar of motor vehicles as the nonresident's agent for service in any action arising from an accident there, and requires that a copy of the process be mailed to the defendant. A driver from another state caused a collision on one of the state's highways. The injured resident served the registrar, mailed a copy to the driver, and sued in the state's courts. Under modern doctrine, what is the best justification for personal jurisdiction over the driver?

q: A Missouri company that makes office furniture has no office, warehouse, or inventory in Kansas. For six years it has employed eight Kansas residents who solicit orders from Kansas businesses, display samples there, and send the orders to Missouri, where they are filled and shipped. Kansas sued the company in a Kansas court for unpaid state payroll taxes on the commissions paid to those eight salespeople. The company was served by delivering process to one salesperson in Kansas and mailing a copy to its Missouri headquarters. The company argued that it was not "present" in Kansas. Does the Kansas court have personal jurisdiction?
o: Yes, because the company's systematic activity in Kansas gave rise to the obligation sued on.
No, because the company has no office or inventory in Kansas and fills all orders from Missouri.
No, because serving one salesperson cannot bring an out-of-state corporation before the court.
Yes, because the company is at home in Kansas by reason of its Kansas employees.
oe: These are essentially the facts of International Shoe. Continuous and systematic activity in the forum, together with a claim arising from that very activity, satisfies minimum contacts and fair play and substantial justice.
Those facts mattered under the old presence test. International Shoe replaced that test with minimum contacts, and soliciting orders through resident employees is a substantial contact.
The service method, coupled with mailing to headquarters, gave adequate notice. The jurisdictional question turns on contacts, not on whom process was handed to.
Right result, wrong reason. A corporation is at home only where it is incorporated or has its principal place of business. This is specific jurisdiction.
topic: Wk 2 · Minimum contacts — Systematic activity, related claim

q: An Arizona insurance company acquired a block of life-insurance policies from another insurer. It mailed one policyholder, a New Mexico resident, an offer to continue his coverage. He accepted and for years mailed his premiums from New Mexico to Arizona. The company has no office, agents, or other policyholders in New Mexico. After the policyholder died, the company refused to pay his beneficiary, a New Mexico resident, who sued it in a New Mexico court. Does the New Mexico court have personal jurisdiction over the company?
o: Yes, because the suit is based on a contract the company deliberately made with a forum resident.
No, because one contract with one forum resident is too isolated to count as a minimum contact.
No, because the company's only contact resulted from the policyholder's unilateral choice to live there.
Yes, because the beneficiary is a New Mexico resident who would be burdened by litigating in Arizona.
oe: Under McGee, a single deliberate contact can support specific jurisdiction over a claim arising from it. The insurer solicited the contract in the forum, and New Mexico has a manifest interest in giving its residents a forum against insurers.
Isolated activity cannot support unrelated claims. A single contact that gives rise to the claim can be enough, as in McGee.
The insurer itself reached into the forum by mailing the offer there. That is the defendant's own act, not unilateral activity of the plaintiff.
The plaintiff's convenience is a fairness factor, but it cannot supply the defendant's contacts. The contract the insurer solicited does that.
topic: Wk 2 · Minimum contacts — One deliberate contract contact

q: While domiciled in Pennsylvania, a settlor created a trust and named a Delaware bank as trustee. Years later, she moved to Florida, where she received trust income and exercised a power of appointment over the trust property. The bank never solicited business in Florida and dealt with the settlor there only because she chose to move. After she died, her heirs sued in a Florida court over the validity of the appointment and named the bank as a defendant. Does the Florida court have personal jurisdiction over the bank?
o: No, because the bank's Florida contacts exist only because of the settlor's own choice to move.
Yes, because the bank sent trust income to Florida and corresponded with the settlor there.
Yes, because Florida has a strong interest in resolving disputes over its domiciliaries' estates.
No, because only Delaware may hear claims involving a trust administered in Delaware.
oe: Hanson v. Denckla: the unilateral activity of those who claim some relationship with a nonresident defendant cannot satisfy the requirement of contact with the forum. The defendant must purposefully avail itself of the forum.
Those acts were performed only because the settlor relocated. They are not deliberate efforts by the bank to do business in Florida.
A forum's interest is a fairness factor that comes into play only after contacts are shown. It cannot create contacts.
Right result, wrong reason. Other states can hear trust disputes when the trustee has the necessary contacts. The bank simply lacked them in Florida.
topic: Wk 2 · Minimum contacts — Unilateral activity of others

q: Variation: Same facts, except that after the settlor moved to Florida, the bank sent her letters in Florida soliciting her to add more assets to the trust, flew a trust officer to Florida to sign her up for an expanded trust agreement, and accepted the new assets there. The heirs' claims concern the expanded agreement. Does the Florida court have personal jurisdiction over the bank?
o: Yes, because the bank itself deliberately reached into Florida to create the relationship at issue.
No, because the settlor's move to Florida is what first brought the bank into contact with the state.
No, because a trustee may be sued only where the trust is administered.
Yes, because the settlor was a Florida domiciliary when she died.
oe: Purposeful availment turns on the defendant's own deliberate acts. Soliciting the settlor in Florida, sending an officer there, and accepting assets there are the bank's contacts, not the settlor's unilateral activity, and the claims arise from them.
The move explains why the bank dealt with her, but the bank then chose to solicit and transact business in Florida itself.
There is no such rule. A trustee is subject to specific jurisdiction wherever it purposefully avails itself of the forum on a related claim.
The settlor's domicile is not the bank's contact. Without the bank's own Florida conduct, this would be Hanson.
topic: Wk 2 · Minimum contacts — Trustee that reaches into the forum
pre: While domiciled in Pennsylvania, a settlor created a trust and named a Delaware bank as trustee. Years later, she moved to Florida, where she received trust income and exercised a power of appointment over the trust property. The bank never solicited business in Florida and dealt with the settlor there only because she chose to move. After she died, her heirs sued in a Florida court over the validity of the appointment and named the bank as a defendant. Does the Florida court have personal jurisdiction over the bank?

q: A Nevada company that makes camping stoves sent one sales representative to a three-day trade show in Ohio four years ago, where she took no orders. The company has no other Ohio contacts. An Ohio resident who bought one of the company's stoves at the company's store in Las Vegas was burned by it while camping in Nevada. He sued the company in an Ohio court. Does the Ohio court have personal jurisdiction over the company?
o: No, because the company's only Ohio contact was isolated and unrelated to the claim.
Yes, because the company purposefully availed itself of Ohio by attending a trade show there.
Yes, because the plaintiff is an Ohio resident who brought the stove home to Ohio.
No, because a company may be sued only in the state where it manufactured the product.
oe: On the International Shoe grid, isolated activity combined with an unrelated claim supports no jurisdiction. The trade show had nothing to do with the purchase or the injury, both of which happened in Nevada.
Attendance might be a purposeful contact, but specific jurisdiction also requires that the claim arise out of or relate to that contact.
The plaintiff's residence and his unilateral acts are not the defendant's contacts with the forum. The plaintiff cannot be the only link.
Right result, wrong reason. Manufacturers are often subject to specific jurisdiction where their products are marketed and cause injury.
topic: Wk 2 · Minimum contacts — Isolated contact, unrelated claim

q: A national pharmacy chain is incorporated in Delaware and has its headquarters in Illinois. It operates 300 stores in Georgia. A Georgia resident sued the chain in a Georgia court over a slip-and-fall at one of its stores in Florida while she was on vacation. The chain moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. How should the court rule?
o: Grant the motion, because Georgia is neither a related forum nor one where the chain is at home.
Deny the motion, because 300 stores is continuous and systematic activity in Georgia.
Deny the motion, because the plaintiff is a Georgia resident and Georgia has an interest in protecting her.
Grant the motion, because a slip-and-fall claim may be brought only where the fall occurred.
oe: Specific jurisdiction fails because the Florida fall is unrelated to the Georgia stores. General jurisdiction requires that the corporation be at home, normally only its state of incorporation (Delaware) or principal place of business (Illinois). Large in-state operations are not enough.
Continuous and systematic activity supports unrelated claims only when it makes the defendant at home. Daimler rejected a test based on the volume of in-state business.
The forum's interest is a fairness factor. Without related contacts or an at-home forum, fairness factors cannot create jurisdiction.
Right result, wrong reason. The claim could also be brought in Delaware or Illinois, where the chain is at home.
topic: Wk 2 · Minimum contacts — Specific versus general jurisdiction

q: A Colorado ski-equipment maker advertises heavily in Utah, ships directly to Utah retailers, and runs a repair center in Salt Lake City. A Utah skier was injured in Utah when the maker's binding failed and sued the maker in a Utah court. The maker conceded that it has minimum contacts with Utah related to the claim but argued that litigating in Utah would be inconvenient because its engineers work in Denver, about 500 miles away. How should the court rule on the maker's motion to dismiss?
o: Deny the motion, because travel inconvenience is not a compelling case of unreasonableness.
Grant the motion, because the burden on the defendant is the most important reasonableness factor.
Grant the motion, because the plaintiff bears the burden of proving that jurisdiction is reasonable.
Deny the motion, because fairness drops out of the analysis once minimum contacts exist.
oe: Once related contacts are shown, the defendant must present a compelling case that other considerations make jurisdiction unreasonable. Ordinary travel inconvenience for a domestic company rarely meets that burden, and Utah has a strong interest in protecting its residents.
Burden is one of five factors and is heaviest for foreign defendants. A domestic company's modest travel burden does not outweigh the other factors.
The plaintiff bears the burden on contacts and relatedness. The defendant must then make the compelling case of unreasonableness.
Right result, wrong reason. Fairness is always part of the analysis. It simply rarely defeats jurisdiction, as Asahi shows it occasionally can.
topic: Wk 2 · Minimum contacts — Fair play and substantial justice

q: A Utah oral surgeon who practices only in Utah traveled once to Idaho, at a patient's request, to perform a procedure on the patient at an Idaho clinic. The patient suffered nerve damage from the procedure and sued the surgeon for malpractice in an Idaho court. The surgeon has had no other contact with Idaho. Does the Idaho court have personal jurisdiction over the surgeon?
o: Yes, because the claim arises from the surgeon's own deliberate act in Idaho.
No, because a single visit is too isolated to amount to minimum contacts.
No, because the surgeon went to Idaho only at the patient's request.
Yes, because performing surgery in Idaho made the surgeon at home in Idaho.
oe: On the International Shoe grid, a single or occasional act can support jurisdiction over a claim arising from it. The surgeon chose to go to Idaho and perform the procedure there, and the claim arises from that very act.
Isolated contacts cannot support unrelated claims, but a single deliberate act can support a claim that arises from it, as McGee shows.
The request does not make the trip the patient's unilateral act. The surgeon chose to travel and perform the procedure in Idaho.
A single visit does not make an individual at home anywhere but the surgeon's domicile. This is specific jurisdiction.
topic: Wk 2 · Minimum contacts — Single act, related claim

q: A married couple who live in Vermont bought a pickup truck from a Vermont dealer. The dealer sells only from its lot in Vermont, does no advertising outside New England, and has no other connection to other states. While moving to Arizona, the couple was rear-ended in New Mexico, and the truck's fuel tank exploded. They sued the dealer in a New Mexico state court. The dealer moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. How should the court rule?
o: Grant the motion, because the couple's decision to drive to New Mexico is not the dealer's contact with that state.
Deny the motion, because it was foreseeable that a truck sold in Vermont would be driven to other states.
Deny the motion, because New Mexico has a strong interest in providing a forum for accidents on its highways.
Grant the motion, because the couple are not New Mexico residents and cannot sue there.
oe: World-Wide Volkswagen: a local dealer that does no business in the forum has no contacts there. The car got there through the buyers' unilateral activity, and the mere foreseeability that a car will travel is not a contact.
Foreseeability that a product will end up in the forum is not enough. The question is whether the defendant's own conduct makes it reasonably anticipate being haled into court there.
The forum's interest is a fairness factor. Fairness factors cannot substitute for missing contacts.
Right result, wrong reason. Nonresident plaintiffs may sue in any forum with jurisdiction over the defendant. The defect is the dealer's lack of contacts.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — Foreseeability and the local dealer

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the couple also sued the truck's manufacturer, which advertises the same model on New Mexico television, sells it through New Mexico dealers, and supplies replacement parts there. This particular truck was assembled in Michigan and first sold in Vermont. Does the New Mexico court have personal jurisdiction over the manufacturer?
o: Yes, because the manufacturer serves the New Mexico market for the very model that exploded there.
No, because this particular truck was not designed, made, or first sold in New Mexico.
No, because the plaintiffs, not the manufacturer, brought the truck into New Mexico.
Yes, because the manufacturer is at home in the states where it sells its vehicles.
oe: World-Wide Volkswagen's dicta said a manufacturer that delivers products into the stream of commerce expecting forum consumers to buy them may be sued there, and Ford holds that relatedness does not require causation when the defendant systematically serves the forum market for the product that injured someone there.
Ford rejected a causation-only test. The claim relates to the manufacturer's New Mexico marketing of the same model even though this vehicle came from elsewhere.
That defeats jurisdiction over the local dealer, which has no New Mexico contacts. The manufacturer has extensive contacts of its own.
Right result, wrong reason. A corporation is at home only in its state of incorporation and principal place of business. This is specific jurisdiction.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — The national manufacturer
pre: A married couple who live in Vermont bought a pickup truck from a Vermont dealer. The dealer sells only from its lot in Vermont, does no advertising outside New England, and has no other connection to other states. While moving to Arizona, the couple was rear-ended in New Mexico, and the truck's fuel tank exploded. They sued the dealer in a New Mexico state court. The dealer moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. How should the court rule?

q: A small maple-syrup producer sells syrup only from a roadside stand in rural Vermont. It knows that many of its customers are tourists who carry the syrup home to other states. A Texas tourist bought a jug, took it home, and became ill after eating syrup contaminated during bottling. He sued the producer in a Texas court. Which is the producer's strongest argument against personal jurisdiction?
o: It did not purposefully direct any activity toward Texas.
Litigating in Texas would impose a heavy burden on a small business.
The plaintiff's injury was caused by negligent bottling that occurred in Vermont.
Texas has no interest in a dispute involving goods sold outside the state.
oe: Specific jurisdiction requires purposeful availment by the defendant itself. Knowing that tourists carry products home makes it foreseeable that the syrup will reach Texas, but foreseeability alone is not a contact.
Burden is a fairness factor that matters only after contacts are shown, and it rarely defeats jurisdiction on its own. The lack of purposeful contacts is the stronger argument.
Where the negligent act occurred does not settle jurisdiction. The question is whether the defendant reached out to Texas.
Texas has an interest in its injured residents. In any case, the forum's interest is a fairness factor, not a substitute for contacts.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — Foreseeability is not enough

q: A Korean company makes valve stems in Korea and sells them to a Chinese bicycle-tire maker. The Korean company knows that about 20% of the finished tires are sold in California. It does nothing else related to California. A California cyclist was injured in California when a valve stem failed, and the litigation now centers on the Korean company's jurisdictional objection. Under the "stream of commerce plus" approach of Justice O'Connor's plurality in Asahi, which additional fact would most strengthen the argument for jurisdiction over the Korean company in California?
o: It designed the valve stem specifically to meet a California safety regulation.
It knew that thousands of the finished tires were sold in California each year.
The injured cyclist is a California resident who bought the bicycle in California.
The Chinese tire maker sells its tires through a California distributor it hired.
oe: O'Connor's approach requires more than awareness that products will reach the forum. Designing the product for the forum market is one of the listed examples of conduct purposefully directed at the forum.
Awareness, even of large volumes, is what Justice Brennan's test asks about. O'Connor requires some additional conduct aimed at the forum.
The plaintiff's residence and purchase are not the defendant's conduct. They bear on relatedness, not purposeful availment.
Marketing through a forum distributor counts only if the defendant itself does so. The Chinese company's choice is not the Korean company's conduct.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — Stream of commerce plus

q: A Japanese company makes circuit boards in Japan and sells them to a Taiwanese company that builds space heaters. The Japanese company knows, from its customer's annual reports, that the Taiwanese company sells about 50,000 heaters a year through national retailers in Oregon. The Japanese company does no advertising, has no distributors, and has no customer-service channel in Oregon. An Oregon homeowner was injured in Oregon when a heater's circuit board overheated. Under the competing tests in Asahi, which is the most accurate analysis of whether the Japanese company has minimum contacts with Oregon?
o: Brennan's test would likely be satisfied, but O'Connor's would likely not be.
O'Connor's test would likely be satisfied, but Brennan's would likely not be.
Both tests would likely be satisfied, because the defendant knew its boards reached Oregon.
Neither test would likely be satisfied, because the company sold only to a foreign manufacturer.
oe: Brennan asks only whether the defendant was aware that its product was being marketed in the forum through the regular, anticipated flow of commerce, which the Japanese company was. O'Connor requires additional conduct aimed at Oregon, such as advertising or design for the forum, and none exists.
This reverses the tests. O'Connor's is the more demanding one, so a case meeting it would also meet Brennan's.
Knowledge alone satisfies only Brennan. O'Connor rejected awareness as sufficient.
Selling to a foreign intermediary does not by itself defeat Brennan's test, which looks to the regular flow of commerce ending in the forum.
