topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — Brennan's awareness test

q: A German company makes industrial pressure valves and, for 15 years, has shipped about 100,000 of them a year to an Ohio assembler that it knows installs them in boilers sold throughout Ohio. The German company does no advertising in Ohio and has no Ohio office. An Ohio worker was injured when a valve burst. Which consideration would Justice Stevens's approach in Asahi treat as most significant to whether the German company purposefully availed itself of Ohio?
o: The volume, value, and hazardous character of the goods regularly delivered into Ohio.
Whether the German company designed the valves specifically for the Ohio market.
Whether the German company is at home in Ohio by reason of its regular shipments.
Whether the injured worker could obtain an adequate remedy in a German court.
oe: Stevens would consider the volume, value, and hazardous character of the components. Regular delivery of large volumes of a hazardous product over many years is likely purposeful availment even without forum advertising.
Designing for the forum is one of O'Connor's plus factors. Stevens did not require such additional conduct.
Regular shipments support at most specific jurisdiction. They do not make a foreign company at home in the forum.
The adequacy of an alternative forum is a forum non conveniens question, not part of the minimum-contacts analysis.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — Stevens's middle position

q: An English manufacturer of industrial saws sells its saws in the United States through an independent distributor in Ohio, which buys the saws and resells them nationwide. The manufacturer's officers attended trade shows in Nevada and Florida to promote sales to American customers. Only one of its saws was ever sold to a buyer in Delaware. A Delaware worker was injured by that saw in Delaware and sued the manufacturer in a Delaware court. How should the court rule on the manufacturer's motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction?
o: Grant the motion, because one sale through an independent distributor fails every test.
Deny the motion, because the manufacturer targeted the United States market, which includes Delaware.
Deny the motion, because the saw caused injury in Delaware to a Delaware resident.
Grant the motion, because a foreign manufacturer may be sued only in a federal court.
oe: In J. McIntyre, Justice Kennedy's plurality required targeting of the forum state, not the United States as a whole. Justice Breyer's concurrence, the narrowest ground, held that a single isolated sale has never been enough. Either way, there is no jurisdiction.
The plurality rejected the idea that targeting the nation as a whole is targeting each state. Jurisdiction depends on submission to a particular sovereign.
The place of injury and the plaintiff's residence matter to relatedness and fairness. They do not show that the manufacturer purposefully availed itself of Delaware.
Right result, wrong reason. Foreign manufacturers are sued in state courts when they have the necessary contacts.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — Targeting the nation is not targeting the state

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the manufacturer also advertised in a Delaware trade journal, sold 40 saws directly to Delaware sawmills over five years, and maintained a toll-free service line for its Delaware customers. How should the court rule on the motion?
o: Deny the motion, because the manufacturer purposefully directed its sales efforts at Delaware.
Grant the motion, because there is still no majority test for stream-of-commerce jurisdiction.
Grant the motion, because the manufacturer has no office or employees in Delaware.
Deny the motion, because the manufacturer is now at home in Delaware.
oe: Advertising in, selling directly into, and providing service channels for the forum satisfy every stream-of-commerce test, including O'Connor's plus test and the McIntyre plurality's targeting requirement.
The lack of a majority test matters only in close cases. When every test is met, the split is irrelevant.
Physical presence is not required for specific jurisdiction. Deliberate sales efforts aimed at the forum are contacts.
Forty sales and some advertising would not make a foreign company at home in Delaware. This is specific jurisdiction.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — Direct marketing into the forum
pre: An English manufacturer of industrial saws sells its saws in the United States through an independent distributor in Ohio, which buys the saws and resells them nationwide. The manufacturer's officers attended trade shows in Nevada and Florida to promote sales to American customers. Only one of its saws was ever sold to a buyer in Delaware. A Delaware worker was injured by that saw in Delaware and sued the manufacturer in a Delaware court. How should the court rule on the manufacturer's motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction?

q: A California motorist injured in California sued a Taiwanese tire maker in a California state court. The tire maker filed a cross-claim for indemnity against a Japanese company that made a component of the tire in Japan and sold it to the tire maker in Taiwan. The motorist then settled, leaving only the cross-claim between the two foreign companies. Assume that the Japanese company has minimum contacts with California. Should the court exercise jurisdiction over the cross-claim?
o: No, because exercising jurisdiction would be unreasonable on these facts.
Yes, because jurisdiction is reasonable once minimum contacts are shown.
Yes, because California has a strong interest in the safety of products used on its highways.
No, because the tire maker, as a foreign company, cannot sue in a California court.
oe: Asahi held, with eight Justices agreeing, that jurisdiction would be unreasonable. The burden on a foreign defendant is heavy, California's interest in an indemnity dispute between foreign companies is slight, and international comity counsels restraint.
Fairness remains part of the test. Asahi is the leading example of contacts, assumed for argument, coupled with unreasonableness.
That interest was largely satisfied when the motorist settled. What remains is a commercial dispute between two foreign companies.
Foreign companies may sue in American courts. The issue is whether jurisdiction over the Japanese defendant is reasonable.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — Unreasonableness can defeat jurisdiction

q: Six hundred people who took a prescription sleep aid sued its maker, a corporation incorporated in Delaware with its headquarters in New Jersey, in a single action in an Illinois state court. One hundred plaintiffs are Illinois residents who bought and took the drug in Illinois. The other 500 live in other states and bought, took, and were injured by the drug there. The maker sells the drug in Illinois and runs a research lab there unrelated to the drug. Does the Illinois court have personal jurisdiction over the maker as to the nonresident plaintiffs' claims?
o: No, because the nonresidents' claims have no connection to the maker's Illinois activities.
Yes, because the nonresidents' claims are identical to the claims of the Illinois residents.
Yes, because the maker's extensive Illinois business makes the Illinois court a fair forum.
No, because a court may not hear a mass action that includes nonresident plaintiffs.
oe: Bristol-Myers Squibb: relatedness is judged claim by claim. The nonresidents did not buy, take, or get hurt by the drug in Illinois. Unrelated Illinois activity, and the residents' similar claims, cannot supply the missing link.
Similar claims by other plaintiffs do not create a connection between the forum and the nonresidents' controversies.

Extensive but unrelated business supports only general jurisdiction, and the maker is not at home in Illinois. The Court rejected a sliding scale that would relax relatedness when contacts are extensive.
Right result, wrong reason. The nonresidents could join a suit in Delaware or New Jersey, where the maker is at home.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — Nonresident plaintiffs in a mass action

q: An appliance maker, incorporated and headquartered in Michigan, designs its dishwashers in Michigan, makes them in Mexico, and sells them nationwide. It advertises its dishwashers on Wisconsin television, sells them through Wisconsin retailers, and has authorized repair shops there. A Wisconsin resident bought a used dishwasher of that model from a private seller in Wisconsin. The dishwasher had originally been sold new in Iowa. It caught fire and burned her Wisconsin home. She sued the maker in a Wisconsin court, and the maker argued that none of its Wisconsin activities caused her injury. Does the court have specific jurisdiction?
o: Yes, because the maker serves the Wisconsin market for that very model.
No, because the dishwasher the plaintiff owned was first sold in Iowa, not Wisconsin.
No, because the plaintiff bought the dishwasher secondhand from a private seller.
Yes, because the maker's Wisconsin activities make it at home in Wisconsin.
oe: Under Ford, a claim relates to the defendant's forum contacts when the defendant serves a market in the forum for the product that malfunctioned and injured a resident there, even if the particular item was first sold elsewhere. Causation is not required.
Ford rejected a strict causation requirement. The claim relates to the maker's Wisconsin marketing of the same model.
A resale by a third party does not break the relationship when the maker cultivates the forum market for the model.
Right result, wrong reason. The maker is at home only in Michigan. Ford is a specific-jurisdiction case.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — Relatedness without causation

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the plaintiff is a Minnesota resident who bought the dishwasher in Minnesota and was injured when it burned her Minnesota home. She sued the maker in Wisconsin because Wisconsin has a longer limitations period. Does the Wisconsin court have specific jurisdiction?
o: No, because the plaintiff, the purchase, and the injury all have no connection to Wisconsin.
Yes, because the maker serves the Wisconsin market for the same dishwasher model.
Yes, because a plaintiff may choose any forum where the defendant does substantial business.
No, because forum shopping for a longer limitations period is prohibited.
oe: Relatedness fails when the plaintiff, the purchase, and the injury are all elsewhere. The maker's Wisconsin marketing is unrelated to this controversy, as in Bristol-Myers Squibb.
Serving the forum market counts only when the product causes injury in the forum. Ford stressed that relatedness still has real limits.
Substantial business supports general jurisdiction only where the defendant is at home, and specific jurisdiction requires a related claim.
Right result, wrong reason. Seeking a favorable limitations period does not itself defeat jurisdiction. The problem is the lack of relatedness.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — Plaintiff, purchase, and injury elsewhere
pre: An appliance maker, incorporated and headquartered in Michigan, designs its dishwashers in Michigan, makes them in Mexico, and sells them nationwide. It advertises its dishwashers on Wisconsin television, sells them through Wisconsin retailers, and has authorized repair shops there. A Wisconsin resident bought a used dishwasher of that model from a private seller in Wisconsin. The dishwasher had originally been sold new in Iowa. It caught fire and burned her Wisconsin home. She sued the maker in a Wisconsin court, and the maker argued that none of its Wisconsin activities caused her injury. Does the court have specific jurisdiction?

q: Two Nevada residents negotiated with a Florida-based restaurant franchisor, partly through its regional office in California and partly through its Miami headquarters, for a 20-year franchise to operate a restaurant in Nevada. The agreement required monthly royalty payments to Miami, provided that Florida law governed, and stated that all notices must be sent to Miami. After the franchisees stopped paying, the franchisor sued them in federal court in Florida. The franchisees, who had never been to Florida, moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because the franchisees reached out to create continuing obligations in Florida.
Grant the motion, because the franchisees never entered Florida or did business there in person.
Grant the motion, because a contract with a forum resident cannot by itself establish minimum contacts.
Deny the motion, because the Florida choice-of-law clause is consent to jurisdiction in Florida.
oe: Burger King: a contract with a forum party is not automatically enough, but here the prior negotiations, the contemplated 20-year relationship, the terms (payments and notices to Miami), and the Florida choice-of-law clause show purposeful availment.
Physical entry is not required. Deliberately reaching out to create continuing obligations with a forum party is a contact.
That is a correct statement of law, but this case involves much more than the bare contract.
Right result, wrong reason. A choice-of-law clause is not a consent to jurisdiction. It reinforces purposeful availment but does not confer jurisdiction by itself.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — Contracts plus

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the dispute involves a single purchase. A Nevada restaurant owner answered a Florida supplier's email, which the supplier sent to restaurants nationwide, and ordered one used pizza oven to be shipped to Nevada. The contract contained no choice-of-law clause and called for no continuing relationship. When the owner refused to pay, the supplier sued him in Florida. How should the court rule on the owner's motion to dismiss?
o: Grant the motion, because answering the seller's solicitation is not purposeful availment.
Deny the motion, because the owner entered a contract with a Florida company.
Deny the motion, because the owner should have foreseen being sued where the seller lives.
Grant the motion, because a seller must sue a buyer in the buyer's home state.
oe: A contract with a forum resident is not automatically a contact. Here the seller initiated the deal, there were no ongoing obligations in Florida, and the buyer did nothing but answer the seller's solicitation.
Burger King held that a contract with a forum resident does not automatically establish minimum contacts. The other factors are missing here.
Foreseeability of suit in the seller's state is not a contact. The defendant's own deliberate conduct must create the connection.
Right result, wrong reason. A buyer who deliberately creates continuing obligations with the forum, as in Burger King, can be sued there.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — One-off purchase from a forum seller
pre: Two Nevada residents negotiated with a Florida-based restaurant franchisor, partly through its regional office in California and partly through its Miami headquarters, for a 20-year franchise to operate a restaurant in Nevada. The agreement required monthly royalty payments to Miami, provided that Florida law governed, and stated that all notices must be sent to Miami. After the franchisees stopped paying, the franchisor sued them in federal court in Florida. The franchisees, who had never been to Florida, moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. How should the court rule?

q: A Florida-based tabloid's reporter and editor, working in Florida, wrote and edited a story accusing a famous Oregon chef of using spoiled ingredients at her Portland restaurant. They relied on phone calls to Oregon sources. The tabloid's largest circulation is in Oregon, with about 200,000 copies sold there. The chef sued the reporter and editor for libel in an Oregon court. They argued that they are not responsible for the tabloid's circulation decisions and acted only in Florida. Does the Oregon court have personal jurisdiction over them?
o: Yes, because they expressly aimed their intentional conduct at Oregon.
No, because they researched, wrote, and edited the story entirely in Florida.
No, because employees are not subject to jurisdiction based on their employer's activities.
Yes, because the chef suffered injury in Oregon, where she lives.
oe: Under Calder's effects test, intentional conduct expressly aimed at the forum, causing harm the defendant knows will be suffered there, supports jurisdiction. Oregon was the focal point of both the story and the harm.
Calder rejected that argument. Acting from another state does not prevent jurisdiction when the conduct is expressly aimed at the forum.
The reporter and editor are judged on their own contacts, but their own intentional conduct was aimed at Oregon.
Injury to a forum resident is not enough by itself (Walden). What matters is that the defendants aimed their conduct at Oregon.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — The effects test

q: A federal agent working at the Denver airport seized $50,000 in cash from two professional poker players who live in Arizona and were flying home. He then drafted an affidavit, allegedly false, to support forfeiture of the cash. All of his conduct occurred in Colorado. The players sued him in federal court in Arizona, arguing that he knew they lived in Arizona and that they suffered the loss there. Does the Arizona court have personal jurisdiction over the agent?
o: No, because none of the agent's own conduct was aimed at Arizona.
Yes, because the agent knew the players lived in Arizona and would feel the harm there.
Yes, because the agent's conduct was intentional rather than negligent.
No, because federal officers are immune from suit in state courts.
oe: Walden v. Fiore: the analysis looks to the defendant's contacts with the forum state itself, not with persons who reside there. The plaintiffs felt the loss in Arizona only because they lived there.
Knowledge of the plaintiff's residence, plus harm there, is not express aiming. Calder involved conduct aimed at the forum, not just at a forum resident.
Intentional conduct triggers the effects test, but the test also requires that the conduct be expressly aimed at the forum.
The suit is in federal court, and the question is personal jurisdiction, not immunity.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — Plaintiff cannot be the only link

q: A Michigan resident posted on his personal Facebook page, from Michigan, that two dentists practicing in Texas were "frauds who overbill their patients." His page is public and viewable anywhere. The post did not mention Texas, was not directed to Texas readers, and was not promoted to any Texas audience. He knew that the dentists lived in Texas. The dentists sued him for defamation in a Texas court. Does the court have personal jurisdiction?
o: No, because nothing shows that the post was aimed at a Texas audience.
Yes, because the post was accessible to readers in Texas.
Yes, because the poster knew the dentists would suffer reputational harm in Texas.
No, because defamation claims must be brought where the statement was written.
oe: Burdick applied Calder and Walden to social media. A public post viewable everywhere is not aimed at the forum without forum-specific content, audience, or distribution. Knowing the plaintiffs live in Texas is not enough.
Accessibility everywhere is not targeting anywhere. If it were, every poster would be subject to jurisdiction in every state.
Walden holds that harm felt in the forum because the plaintiff lives there is not the defendant's contact with the forum.
Right result, wrong reason. Defamation claims can be brought where the statement was expressly aimed, as in Calder.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — Social-media posts

q: Two Maine newspapers published articles, also posted on their websites, criticizing conditions at a private prison in Georgia where Maine had sent some of its inmates. The articles focused on whether Maine's policy of shipping inmates out of state was wise, and they suggested that the Georgia prison's warden tolerated abuse. The newspapers' websites carry Maine news and Maine advertising. The warden, a Georgia resident, sued the newspapers for libel in federal court in Georgia. Does the court have personal jurisdiction?
o: No, because the newspapers did not aim their content at Georgia readers.
Yes, because the articles concerned a Georgia prison and a Georgia warden.
Yes, because the websites could be read by anyone in Georgia.
No, because a newspaper may be sued only where it is published.
oe: Young v. New Haven Advocate: the question is where the content was aimed, not where it could be read. The articles addressed a Maine policy debate for Maine readers, so there was no manifest intent to target Georgia.
Writing about a forum subject is not the same as aiming the publication at a forum audience. The focus was Maine's inmate policy.
Being accessible everywhere is not targeting anywhere.
Right result, wrong reason. A publisher that targets a forum audience, as in Calder, can be sued there.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — Websites aimed at a local audience

q: A Pennsylvania company sued a California company in federal court in Pennsylvania for trademark infringement arising from the California company's use of a confusingly similar domain name. Which fact pattern most strongly supports specific jurisdiction in Pennsylvania?
o: The company sold subscriptions through its website to 3,000 Pennsylvania residents.
The company's website describes its products and can be viewed by Pennsylvania residents.
The company's website lets visitors in any state email questions, and some Pennsylvanians have.
The company knew that the Pennsylvania company's headquarters was located in Pennsylvania.
oe: On the Zippo sliding scale, a defendant that knowingly and repeatedly does business with forum residents over the internet has purposefully availed itself of the forum, and the infringement claim arises from that business.
A passive website that merely posts information is at the no-jurisdiction end of the scale.
Limited interactivity without commercial dealings with forum residents is a weak basis. It sits in the middle of the scale and usually fails.
Knowing where the plaintiff lives is not purposeful direction at the forum (Walden).
topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — Interactive commercial websites

q: A plaintiff sued an out-of-state defendant in federal court, alleging specific jurisdiction. The defendant moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. Which statement correctly describes the burdens on the motion?
o: The plaintiff must show contacts and relatedness; the defendant must then show unreasonableness.
The defendant must disprove purposeful availment, relatedness, and reasonableness.
The plaintiff must prove purposeful availment, relatedness, and reasonableness, each by a preponderance.
The court must decide all three elements on its own, without allocating any burden.
oe: The plaintiff bears the burden on the first two elements. Once they are shown, Burger King places on the defendant the burden of presenting a compelling case that jurisdiction would offend fair play and substantial justice.
The party invoking the court's power bears the burden of showing the basis for jurisdiction.
The plaintiff need not prove reasonableness. The defendant bears the burden of showing unreasonableness.
Burdens are allocated. A court does not investigate jurisdictional facts on its own initiative.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — Burden allocation

q: A Maine contractor renovated a house in Maine for a client who lived there. Two years after the work was done, the client moved to Florida. She then discovered that the roof leaked, and she sued the contractor in a Florida court for breach of warranty. The contractor has never worked in Florida, solicited business there, or sent anything there apart from one email answering her complaint about the roof. Does the Florida court have personal jurisdiction?
o: No, because the client's own move is the only link to Florida.
Yes, because the contractor sent an email to Florida about the very roof at issue.
Yes, because the warranty obligation follows the client to whatever state she moves to.
No, because warranty claims may be brought only where the work was performed.
oe: Specific jurisdiction rests on the defendant's own deliberate contacts with the forum. A plaintiff's unilateral move cannot create them, and one reply email sent because she happened to live there is not purposeful availment.
A reply prompted by the plaintiff's own relocation is not the defendant reaching out to Florida. The plaintiff cannot be the only link.
The location of a contractual obligation's beneficiary does not determine the defendant's contacts.
Right result, wrong reason. A warranty claim could be brought wherever the contractor has related contacts or is at home.
topic: Wks 3–4 · Specific jurisdiction & stream of commerce — Plaintiff's later move

q: A corporation is incorporated in Delaware and has its headquarters, where its senior officers direct its business, in Texas. Its largest factory is in Ohio, and California accounts for 30% of its nationwide sales, more than any other state. A plaintiff wants to sue the corporation on a claim that has no connection to any of these states. In which states may the plaintiff sue the corporation based on general jurisdiction?
o: Delaware and Texas only.
Delaware, Texas, Ohio, and California, because the corporation does substantial business in each.
Texas and California only, where its headquarters and largest market are located.
Delaware only, because a corporation is a citizen only of its state of incorporation.
oe: A corporation is essentially at home, and subject to general jurisdiction, in its state of incorporation and its principal place of business. Absent an exceptional case, no other state qualifies, however large the corporation's operations there.
Daimler rejected a test based on substantial, continuous, and systematic business as unacceptably grasping. A factory or a large share of sales does not make a corporation at home.
The state of incorporation is always a place where a corporation is at home, and a large market is not.
A corporation is also at home where it has its principal place of business, its nerve center in Texas.
topic: Wk 4 · General, consent & tag jurisdiction — Where a corporation is at home

q: Twenty residents of Brazil sued a German automaker in federal court in California, alleging that the automaker's Brazilian subsidiary helped Brazilian security forces abuse workers in Brazil during the 1970s. No relevant conduct occurred in the United States. The plaintiffs rely on the California sales of the automaker's American distributor, a subsidiary incorporated in Delaware and headquartered in New Jersey. Those sales make up about 3% of the automaker's worldwide sales. Assume that the distributor's contacts may be attributed to the automaker. Does the court have personal jurisdiction over the automaker?
o: No, because the automaker is not at home in California.
Yes, because the distributor's California sales are substantial, continuous, and systematic.
Yes, because the subsidiary's contacts are attributed to the parent for jurisdictional purposes.
No, because foreign plaintiffs may not sue in United States courts for conduct abroad.
oe: Daimler held that general jurisdiction over a corporation is essentially limited to its place of incorporation and principal place of business. Even with the subsidiary's contacts attributed to it, a German company is not at home in California, and nothing about the claims relates to California.
Daimler called that test unacceptably grasping. The relevant comparison is the defendant's forum activity relative to its activity everywhere.
Attribution was assumed in Daimler, and jurisdiction still failed. The attributed contacts did not make the parent at home.
Foreign plaintiffs may sue in American courts if a court has jurisdiction. The defect here is the absence of general jurisdiction.
topic: Wk 4 · General, consent & tag jurisdiction — Large sales through a subsidiary

q: Two Ohio teenagers were killed when a bus overturned in Spain. Their families sued three foreign subsidiaries of an American tire company in an Ohio state court, alleging that a defective tire made by one of the subsidiaries in Turkey caused the crash. A small number of the subsidiaries' tires reached Ohio through other affiliates' distribution channels. The subsidiaries have no offices, employees, or bank accounts in Ohio. Does the Ohio court have general jurisdiction over the subsidiaries?
o: No, because occasional stream-of-commerce sales into Ohio do not make them at home there.
Yes, because their tires regularly reach the Ohio market through the stream of commerce.
Yes, because the plaintiffs are Ohio residents whose decedents were killed by the defendants' product.
No, because general jurisdiction does not reach corporations organized abroad.
oe: Goodyear coined the essentially-at-home test and held that sales through the stream of commerce may support specific jurisdiction over related claims, but never general jurisdiction. The crash and the tire had nothing to do with Ohio.
Stream-of-commerce sales bear only on specific jurisdiction, and even then only for claims arising from in-forum products.
The plaintiffs' residence is not the defendants' contact. General jurisdiction depends on the defendants being at home.
Right result, wrong reason. Foreign corporations can be at home in a state, as in the exceptional Perkins case.
topic: Wk 4 · General, consent & tag jurisdiction — Stream-of-commerce sales and general jurisdiction

q: A Peruvian helicopter company bought 80% of its fleet from a manufacturer in Texas over seven years, sent its pilots to Texas for training, and sent its chief executive to Houston once to negotiate a contract. One of its helicopters crashed in Peru, killing four American workers. Their survivors sued the Peruvian company in a Texas court, relying solely on general jurisdiction. How should the court rule on the company's motion to dismiss?
o: Grant the motion, because purchases and related trips do not make the company at home in Texas.
Deny the motion, because the company's Texas purchases were regular and substantial over seven years.
Deny the motion, because the company's chief executive negotiated a contract while in Texas.
Grant the motion, because a wrongful-death claim may be brought only where the death occurred.
oe: Helicopteros held that purchases in the forum, even at regular intervals, and related training trips are not enough for general jurisdiction over an unrelated claim. After Daimler, the at-home test makes the answer clearer still.
Regular purchases are not the kind of contact that makes a corporation at home. Helicopteros rejected this argument.
One negotiating trip is far short of the at-home standard, and the claim did not arise from that contract.
Right result, wrong reason. The claim could be brought wherever the company is at home or has related contacts.
topic: Wk 4 · General, consent & tag jurisdiction — Purchases and training trips

q: A railroad incorporated in Delaware with its headquarters in Texas operates about 2,000 miles of track in Montana and employs about 2,000 people there, roughly 6% of its workforce. A former employee who lives in North Dakota sued the railroad in a Montana court for injuries he suffered while working for it in South Dakota. Does the Montana court have personal jurisdiction over the railroad?
o: No, because the railroad is not at home in Montana, and the claim is unrelated to its Montana activities.
Yes, because the railroad's Montana operations are continuous and systematic.
Yes, because the railroad's Montana operations are as large as those of many companies headquartered there.
No, because an employee's injury claim must be brought in the state where he lives.
oe: In BNSF Railway v. Tyrrell, the Court held that thousands of miles of track and thousands of employees in a state did not make a railroad at home there. Its Montana activity is a small part of its activity everywhere, and the claim arose elsewhere.
Continuous and systematic activity is not the test after Daimler. The question is whether the corporation is essentially at home.
The comparison is to the defendant's own activity nationwide, not to other companies' activity in the forum.
Right result, wrong reason. The claim could be brought in Delaware or Texas, or in South Dakota on specific jurisdiction.
topic: Wk 4 · General, consent & tag jurisdiction — Railroad with track in the forum

q: During a war, a Philippine mining company's operations in the Philippines were halted by enemy occupation. Its president moved to Ohio, where he kept the company's files, held directors' meetings, paid salaries from Ohio bank accounts, and supervised the company's limited wartime activities. A shareholder sued the company in an Ohio court on a claim unrelated to Ohio. Does the Ohio court have general jurisdiction over the company?
o: Yes, because Ohio became the company's de facto principal place of business.
No, because a corporation is at home only in its place of incorporation.
No, because the shareholder's claim did not arise from the company's Ohio activities.
Yes, because the company kept bank accounts and paid salaries in Ohio.
oe: This is Perkins v. Benguet, the exceptional case. With its president running the company from Ohio, Ohio was effectively its headquarters, so the company was at home there.
A corporation is also at home in its principal place of business. Perkins found that Ohio had become the company's headquarters in fact.
Relatedness is required for specific jurisdiction, not general. General jurisdiction permits any claim where the defendant is at home.
Bank accounts and payroll alone would not suffice. What mattered was that Ohio was where the company was being directed and controlled.
topic: Wk 4 · General, consent & tag jurisdiction — The exceptional case

q: A woman domiciled in Arizona caused a car accident in Nevada while on vacation. The other driver, a California resident, sued her in an Arizona state court. The woman argued that Arizona had no connection to the accident. Does the Arizona court have personal jurisdiction over her?
o: Yes, because an individual is always subject to general jurisdiction in her domicile.
No, because the claim did not arise from her contacts with Arizona.
No, because only Nevada may hear claims arising from accidents on its roads.
Yes, but only if she is personally served while physically present in Arizona.
oe: An individual is at home in her domicile, which supports jurisdiction over any claim against her, including one arising entirely elsewhere.
Relatedness is required only for specific jurisdiction. At home, she may be sued on any claim.
Nevada also has specific jurisdiction, but it is not exclusive. The plaintiff may choose any forum with jurisdiction.
In-state service is one basis for jurisdiction, but domicile is independently sufficient. She may be served outside Arizona.
topic: Wk 4 · General, consent & tag jurisdiction — Domicile of an individual

q: A man domiciled in New Jersey flew to California for three days to attend a business meeting and to visit his children, who lived there with his estranged wife. While he was there, he was personally handed a summons and complaint in her California divorce action. He has no other contacts with California. He moved to quash for lack of personal jurisdiction. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because he was personally served while voluntarily present in California.
Grant the motion, because his brief visit does not amount to minimum contacts with California.
Grant the motion, because the divorce action is unrelated to his business meeting.
Deny the motion, because California is the domicile of the children.
oe: Burnham: in-state personal service on an individual who is voluntarily present satisfies due process, even for a claim unrelated to the visit. Scalia's plurality relied on tradition; Brennan's on fairness, since a visitor enjoys the state's benefits.
Minimum contacts is a substitute for physical presence, not a limit on it. Tag jurisdiction requires no further contacts.
Transient jurisdiction does not require that the claim relate to the visit.
Right result, wrong reason. The children's domicile does not supply jurisdiction over the father. The in-state service does.
topic: Wk 4 · General, consent & tag jurisdiction — Tag jurisdiction

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the man came to California only because his wife falsely told him that one of the children had been hospitalized and needed him there. He was served when he stepped off the plane. How should the court rule on the motion to quash?
o: Grant the motion, because his presence in California was obtained by fraud.
Deny the motion, because he was personally served while physically present in the state.
Deny the motion, because his visit to see his children was a purposeful contact with California.
Grant the motion, because divorce actions may be filed only in the defendant's domicile.
oe: Tag jurisdiction depends on voluntary presence. Presence procured by fraud or force is a recognized exception, so the in-state service does not support jurisdiction.
Physical presence is not enough when the plaintiff lured the defendant into the state by fraud.
The visit was induced by the plaintiff's deception, so it is not his own voluntary contact.
Right result, wrong reason. Divorce actions are often filed in the plaintiff's state. The fraud is what defeats tag jurisdiction here.
topic: Wk 4 · General, consent & tag jurisdiction — Presence obtained by fraud
pre: A man domiciled in New Jersey flew to California for three days to attend a business meeting and to visit his children, who lived there with his estranged wife. While he was there, he was personally handed a summons and complaint in her California divorce action. He has no other contacts with California. He moved to quash for lack of personal jurisdiction. How should the court rule?

q: A Colorado resident traveled to Utah under subpoena to testify as a witness in an unrelated Utah trial. As he left the courthouse after testifying, a process server handed him a summons and complaint in a Utah breach-of- contract action against him. He has no other contacts with Utah. Under the traditional exception to transient jurisdiction, how should the Utah court rule on his motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction?
o: Grant the motion, because witnesses attending court are traditionally immune from service there.
Deny the motion, because he was personally served while voluntarily present in Utah.
Deny the motion, because his testimony in Utah was a purposeful contact with the state.
Grant the motion, because the contract claim is unrelated to his testimony.
oe: Immunity for parties and witnesses who enter a state to attend court is a recognized exception to tag jurisdiction. It encourages participation in judicial proceedings.
Ordinarily that would suffice, but the witness immunity exception applies to someone in the state to testify.
Testifying under subpoena is not purposeful availment, and the contract claim is unrelated to it anyway.
Right result, wrong reason. Unrelated claims are normally fine for tag jurisdiction. The immunity is what defeats it here.
topic: Wk 4 · General, consent & tag jurisdiction — Immunity for witnesses

q: The president of a corporation incorporated and headquartered in Georgia changed planes at the Denver airport. During her layover, a process server handed her a summons and complaint naming the corporation as defendant in a Colorado action over a contract performed entirely in Georgia. The corporation has no Colorado contacts. Under the approach most courts take, does the Colorado court have personal jurisdiction over the corporation?
o: No, because serving a traveling officer does not create jurisdiction over the corporation.
Yes, because the corporation's president was personally served while voluntarily present in Colorado.
Yes, because a corporation is present wherever its officers conduct its business.
No, because a corporation may be served only at its registered office.
oe: Most courts do not apply tag jurisdiction to corporations. Serving the president may be a valid method of service under Rule 4(h), but it supplies no basis for jurisdiction over a corporation that is not at home in Colorado and has no related contacts there.
Burnham's tag rule concerns individuals. Most courts refuse to extend it to corporations served through their officers.
That corporate presence fiction was abandoned with International Shoe. Today the question is whether the corporation is at home or has related contacts.
Right result, wrong reason. A corporation may be served by delivery to an officer anywhere. The problem is jurisdiction, not the method of service.
topic: Wk 4 · General, consent & tag jurisdiction — Tag jurisdiction and corporations

q: A state's business-registration statute provides that a foreign corporation's registration to do business in the state "shall constitute consent to the exercise of general personal jurisdiction" by the state's courts. A railroad incorporated and headquartered in Virginia registered under the statute. A former employee who lives in Virginia sued the railroad in the registering state's courts for an illness he attributes to work he performed in Ohio and Virginia. Does the court have personal jurisdiction over the railroad?
o: Yes, because the railroad consented to general jurisdiction by registering under the statute.
No, because the railroad is not at home in the state and the claim is unrelated to it.
No, because a state may not condition the right to do business on consent to jurisdiction.
Yes, because registering to do business makes a corporation at home in the state.
oe: Mallory v. Norfolk Southern upheld this kind of statute. Registration that the statute expressly makes consent to general jurisdiction satisfies due process, even for a claim unrelated to the state.
That would defeat general and specific jurisdiction based on contacts, but consent is an independent basis.
Mallory rejected that due process argument.
Right result, wrong reason. Registration does not make a corporation at home. It operates as consent only because the statute expressly says so.
topic: Wk 4 · General, consent & tag jurisdiction — Consent by registration statute

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the statute requires a registering corporation only to appoint an in-state agent for service of process and says nothing about consenting to jurisdiction. Does the court have personal jurisdiction over the railroad?
o: No, because the statute does not expressly make registration consent to general jurisdiction.
Yes, because a corporation that appoints an in-state agent consents to suit in that state.
Yes, because the railroad was properly served through its registered agent.
No, because consent to jurisdiction may be given only in a contract.
oe: Registration is a route to general jurisdiction only where the state's statute expressly provides it. Appointing an agent to receive service is a method of service, not a jurisdictional basis.
Treating registration as consent without statutory language is a pre-International Shoe fiction. Mallory turned on Pennsylvania's express consent provision.
Valid service is not the same as jurisdiction. Service and personal jurisdiction are separate requirements.
Right result, wrong reason. Consent may also come from a registration statute that expressly provides it, a stipulation, or a waiver.
topic: Wk 4 · General, consent & tag jurisdiction — Statute silent on jurisdiction
pre: A state's business-registration statute provides that a foreign corporation's registration to do business in the state "shall constitute consent to the exercise of general personal jurisdiction" by the state's courts. A railroad incorporated and headquartered in Virginia registered under the statute. A former employee who lives in Virginia sued the railroad in the registering state's courts for an illness he attributes to work he performed in Ohio and Virginia. Does the court have personal jurisdiction over the railroad?

q: A Washington couple bought tickets for a cruise departing from Los Angeles. The tickets, which they received after paying, stated in fine print that the passengers agreed to litigate all disputes in the courts of Florida, where the cruise line has its headquarters. The couple did not negotiate the clause and had a chance to cancel for a full refund after receiving the tickets. After the cruise, the cruise line sued them in a Florida court for unpaid onboard charges, and they moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. They have never been to Florida. Which is the cruise line's strongest response?
o: The couple consented to jurisdiction in Florida through an enforceable forum-selection clause.
The couple purposefully availed themselves of Florida by buying tickets from a Florida company.
Florida has a strong interest in providing a forum for its corporations to collect debts.
Personal jurisdiction is satisfied whenever service of process is made in compliance with Rule 4.
oe: Carnival Cruise Lines v. Shute enforced a non-negotiated forum clause on a cruise ticket. The cruise line had a legitimate interest in a single forum, there was no fraud or bad faith, and the passengers could have rejected the contract. Consent makes contacts unnecessary.
Buying from a forum company is not automatically purposeful availment. The consent clause is the stronger ground.
The forum's interest is a fairness factor that cannot replace consent or contacts.
Proper service does not create jurisdiction over a defendant who has no contacts with the forum and has not consented.
topic: Wk 4 · General, consent & tag jurisdiction — Non-negotiated forum-selection clause

q: A state statute allows a bank that pools many small trusts into a common fund to obtain a judicial settlement of its accounts, which cuts off any claims by beneficiaries for mismanagement. The statute requires only publication of notice in a newspaper. The bank has the mailing addresses of 900 beneficiaries in its own records. It published the required notice and obtained a settlement decree. A beneficiary whose address the bank had on file later sued, arguing that the decree does not bind her. Is the decree binding on her?
o: No, because notice by publication was not reasonably calculated to reach a beneficiary with a known address.
Yes, because the proceeding was in rem, and publication is sufficient for in rem proceedings.
Yes, because the bank complied with the notice procedure prescribed by the state statute.
No, because each beneficiary was entitled to personal service of process within the state.
oe: Mullane requires notice reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to apprise interested parties of the action. For beneficiaries whose names and addresses are known, publication is not a means one desirous of informing them would use. At least ordinary mail is required.
Mullane held that the notice standard applies whether a proceeding is labeled in rem or in personam.
Statutory compliance does not satisfy due process if the statutory method is constitutionally inadequate.
Due process does not require personal service. Mail would have been enough for known beneficiaries.
topic: Wk 4 · Notice & service of process — Publication to known beneficiaries

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the beneficiary challenging the decree holds a contingent interest, and neither her identity nor her address could have been found through diligent inquiry when the bank sought the decree. Is the decree binding on her?
o: Yes, because publication suffices for persons who cannot reasonably be found.
No, because due process requires actual notice to each person whose rights are adjudicated.
No, because notice by publication does not satisfy due process.
Yes, because a beneficiary with only a contingent interest has no right to notice at all.
oe: Mullane held that publication suffices for beneficiaries whose interests or whereabouts are unknown or could not be ascertained with due diligence. There is no better practicable means of reaching them.
Actual receipt is not required. Due process requires notice reasonably calculated to inform, which publication is when nothing better is feasible.
Publication is sufficient when the party's identity or location cannot reasonably be determined.
Right result, wrong reason. Contingent beneficiaries are entitled to constitutionally adequate notice. Publication satisfies it here because they could not be found.
topic: Wk 4 · Notice & service of process — Unknown beneficiaries
pre: A state statute allows a bank that pools many small trusts into a common fund to obtain a judicial settlement of its accounts, which cuts off any claims by beneficiaries for mismanagement. The statute requires only publication of notice in a newspaper. The bank has the mailing addresses of 900 beneficiaries in its own records. It published the required notice and obtained a settlement decree. A beneficiary whose address the bank had on file later sued, arguing that the decree does not bind her. Is the decree binding on her?

q: A homeowner moved out of his house but continued to own it. After his mortgage was paid off, the property taxes went unpaid. The county sent a certified letter to the house warning of a tax sale, and the post office returned it marked "unclaimed." The county then published notice in a local newspaper and sold the house. The homeowner learned of the sale only when the buyer began eviction proceedings against his tenant. Was the notice constitutionally adequate?
o: No, because the county ignored a known failure of its mailed notice.
Yes, because the county mailed the notice to the owner's address of record.
Yes, because the county also published notice after the letter was returned.
No, because due process requires that the owner actually receive notice before a tax sale.
oe: Jones v. Flowers: when the government learns before acting that its attempt at notice failed, it must take additional reasonable steps if practicable, such as resending by regular mail, posting at the property, or addressing mail to the occupant.
Mailing to the address of record is ordinarily enough, but not when the sender learns that the mailing failed and ignores that knowledge.
Publication is a fallback for unknown or unfindable parties. The owner and the property's address were known, and cheaper, more effective steps were available.
Right result, wrong reason. Actual receipt is not required. What is required is a reasonable response when notice is known to have failed.
topic: Wk 4 · Notice & service of process — Notice that is known to have failed

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the certified letter was signed for by the homeowner's tenant and was never returned to the county. The tenant threw it away, and the homeowner never saw it. Was the notice constitutionally adequate?
o: Yes, because the mailing was reasonably calculated to reach him and was not known to fail.
No, because the homeowner never actually received or read the notice before the sale.
No, because the county was required to serve the homeowner personally before selling his property.
Yes, because the tenant was the homeowner's agent for receiving official mail.
oe: Due process requires notice reasonably calculated to inform, not actual receipt. The duty to take additional steps arises only when the sender learns that its notice failed.
Actual receipt is not required. Jones confirmed this even as it required additional steps when failure is known.
Personal service is not constitutionally required. Mail reasonably calculated to reach the owner is enough.
Right result, wrong reason. Nothing shows the tenant was an agent. The notice was adequate because it was reasonably calculated to reach the owner.
topic: Wk 4 · Notice & service of process — No sign of failure
pre: A homeowner moved out of his house but continued to own it. After his mortgage was paid off, the property taxes went unpaid. The county sent a certified letter to the house warning of a tax sale, and the post office returned it marked "unclaimed." The county then published notice in a local newspaper and sold the house. The homeowner learned of the sale only when the buyer began eviction proceedings against his tenant. Was the notice constitutionally adequate?

q: A Nevada casino sued a Costa Rican online gambling business in federal court in Nevada for trademark infringement. The business had no United States address where it could be served, conducted its business through its website, and told customers to contact it by email. Without first attempting service by any other means, the casino asked the court to authorize service by email under Rule 4(f)(3), and the court did so. No international agreement prohibits email service in Costa Rica. The business moved to quash, arguing that court- ordered service is a last resort. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because Rule 4(f)(3) needs only a court order and a method not prohibited by international agreement.
Grant the motion, because a plaintiff must try the methods in Rule 4(f)(1) and (2) before seeking a court order.
Grant the motion, because email is not a method of service authorized by any of the Federal Rules.
Deny the motion, because the business consented to email service by listing an email address on its website.
oe: Rio Properties: Rule 4(f)(3) is not a last resort and requires no prior attempt at other methods. The method must also satisfy Mullane, and email was the method most likely to reach a business that chose to operate by email.
Rule 4(f) is not a hierarchy. Subsection (f)(3) stands on equal footing with the others.
Rule 4(f)(3) authorizes any means the court orders that is not prohibited by international agreement. That includes email.
Right result, wrong reason. Listing an email address is not consent to service. The court order under Rule 4(f)(3) is what made the service valid.
topic: Wk 4 · Notice & service of process — Court-ordered email service abroad

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the casino never asked the court for an order. It simply emailed the summons and complaint to the business, which acknowledged receiving them and then moved to dismiss for insufficient service of process. How should the court rule?
o: Grant the motion, because email service on a foreign defendant requires a court order under Rule 4(f)(3).
Deny the motion, because the business actually received the summons and complaint.
Deny the motion, because email is reasonably calculated to reach a business that operates by email.
Grant the motion, because email is not a permissible way to serve a foreign business.
oe: Rule 4(f)(3) authorizes email service only when the court orders it. Actual receipt does not cure noncompliance with Rule 4, so a Rule 12(b)(5) motion succeeds.
Notice and service are separate requirements. A defendant who receives the papers can still win a 12(b)(5) motion if service did not follow Rule 4.
That satisfies Mullane's notice standard, but service must also comply with Rule 4, which requires a court order for this method.
Right result, wrong reason. Email service is permitted when a court orders it under Rule 4(f)(3).
topic: Wk 4 · Notice & service of process — Email without a court order
pre: A Nevada casino sued a Costa Rican online gambling business in federal court in Nevada for trademark infringement. The business had no United States address where it could be served, conducted its business through its website, and told customers to contact it by email. Without first attempting service by any other means, the casino asked the court to authorize service by email under Rule 4(f)(3), and the court did so. No international agreement prohibits email service in Costa Rica. The business moved to quash, arguing that court- ordered service is a last resort. How should the court rule?

q: A plaintiff filed a federal action against an individual defendant in Kansas. The process server went to the defendant's house and, finding him away, attempted service in one of four ways. Assume that Kansas law authorizes no other method. Which attempt is valid service under Rule 4(e)?
o: Leaving the papers with the defendant's adult live-in housekeeper at the house.
Leaving the papers with the defendant's next-door neighbor, who promised to deliver them.
Leaving the papers with the defendant's adult daughter at her own apartment across town.
Taping the papers to the defendant's front door after no one answered.
oe: Rule 4(e)(2)(B) permits leaving copies at the individual's dwelling or usual place of abode with someone of suitable age and discretion who resides there. An adult housekeeper who lives in the home qualifies.
The person must reside at the defendant's dwelling. A neighbor does not.
Abode service must be made at the defendant's own dwelling or usual place of abode.
Posting is not a method listed in Rule 4(e)(2), and the facts say Kansas law authorizes no other method.
topic: Wk 4 · Notice & service of process — Abode service

q: A plaintiff sued an individual in federal court in State A. State A's law permits service on an individual by certified mail, return receipt requested. The plaintiff mailed the summons and complaint by certified mail to the defendant's home in State A, and the defendant signed the return receipt. The defendant moved to dismiss for insufficient service, arguing that the Federal Rules do not authorize service by mail. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because Rule 4(e)(1) permits service under the law of the state where the court sits.
Grant the motion, because the only mail procedure in Rule 4 is a request to waive service.
Grant the motion, because the Federal Rules preempt state service methods in federal court.
Deny the motion, because the defendant actually received the papers and signed for them.
oe: Rule 4(e)(1) incorporates the service methods of the state where the district court is located or where service is made. State A's law authorizes certified mail, so service was valid.
Rule 4(d) waiver is the only mail procedure the Rule itself creates, but Rule 4(e)(1) also borrows state methods, including mail where state law allows it.
Rule 4 expressly incorporates state methods. There is no conflict to preempt.
Right result, wrong reason. Receipt alone does not validate service. Compliance with a method incorporated by Rule 4(e)(1) does.
topic: Wk 4 · Notice & service of process — Following state-law service methods

q: A plaintiff who was representing himself sued his former landlord in federal court. To save money, he drove to the landlord's office and personally handed her the summons and complaint. The landlord filed a timely motion to dismiss for insufficient service of process. How should the court rule?
o: Grant the motion, because a party may never serve the summons and complaint himself.
Deny the motion, because the landlord received the papers by personal delivery.
Deny the motion, because a pro se plaintiff is exempt from the technical requirements of Rule 4.
Grant the motion, because only a United States marshal may serve process in federal cases.
oe: Rule 4(c)(2) allows service by any person who is at least 18 and not a party. A party's own delivery is not valid service, even though the landlord got the papers. Dismissal is typically without prejudice, or the court may quash service and allow re-service.
Personal delivery is a valid method only when made by a proper server. Receiving the papers does not cure the defect.
Self-represented parties must comply with Rule 4, although the court may order service by a marshal on request.
Right result, wrong reason. Any nonparty adult may serve. The marshal serves only when the court orders it.
topic: Wk 4 · Notice & service of process — Who may serve

q: A plaintiff sued a corporation located in Ohio in federal court. She mailed the corporation a properly completed request to waive service, with a copy of the complaint and a prepaid means of return, giving it 30 days to respond. The corporation ignored the request without any reason. The plaintiff then had it formally served by a process server at a cost of $400, and she spent $1,500 in attorney's fees on a motion to collect those costs. What may the court order?
o: The corporation must pay both the $400 service costs and the $1,500 in fees for the collection motion.
The corporation must pay the $400 service costs, but not the fees for the motion.
Nothing, because waiver of service is entirely voluntary for the defendant.
The corporation is in default, because it failed to respond to the request within 30 days.
oe: A defendant located in the United States that fails without good cause to sign and return a waiver must pay the expenses of formal service and the reasonable expenses, including attorney's fees, of any motion required to collect them (Rule 4(d)(2)).
Rule 4(d)(2)(B) expressly includes the reasonable expenses of a motion to collect the service costs.
Waiver is voluntary, but refusing without good cause shifts the costs of formal service to the defendant.
Ignoring a waiver request is not a failure to plead or defend. The plaintiff must serve formally, and the remedy is cost-shifting.
topic: Wk 4 · Notice & service of process — Refusing to waive service

q: On March 1, a plaintiff mailed a waiver-of-service request to an individual defendant who lives in Illinois. The defendant signed and returned the waiver on March 10, and the plaintiff filed it with the court. The defendant intends to contest personal jurisdiction. Which statement is correct?
o: The defendant must answer or move by April 30 and may still object to personal jurisdiction.
The defendant must answer or move by March 31 and may still object to personal jurisdiction.
The defendant must answer or move by May 9, but waived any objection to personal jurisdiction.
The defendant must answer or move by April 30, but waived any objection to personal jurisdiction.
oe: A defendant who timely waives service has 60 days after the request was sent (here, from March 1) to answer or move. Waiving service does not waive any objection to personal jurisdiction or venue (Rule 4(d)(5)).
Twenty-one days applies to formally served defendants, and it would run from service, not the request. A waiving defendant gets 60 days from when the request was sent.
The 60 days run from when the request was sent, not when the waiver was returned, and waiving service preserves jurisdictional objections.
The deadline is right, but signing a waiver of service does not waive objections to personal jurisdiction or venue.
topic: Wk 4 · Notice & service of process — Answer deadline after waiver

q: A plaintiff sued a corporation in federal court in Missouri. The process server walked into the corporation's Missouri headquarters and handed the summons and complaint to a receptionist at the front desk, who had no authority to accept legal papers and no management duties. Missouri law permits service on a corporation only by delivery to an officer, a managing or general agent, or a registered agent. Was service valid?
o: No, because the receptionist is not an officer, managing or general agent, or authorized agent.
Yes, because the papers were delivered at the corporation's principal place of business.
Yes, because a receptionist is a person of suitable age and discretion at the corporation's office.
No, because a corporation may be served only through its registered agent.
oe: Rule 4(h)(1) permits service on a corporation in the United States by the state-law method or by delivery to an officer, a managing or general agent, or an agent authorized by appointment or law. A receptionist with no authority is none of these, and Missouri law adds no broader method.
Where papers are delivered is not the test. Rule 4(h) requires delivery to particular people.
That standard applies to abode service on an individual under Rule 4(e)(2)(B), not to corporations.
Right result, wrong reason. Service on an officer or a managing or general agent is also valid.
topic: Wk 4 · Notice & service of process — Serving a corporation

q: A veteran sued the Department of Veterans Affairs, a federal agency, in federal district court, challenging the denial of benefits. He sent the summons and complaint by certified mail to the agency's headquarters and did nothing else. The government moved to dismiss for insufficient service. Which additional steps did Rule 4(i) require?
o: Serving the U.S. attorney for the district and mailing to the Attorney General.
Personal delivery of the papers to the Secretary of Veterans Affairs.
Filing a waiver-of-service request with the clerk of the district court.
Nothing, because certified mail to the agency is sufficient by itself.
oe: To serve a federal agency, a party must serve the United States, by delivering to the U.S. attorney for the district (or mailing to the civil-process clerk) and mailing to the Attorney General, and also mail the papers to the agency.
Rule 4(i) does not require personal delivery to the agency head. It requires serving the United States through the U.S. attorney and the Attorney General.
Waiver requests go to the defendant, and Rule 4(d) does not apply to the United States.
Mailing to the agency is only one part. Without serving the United States as well, service is incomplete.
topic: Wk 4 · Notice & service of process — Serving the United States

q: A plaintiff filed a federal complaint on January 10 against a defendant living in Texas. Through her lawyer's oversight, she did not serve the defendant until May 1, 111 days after filing. She has no excuse other than the oversight. The defendant moved to dismiss under Rule 4(m). What may the court do?
o: Dismiss the action without prejudice or order that service be made within a specified time.
Dismiss the action with prejudice, because the plaintiff had no good cause for the delay.
Nothing, because service was completed before the defendant filed the motion.
Extend the time, because the court must extend the time whenever service is eventually made.
oe: Rule 4(m) requires service within 90 days after the complaint is filed. If service is late, the court must dismiss without prejudice or order service within a specified time. An extension is mandatory only on good cause, which a lawyer's oversight usually is not, but the court may still extend in its discretion.
A Rule 4(m) dismissal is without prejudice. It may still bar the claim if the limitations period has run, but that is a separate consequence.
Late service does not become timely because it was finished before the motion. The 90-day period still governs.
The court must extend only for good cause. Otherwise it has a choice between dismissal and a discretionary extension.
topic: Wk 4 · Notice & service of process — The 90-day service limit

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the defendant lives in France, and the plaintiff spent seven months completing service through France's central authority under the Hague Service Convention. What should the court do with the defendant's Rule 4(m) motion?
o: Deny it, because the 90-day limit does not apply to service in a foreign country.
Grant it, because service was made more than 90 days after the complaint was filed.
Grant it, because the plaintiff should have used email service to avoid delay.
Deny it, but only because the Hague Convention extends the 90-day limit to 180 days.
oe: Rule 4(m) expressly does not apply to service in a foreign country under Rule 4(f) or 4(h)(2). International service often takes far longer than 90 days.
The 90-day limit does not govern foreign service.
Email service requires a court order and is not a duty. Using the Hague Convention is entirely proper.
The Convention sets no such period. The exemption comes from the text of Rule 4(m).
topic: Wk 4 · Notice & service of process — Service abroad
pre: A plaintiff filed a federal complaint on January 10 against a defendant living in Texas. Through her lawyer's oversight, she did not serve the defendant until May 1, 111 days after filing. She has no excuse other than the oversight. The defendant moved to dismiss under Rule 4(m). What may the court do?

q: A process server properly delivered a summons and complaint to a defendant personally. The plaintiff's lawyer forgot to file the server's affidavit of service with the court until two months later. The defendant moved to dismiss for insufficient service, pointing to the missing proof. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because failure to prove service does not affect the validity of the service.
Grant the motion, because service is not complete until proof is filed with the court.
Grant the motion, because the plaintiff must file proof of service within 21 days.
Deny the motion, because the defendant waived the objection by not raising it within 14 days.
oe: Rule 4(l) requires proof of service by the server's affidavit unless service is waived, but Rule 4(l)(3) provides that failure to prove service does not affect its validity. The court may permit the proof to be amended or filed late.
Service is complete on delivery. Proof is evidence of service, not a part of it.
There is no 21-day filing deadline in Rule 4(l), and late filing would not invalidate the service anyway.
Right result, wrong reason. There is no 14-day limit. Service objections are raised in the first Rule 12 motion or the answer.
topic: Wk 4 · Notice & service of process — Proof of service

q: A defendant was personally served with a copy of the complaint and a document labeled "summons" that the plaintiff's lawyer had prepared. It named the parties and the court but bore neither the clerk's signature nor the court's seal and did not state the time within which the defendant had to appear. The defendant moved to dismiss. Which Rule 12(b) defense best describes the defect?
o: Insufficient process, because the summons itself was defective in form.
Insufficient service of process, because the method of delivery was improper.
Lack of personal jurisdiction, because a defective summons deprives the court of power over the defendant.
Failure to state a claim, because the complaint was not accompanied by a valid summons.
oe: Rule 4(a)-(b) requires the summons to be signed by the clerk, bear the court's seal, and state the time to appear and defend. A defect in the summons is insufficient process under Rule 12(b)(4). The plaintiff can cure it by having a proper summons issued and served.
Rule 12(b)(5) addresses defects in the manner of delivery. Personal delivery was proper; the document itself was defective.
A defective summons is a service-related defect, separate from personal jurisdiction, and is curable.
Rule 12(b)(6) tests the legal sufficiency of the complaint's allegations, not the summons.
topic: Wk 4 · Notice & service of process — Insufficient process

q: A plaintiff sued a 15-year-old who lives in Ohio in federal court in Ohio over a skateboarding collision. The plaintiff's process server handed the summons and complaint directly to the minor at school. Ohio law requires that service on a minor under 16 be made on the minor's parent or guardian. Was service valid?
o: No, because service on a minor must follow Ohio's rules for serving minors.
Yes, because personal delivery to the defendant is valid under Rule 4(e)(2).
Yes, because a 15-year-old is a person of suitable age and discretion.
No, because a minor may be sued only in a state court where the minor resides.
oe: Rule 4(g) provides that a minor or incompetent person in a judicial district of the United States must be served by following the law of the state where service is made. Ohio requires service on the parent or guardian.
Rule 4(g), not Rule 4(e), governs service on minors.
That standard concerns who may receive papers at an individual's abode, not how a minor must be served.
Minors may be sued in federal court like anyone else. The issue is how they must be served.
topic: Wk 4 · Notice & service of process — Serving a minor

q: In settlement of an injury claim, a railroad promised a couple free lifetime passes. Years later, the railroad refused to renew the passes, citing a new federal statute that prohibits free passes. The couple, who share citizenship with the railroad, sued in federal court for specific performance. Their complaint alleged that the federal statute does not apply to their passes and, if it does, is unconstitutional. Neither party questioned jurisdiction, and the trial court ruled for the couple. On appeal, how should the appellate court proceed?
o: Order dismissal for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction on its own motion.
Decide the constitutional question, because the complaint expressly raised it.
Affirm, because the railroad waived any objection by failing to raise it in the trial court.
Affirm, because the case necessarily required interpretation of a federal statute.
oe: Mottley: the couple's claim is for breach of a state-law contract. The federal statute enters only as the railroad's anticipated defense, which does not appear in a well-pleaded complaint. Federal courts must police their own subject-matter jurisdiction, so the court must dismiss on its own motion.
Mentioning an anticipated defense in the complaint does not make the claim arise under federal law. The well-pleaded complaint rule ignores such allegations.
Subject-matter jurisdiction cannot be waived or created by consent, and it may be raised for the first time on appeal.
The federal issue arises from the defense, not from the plaintiffs' claim. The embedded-issue test applies only when the federal issue is an element of the plaintiff's own state claim.
topic: Wk 5 · SMJ basics & federal question — Anticipated federal defense

q: A plaintiff sued a defendant in federal court, alleging diversity jurisdiction. After losing at trial, the plaintiff discovered that the defendant had been a citizen of the plaintiff's own state when the complaint was filed. The plaintiff then moved to vacate the judgment for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. The defendant argued that the plaintiff, having chosen the federal forum, could not now attack its jurisdiction. Should the court vacate the judgment?
o: Yes, because the parties' conduct can never create subject-matter jurisdiction.
No, because a party that invokes federal jurisdiction is estopped from denying it later.
No, because the defendant waived the citizenship issue by not raising it before trial.
Yes, but only because the defendant concealed his true citizenship from the court.
oe: Subject-matter jurisdiction cannot be waived, forfeited, or created by consent or estoppel. Any party, including the one that invoked jurisdiction, may raise its absence, and the court must dismiss (Rule 12(h)(3)).
Estoppel cannot create subject-matter jurisdiction. The rule protects the limits on federal judicial power, not the parties.
Neither party can waive a lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.
Right result, wrong reason. Concealment is irrelevant. The judgment falls because the court never had jurisdiction.
topic: Wk 5 · SMJ basics & federal question — Party that invoked jurisdiction may challenge it

q: An employee sued her former employer in federal court under Title VII, a federal statute that creates a cause of action for employment discrimination. She seeks $12,000 in back pay. She and the employer are citizens of the same state. The employer moved to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because the claim is created by federal law.
Grant the motion, because the amount in controversy does not exceed $75,000.
Grant the motion, because the parties are citizens of the same state.
Deny the motion, because employment cases are within the exclusive jurisdiction of federal courts.
oe: Under the creation test, a suit arises under the law that creates the cause of action. A claim under a federal statute satisfies § 1331, which has no amount-in-controversy requirement.
The $75,000 requirement applies to diversity jurisdiction under § 1332, not to federal-question jurisdiction.
Citizenship matters only for diversity jurisdiction. Federal-question jurisdiction does not depend on the parties' citizenship.
Right result, wrong reason. State courts may also hear Title VII claims. The point is that federal law creates this claim.
topic: Wk 5 · SMJ basics & federal question — Federal cause of action, small amount

q: A supplier sued a retailer in a state court for $300,000 in unpaid invoices under state contract law. Both are citizens of the same state. The retailer filed a counterclaim under the federal antitrust laws, alleging that the supplier's pricing violated the Sherman Act, and then filed a notice of removal based on the federal counterclaim. Was removal proper?
o: No, because a federal counterclaim cannot make the action arise under federal law.
Yes, because the counterclaim arises under a federal statute and seeks more than $75,000.
Yes, because antitrust claims are within the federal courts' exclusive jurisdiction.
No, because only the plaintiff may remove a case once a counterclaim is filed.
oe: Under the well-pleaded complaint rule, jurisdiction is judged by the plaintiff's claims. A federal counterclaim does not make the action one arising under federal law (Holmes Group v. Vornado), so there is nothing to remove.
The counterclaim's federal character and size are irrelevant to removal, which looks only to the plaintiff's complaint.
Exclusive jurisdiction over the counterclaim does not make the whole action removable. The state court's lack of power over the counterclaim is a separate problem.
Plaintiffs can never remove, even when facing a counterclaim. Only defendants to the plaintiff's claims may remove.
topic: Wk 5 · SMJ basics & federal question — Federal counterclaim

q: A distributor fears that a manufacturer will sue it under state law for breaching an exclusive-dealing contract. The distributor believes that a federal statute preempts the contract's exclusivity term. Before the manufacturer sues, the distributor files a federal action under the Declaratory Judgment Act seeking a declaration that the federal statute preempts the term. The parties are citizens of the same state. Does the court have federal- question jurisdiction?
o: No, because the anticipated coercive action would be a state contract claim with a federal defense.
Yes, because the distributor's own complaint asks the court to interpret a federal statute.
Yes, because the Declaratory Judgment Act is a federal statute that creates the cause of action.
No, because declaratory judgments may be sought only in state court.
oe: A declaratory-judgment action is judged by the coercive suit it anticipates (Skelly Oil). The manufacturer's suit would be a state-law contract claim, with preemption arising only as a defense, so the well-pleaded complaint rule bars jurisdiction.
