o: A short and plain statement of the grounds for removal, signed under Rule 11.
A sworn affidavit from each plaintiff stating that the damages exceed $75,000.
A copy of an order from the state court granting leave to remove.
A bond securing the plaintiffs' costs in case the federal court remands.
oe: Section 1446(a) requires a short and plain statement of the grounds for removal, signed under Rule 11. As in the Lara notice, a diversity removal should plead each party's citizenship, the amount in controversy, timeliness, and every served defendant's consent.
The defendant may assert the amount in controversy in the notice and must prove it by a preponderance only if challenged. No affidavit from the plaintiffs is needed.
Removal requires no state-court permission. The defendant files the notice in federal court and a copy in the state court, which then may proceed no further.
The current removal statute requires no bond.
topic: Wk 6 · Removal — What a notice of removal must show

q: A defendant filed a notice of removal in federal court, promptly gave written notice to the plaintiff, and filed a copy of the notice with the clerk of the state court. The next day, the state judge, believing removal improper, granted the plaintiff's pending motion for a preliminary injunction. Is the injunction valid?
o: No, because the state court may proceed no further once the notice copy is filed.
Yes, because a state court retains jurisdiction until the federal court rules on removal.
Yes, because the state judge believed in good faith that removal was improper.
No, because only a federal court may issue a preliminary injunction in a removable case.
oe: Under § 1446(d), filing a copy of the notice with the state court effects the removal, and the state court "shall proceed no further unless and until the case is remanded."
The state court loses power as soon as removal is effected by filing the copy. The federal court decides whether removal was proper.
The state court's view of the removal's validity does not matter. The question goes to the federal court.
State courts issue injunctions all the time. The problem is that this one acted after removal.
topic: Wk 6 · Removal — Effect of the notice on the state court

q: A Nevada plaintiff sued an Arizona corporation in a Nevada state court for injuries in a car accident. Nevada's rules forbid stating a specific dollar amount in the complaint, which seeks "damages in excess of $15,000." The corporation removed on diversity, asserting in its notice that the amount in controversy exceeds $75,000. The plaintiff challenged that assertion. How is the amount determined?
o: The corporation must prove by a preponderance of the evidence that the amount exceeds $75,000.
The case must be remanded, because the complaint does not demand more than $75,000.
The plaintiff must prove to a legal certainty that the amount is $75,000 or less.
The corporation's good-faith assertion controls unless the plaintiff stipulates otherwise.
oe: When the complaint does not state an amount, § 1446(c)(2) lets the defendant assert one in the notice of removal. If the plaintiff challenges it, the court decides by a preponderance of the evidence whether the amount exceeds $75,000.
The statute addresses exactly this situation by letting the defendant assert the amount.
The legal-certainty test governs when the plaintiff's own complaint claims an amount. Here the defendant asserts the amount and bears the burden.
The defendant's assertion is accepted only if unchallenged. Once challenged, it must be proved.
topic: Wk 6 · Removal — Amount in controversy on removal

q: A New York citizen sued two individuals in federal court for fraud in the sale of a business located in New Jersey. One defendant is domiciled in Philadelphia, in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania. The other is domiciled in Pittsburgh, in the Western District of Pennsylvania. All of the events giving rise to the claim occurred in New Jersey. Which of the following is a proper venue?
o: The Western District of Pennsylvania.
The Southern District of New York, where the plaintiff lives.
The Middle District of Pennsylvania, because both defendants reside in Pennsylvania.
None of the Pennsylvania districts, because the events occurred in New Jersey.
oe: Under § 1391(b)(1), venue is proper in a district where any defendant resides if all defendants are residents of the state in which the district is located. Both defendants are Pennsylvania residents, so either Pennsylvania district where one of them resides is proper.
The plaintiff's residence plays no role in venue under § 1391(b).
Section 1391(b)(1) permits venue only in a district where a defendant actually resides, not in any district of the state.
Residence-based venue under § 1391(b)(1) is an alternative to events-based venue under § 1391(b)(2). The District of New Jersey is also proper, but it is not the only proper venue.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — All defendants reside in the same state

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the second defendant is domiciled in Wilmington, Delaware. Which is a proper venue?
o: The District of New Jersey.
The Eastern District of Pennsylvania, where one defendant resides.
Any district where either defendant is subject to personal jurisdiction.
The District of Delaware, because one defendant resides there.
oe: Because the defendants reside in different states, § 1391(b)(1) is unavailable. Section 1391(b)(2) makes venue proper where a substantial part of the events occurred, which is New Jersey.
Residence-based venue requires that all defendants reside in the same state.
The fallback in § 1391(b)(3) applies only when no district satisfies (b)(1) or (b)(2). New Jersey satisfies (b)(2).
As with Pennsylvania, one defendant's residence is not enough when the defendants live in different states.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — Defendants in different states
pre: A New York citizen sued two individuals in federal court for fraud in the sale of a business located in New Jersey. One defendant is domiciled in Philadelphia, in the Eastern District of Pennsylvania. The other is domiciled in Pittsburgh, in the Western District of Pennsylvania. All of the events giving rise to the claim occurred in New Jersey. Which of the following is a proper venue?

q: A trucking company sued a shipper in federal court for breach of contract. The contract was negotiated by phone and email between the company's office in the Northern District of Illinois and the shipper's office in the District of Minnesota, and it was signed in Minnesota. The goods were loaded in Illinois, and the shipper refused to pay after delivery in Minnesota. The shipper resides in Minnesota. The trucking company filed in the Northern District of Illinois, and the shipper moved to dismiss for improper venue, arguing that most of the events occurred in Minnesota. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because a substantial part of the events occurred in Illinois.
Grant the motion, because venue lies only in the district where the most substantial events occurred.
Grant the motion, because the shipper resides only in Minnesota, not in Illinois.
Deny the motion, because the plaintiff resides in the Northern District of Illinois.
oe: Section 1391(b)(2) asks whether significant events material to the claim occurred in the district, not where the most substantial events occurred. Venue can be proper in more than one district, and negotiation and performance in Illinois are significant.
The statute does not require choosing the single best district. Several districts can each host a substantial part.
Residence-based venue is only one option. Events-based venue in Illinois is an independent basis.
Right result, wrong reason. The plaintiff's residence is irrelevant to venue.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — More than one substantial-part district

q: A plaintiff sued an individual defendant in federal court in the District of Colorado over a car accident in Kansas. The defendant is domiciled in Omaha, Nebraska, but owns a ski condominium in Colorado where he spends six weeks a year. He was personally served at the condominium, so the court has personal jurisdiction over him. He moved to dismiss for improper venue. How should the court rule?
o: Grant the motion, because the defendant does not reside in Colorado for venue.
Deny the motion, because the defendant was personally served in Colorado.
Deny the motion, because the defendant owns property and regularly spends time in Colorado.
Grant the motion, because venue is proper only where the events occurred.
oe: Under § 1391(c)(1), a natural person resides in the judicial district of domicile. Being subject to personal jurisdiction in Colorado does not make him a Colorado resident for venue, and no events occurred there.
In-state service establishes personal jurisdiction, not venue. Venue is a separate requirement.
A vacation home is not a domicile. Individuals reside for venue only where they are domiciled.
Right result, wrong reason. Venue is also proper where the defendant resides. Colorado is neither.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — Individual's venue residence

q: A plaintiff sued a corporation incorporated in Delaware with its headquarters in Atlanta, Georgia, in federal court in the Northern District of Illinois. The claim arises from a defective furnace the corporation sold to the plaintiff through its Chicago showroom, and the corporation is subject to specific jurisdiction in that district for this claim. The furnace exploded in Indiana. The corporation moved to dismiss for improper venue, arguing that it resides only in Delaware and Georgia. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because the corporation resides in the district for venue purposes.
Grant the motion, because a corporation resides only in its state of incorporation and principal place of business.
Grant the motion, because the furnace exploded and caused the injury in Indiana.
Deny the motion, because the plaintiff purchased the furnace in the district.
oe: Under § 1391(c)(2), an entity resides, as a defendant, in any district where it is subject to personal jurisdiction with respect to the action. Corporate venue residence is much broader than diversity citizenship.
That is the rule for diversity citizenship and general jurisdiction, not for venue.
Events-based venue is only one alternative. Residence-based venue makes the Northern District of Illinois proper.
That may also support venue under § 1391(b)(2), but the corporation's argument fails most clearly because it resides in the district.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — Corporate venue residence

q: A corporation incorporated and headquartered in Ohio operates a single retail store in Texas, located in the Southern District of Texas. A customer sued it in federal court in the Northern District of Texas over a dispute arising from a purchase at that store, with no events in the Northern District. Texas's long-arm statute reaches as far as due process permits. Does the corporation reside in the Northern District of Texas for venue purposes?
o: No, because it lacks contacts with the Northern District itself.
Yes, because it is subject to personal jurisdiction in Texas.
Yes, because a corporation resides in each district of a state in which it does business.
No, because a corporation resides only in the district where its headquarters is located.
oe: Under § 1391(d), in a state with multiple districts, a corporation resides in any district within which its contacts would be sufficient for personal jurisdiction if that district were a separate state. Its only Texas contacts are in the Southern District.
Statewide jurisdiction is not enough. Section 1391(d) asks district by district.
Residence is assessed separately for each district in a multi-district state.
Right result, wrong reason. A corporation may reside in many districts. It just lacks contacts in the Northern District.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — Corporation in a multi-district state

q: A Florida plaintiff sued two individuals, one domiciled in Ohio and one domiciled in Oregon, in federal court for breach of a contract negotiated and performed entirely in France. Both defendants are subject to personal jurisdiction in the Southern District of Ohio for this action. Is venue proper there?
o: Yes, under the fallback provision of § 1391(b)(3).
No, because one of the defendants resides in Oregon, not Ohio.
No, because venue must lie where a substantial part of the events occurred.
Yes, because the Ohio defendant resides in the Southern District of Ohio.
oe: Section 1391(b)(1) fails because the defendants live in different states, and (b)(2) fails because no events occurred in the United States. The fallback in (b)(3) then permits any district where any defendant is subject to personal jurisdiction for the action.
That defeats (b)(1), but the fallback provision still applies.
That is only one of three options, and it is unavailable here because the events occurred abroad.
Right result, wrong reason. One defendant's residence is not enough under (b)(1) when the defendants live in different states.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — The fallback provision

q: A California plaintiff sued a Japanese corporation with no United States offices, and its Washington-resident sales agent, in federal court in the Western District of Washington. The claims arise from a sale that took place in Oregon. The court has personal jurisdiction over both defendants. Is venue proper?
o: Yes, because the sales agent resides in the district, and the foreign corporation is disregarded.
No, because the sale giving rise to the claims took place in Oregon, not Washington.
No, because a foreign corporation resides only where it is incorporated.
Yes, because a foreign corporation may be sued in any district where the plaintiff chooses.
oe: Under § 1391(c)(3), a defendant not resident in the United States may be sued in any district, and its joinder is disregarded in deciding venue for the other defendants. The sales agent resides in the Western District of Washington, so (b)(1) is satisfied.
Events-based venue is one option, not a requirement. Residence-based venue is satisfied here.
A non-U.S. defendant may be sued in any district.
That correctly states the rule for the corporation, but venue must also be proper as to the sales agent, which it is because he resides in the district.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — Foreign defendant

q: A corporation with its principal place of business in Boston sued a New Hampshire individual in federal court in the District of Massachusetts for breach of a contract negotiated and performed in New Hampshire. The defendant has no connection to Massachusetts. Which is the defendant's strongest objection to the choice of forum?
o: Venue is improper, because neither the defendant nor the events are in Massachusetts.
Venue is improper, because a corporation may sue only in its state of incorporation.
Subject-matter jurisdiction is lacking, because the plaintiff is a corporation.
Notice is defective, because the defendant must be served in Massachusetts.
oe: Venue under § 1391(b) depends on the defendants' residence or the location of events. A plaintiff entity's residence, its principal place of business, matters only in limited situations and does not make its home district proper.
There is no such limit. The problem is the lack of any connection to the defendant or the events.
Corporations may invoke diversity jurisdiction like anyone else.
Service outside the forum state is common. Notice is not the problem here.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — Plaintiff's residence is irrelevant

q: A defendant sued in federal court filed a pre-answer motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim. The court denied it. The defendant then filed an answer asserting, for the first time, that venue was improper. The plaintiff argued that the venue objection was waived. Is it?
o: Yes, because it was omitted from the defendant's first Rule 12 motion.
No, because a venue objection may be raised in the answer.
No, because venue is a jurisdictional requirement that cannot be waived.
Yes, because venue objections must be raised within 14 days of service.
oe: Under Rule 12(g)(2) and (h)(1), a defense of improper venue is waived if it is omitted from a pre-answer motion that raises other Rule 12 defenses. Raising it in the later answer is too late.
It could have been raised in the answer only if the defendant had not first made a Rule 12 motion.
Venue is not jurisdictional. It protects the defendant's convenience and can be waived.
Right result, wrong reason. There is no 14-day rule. The objection is waived because it was left out of the first Rule 12 motion.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — Waiver of venue objection

q: A plaintiff sued a defendant in a state court in Austin, Texas, which is in the Western District of Texas. No events occurred in that district, and the defendant does not reside there. The defendant removed to the Western District of Texas and then moved to dismiss for improper venue under § 1391. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because § 1391 does not govern venue in removed cases.
Grant the motion, because venue in the Western District is improper under § 1391(b).
Grant the motion, because the defendant was entitled to remove to any district with proper venue.
Deny the motion, because the defendant waived venue by removing.
oe: Section 1441(a) fixes venue in a removed case in the district and division embracing the place where the state action was pending. Section 1391 does not govern removed cases.
Section 1391 does not apply to removed cases. The defendant's remedy, if any, is a motion to transfer under § 1404(a).
A defendant must remove to the district embracing the state court, not to a district of its choosing.
Right result, wrong reason. Venue is proper by statute, so there was nothing to waive.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — Venue in removed cases

q: A plaintiff sued a manufacturer in federal court in the District of Oregon, where venue is proper. The accident occurred in Idaho, and nearly all of the witnesses and the physical evidence are in Idaho. The manufacturer is subject to personal jurisdiction in Idaho, and venue would be proper there. The manufacturer moved to transfer the case to the District of Idaho. What standard governs?
o: The court may transfer after weighing convenience and the interest of justice.
The court must dismiss the action, because a more convenient federal forum exists.
The court must transfer, because venue is improper in Oregon.
The court may transfer only if the plaintiff consents to litigating in Idaho.
oe: Under § 1404(a), when venue is proper the court may transfer to any district where the case might have been brought, balancing private-interest factors (access to proof, witnesses, cost) and public-interest factors. The plaintiff's choice of forum gets deference.
When venue is proper, convenience supports transfer, not dismissal.
Venue in Oregon is proper. Section 1406(a) applies only when venue is wrong.
The court may transfer over the plaintiff's objection to any district where the action might have been brought.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — Transfer for convenience

q: A plaintiff sued a defendant in federal court in Arizona, where venue and personal jurisdiction are proper. The defendant moved under § 1404(a) to transfer the case to the District of Montana, where most witnesses live. The defendant is not subject to personal jurisdiction in Montana, but it offered to waive any objection there. The plaintiff does not consent. May the court transfer the case to Montana?
o: No, because the action could not have been brought in Montana.
Yes, because the defendant waived its personal-jurisdiction objection in Montana.
Yes, because the convenience of the witnesses strongly favors Montana.
No, because § 1404(a) transfers require a forum-selection clause.
oe: Section 1404(a) permits transfer only to a district where the case might have been brought (proper venue, personal jurisdiction, and subject-matter jurisdiction there) or to which all parties have consented. The defendant's unilateral waiver does not count.
Whether the action might have been brought there is judged without the defendant's after-the-fact consent, unless all parties consent.
Convenience matters only among eligible transferee districts.
Forum-selection clauses change how § 1404(a) applies, but transfer is available without one.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — Where the action might have been brought

q: A plaintiff sued in federal court in Mississippi, invoking diversity jurisdiction, within Mississippi's six-year limitations period. Venue and jurisdiction were proper. The defendant obtained a § 1404(a) transfer to the District of Pennsylvania for convenience. Pennsylvania's limitations period is two years, which had run before filing. Mississippi's choice-of-law rules would apply Mississippi's limitations period. Which state's limitations period should the transferee court apply?
o: Mississippi's, because the transferor's law goes with the case.
Pennsylvania's, because the transferee court applies the law of the state where it sits.
Pennsylvania's, because the defendant was entitled to the shorter limitations period.
Federal law's, because the case is now in a federal court in a different state.
oe: Under Van Dusen v. Barrack, a § 1404(a) transfer is a change of courtrooms, not of law. The transferee court applies the law that the transferor court would have applied.
That is the rule after a § 1406(a) transfer from an improper venue, not after a convenience transfer.
A defendant who seeks a convenience transfer does not gain a change in governing law.
In a diversity case, Erie and Klaxon require state law, including state choice-of-law rules.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — Law applied after a § 1404(a) transfer

q: A plaintiff sued a defendant in federal court in the District of Nevada, where venue is improper. Venue would be proper in the District of Utah. The limitations period expired after the plaintiff filed but before the court could rule, so a new suit in Utah would be time-barred. The defendant moved to dismiss for improper venue. What is the court's best course?
o: Transfer the case to the District of Utah in the interest of justice.
Dismiss the case, because venue in Nevada is improper.
Keep the case, because the defendant waived venue by not raising it in a timely answer.
Transfer the case under § 1404(a) for the convenience of the parties.
oe: Section 1406(a) requires the court to dismiss, or if it is in the interest of justice, transfer to a district where the case could have been brought. Transfer is favored when dismissal would leave the plaintiff time-barred.
Dismissal is permitted, but transfer is favored where refiling would be barred by the statute of limitations.
The defendant raised venue by a pre-answer motion, which is timely.
Section 1404(a) applies only when venue is proper in the transferor district.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — Improper venue and a lapsed limitations period

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the Nevada court also lacks personal jurisdiction over the defendant. The defendant argues that a court without personal jurisdiction has no power to transfer and must dismiss. After a transfer, which state's law would govern?
o: The court may transfer, and Utah law would govern after transfer.
The court may transfer, and Nevada law would govern after transfer.
The court must dismiss, because it lacks power over the defendant.
The court must dismiss, but the plaintiff may refile in Utah with Nevada law applying.
oe: Goldlawr v. Heiman permits a § 1406(a) transfer even when the transferor court lacks personal jurisdiction. After a § 1406(a) transfer, the transferee's law applies, because the plaintiff gets no benefit from filing in the wrong place.
The transferor's law follows the case only after a § 1404(a) transfer from a proper venue.
Goldlawr rejected this argument. Transfer is a way to cure the defect, not an exercise of power over the defendant.
Dismissal is not required, and Nevada law would not travel with a refiled case.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — No personal jurisdiction in the transferor
pre: A plaintiff sued a defendant in federal court in the District of Nevada, where venue is improper. Venue would be proper in the District of Utah. The limitations period expired after the plaintiff filed but before the court could rule, so a new suit in Utah would be time-barred. The defendant moved to dismiss for improper venue. What is the court's best course?

q: A Virginia general contractor and a Texas subcontractor signed a subcontract for work in Texas providing that all disputes "shall be litigated in the state or federal courts in Norfolk, Virginia." The subcontractor sued the contractor in federal court in Texas, where venue is proper under § 1391. The contractor moved to dismiss for improper venue under Rule 12(b)(3) and § 1406(a). How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because the clause does not make venue in Texas improper.
Grant the motion, because a forum-selection clause makes venue improper in any other district.
Grant the motion, because the clause is a waiver of venue in Texas.
Deny the motion, because forum-selection clauses are unenforceable in federal court.
oe: Atlantic Marine: venue is wrong only when § 1391 is not satisfied, so a forum-selection clause does not make venue improper. A clause pointing to another federal district is enforced through § 1404(a).
Atlantic Marine rejected that view. Whether venue is wrong depends only on the venue statute.
The clause is enforceable, but by transfer under § 1404(a), not by dismissal.
Valid forum-selection clauses are enforced and get controlling weight in all but the most exceptional cases.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — Enforcing a forum-selection clause

q: In a federal case in Texas, the defendant moved under § 1404(a) to transfer to the Eastern District of Virginia under a valid forum-selection clause. The plaintiff argued that its witnesses are in Texas, that it would be costly to litigate in Virginia, and that its choice of forum deserves deference. How should the court treat those arguments?
o: It should give them no weight in deciding the motion.
It should weigh them against the clause, because the plaintiff's choice of forum deserves deference.
It should deny transfer if the private-interest factors, taken together, favor Texas.
It should dismiss the case, because the plaintiff breached the clause by filing in Texas.
oe: Under Atlantic Marine, the plaintiff's choice gets no weight, the plaintiff bears the burden of showing transfer is unwarranted, and the court considers only public-interest factors, since the parties waived their private interests by contract.
A valid clause changes the usual § 1404(a) analysis and removes the deference ordinarily given to the plaintiff's choice.
Private-interest factors are deemed to favor the preselected forum and are not weighed.
The remedy for a clause pointing to another federal district is transfer, not dismissal.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — Atlantic Marine's modified analysis

q: A contract between a Delaware corporation and a German company provides that all disputes "shall be resolved exclusively in the courts of Munich, Germany." The Delaware corporation sued the German company in federal court in Delaware, where venue is proper. How should the German company seek to enforce the clause?
o: By a motion to dismiss for forum non conveniens.
By a motion to transfer under § 1404(a) to the courts of Munich.
By a motion to dismiss for improper venue under Rule 12(b)(3).
By a motion to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction.
oe: A forum-selection clause pointing to a state or foreign court is enforced through forum non conveniens, because a federal court cannot transfer a case to a foreign court. The Atlantic Marine modifications apply in that analysis too.
Section 1404(a) transfers only to other federal district courts.
Venue in Delaware is proper under § 1391, so Rule 12(b)(3) does not apply.
A clause selecting another forum does not deprive the Delaware court of personal jurisdiction.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — Clause pointing to a foreign court

q: A small plane made in Pennsylvania crashed in Scotland, killing the Scottish pilot and five Scottish passengers. The plane was owned and operated by Scottish companies. A California administrator of the estates sued the Pennsylvania manufacturer in federal court in Pennsylvania, admitting that she chose the United States because American tort law is more favorable. Scottish courts are available, but Scottish law does not recognize strict liability. Most witnesses and evidence are in Scotland. The manufacturer moved to dismiss for forum non conveniens. May the court grant the motion?
o: Yes, because the less favorable Scottish law does not make Scotland inadequate.
No, because Scottish law would be less favorable to the plaintiffs than American law.
No, because the defendant is at home in Pennsylvania and may be sued there.
Yes, but only by transferring the case to a federal court in Scotland.
oe: Piper Aircraft: an unfavorable change in law does not make the foreign forum inadequate unless its remedy is so clearly inadequate that it is no remedy at all. The real plaintiffs are foreign, so their choice gets less deference, and the private and public factors point to Scotland.
Piper held that this consideration gets no conclusive or even substantial weight.
Forum non conveniens assumes the court has jurisdiction and venue. The question is whether another forum is far more appropriate.
Forum non conveniens results in dismissal. There is no federal court in Scotland to transfer to.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — Less favorable foreign law

q: A Brazilian plaintiff sued an Illinois corporation in federal court in Illinois for injuries suffered in Brazil. The corporation moved to dismiss for forum non conveniens in favor of the Brazilian courts. The plaintiff showed that the Brazilian courts would lack jurisdiction over the corporation and that the Brazilian limitations period has run. The corporation has not offered to submit to Brazilian jurisdiction or waive any limitations defense. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because an adequate alternative forum is not available.
Grant the motion, because a foreign plaintiff's choice of a United States forum gets little deference.
Grant the motion, because the injury occurred in Brazil.
Deny the motion, because forum non conveniens is unavailable against a domestic defendant.
oe: Forum non conveniens requires an available alternative forum, which means the defendant must be amenable to process there. Courts often cure this by conditioning dismissal on the defendant's consent to jurisdiction abroad and waiver of limitations, but no such conditions are offered here.
Reduced deference matters only after an available, adequate alternative forum is shown.
Where the injury occurred is one factor in the balance, but the threshold requirement of an available forum is not met.
Right result, wrong reason. Domestic defendants, like the manufacturer in Piper, may seek dismissal in favor of a foreign forum.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — Unavailable alternative forum

q: An Ohio resident sued a Japanese manufacturer in federal court in Ohio for injuries suffered in Ohio from the manufacturer's product. The manufacturer moved to dismiss for forum non conveniens in favor of the courts of Japan, where its engineers and design documents are located. How much deference should the court give the plaintiff's choice of forum?
o: Strong deference, because she is suing in her home forum.
Little deference, because the defendant is a foreign corporation.
No deference, because the design evidence and engineers are located abroad in Japan.
The same deference as any other factor, because all factors are weighed equally.
oe: A home plaintiff's choice of forum gets strong deference. A foreign plaintiff's choice gets less, because it is less likely to rest on convenience.
Deference turns on the plaintiff's connection to the forum, not the defendant's nationality.
The location of evidence is a private-interest factor to be balanced, not a reason to ignore the plaintiff's choice.
The plaintiff's choice is not just one factor. It sets the presumption against which the defendant must show the balance strongly favors dismissal.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — Home plaintiff's choice of forum

q: A plaintiff sued in federal court in Florida. The defendant argues that the District of Colorado would be a far more convenient forum and moves to dismiss for forum non conveniens. How should the court treat the motion?
o: As a motion to transfer under § 1404(a).
As a motion to dismiss, because the doctrine permits dismissal whenever another forum is more convenient.
As a request for transfer under § 1406(a), because venue in Florida is improper.
As a request to remand the case to a Colorado state court with jurisdiction.
oe: Section 1404(a) codified forum non conveniens for moves between federal districts. Today dismissal for forum non conveniens is used mainly when the more convenient forum is a foreign (or state) court.
Within the federal system, the remedy is transfer, which avoids the costs of dismissal and refiling.
Nothing suggests venue is improper. Inconvenience does not make venue wrong.
Remand applies only to removed cases, and only to the state court from which the case came.
topic: Wk 7 · Venue, transfer & forum non conveniens — Forum non conveniens between federal courts

q: A Pennsylvania citizen walking at night on a well-worn path beside railroad tracks in Pennsylvania was struck by an object protruding from a passing train. He sued the railroad, a New York corporation, in federal court in New York on the basis of diversity. Pennsylvania's highest court has held that a person using such a path is a trespasser to whom the railroad owes a duty only to avoid willful or wanton injury. No Pennsylvania statute addresses the question. What standard of care should the federal court apply?
o: Pennsylvania's standard, as stated by its highest court.
The general common law of negligence, as the federal court independently determines it.
New York's standard, because the federal court sits in New York.
Pennsylvania's standard only if it has been codified in a state statute.
oe: Erie overruled Swift: except where the Constitution or Acts of Congress govern, federal courts in diversity apply state law, and state law includes the decisions of the state's highest court, not just its statutes.
That was the Swift regime, which Erie overruled. There is no federal general common law.
The forum state's choice-of-law rules decide which state's law applies, but nothing suggests New York law would govern an accident in Pennsylvania between these parties.
Erie rejected Swift's limitation of state law to statutes and local law. State court decisions are state law.
topic: Wk 7 · From Swift to Erie — State decisional law governs

q: In 1880, a holder sued the acceptor of a bill of exchange in federal court in New York on the basis of diversity. The acceptor raised a fraud defense that would fail against a holder who took the bill for value. The holder had taken it in payment of a pre-existing debt. New York decisions suggested that a pre-existing debt is not value, but the federal court believed that the general commercial law treats it as value. Under the law then in force, what should the federal court have done?
o: Apply its own view of the general commercial law and hold that the debt was value.
Follow the New York decisions, because they are the law of the state where the court sits.
Certify the question to New York's highest court and follow its answer.
Dismiss the case, because commercial-paper disputes were outside federal jurisdiction.
oe: Swift v. Tyson read the Rules of Decision Act's "laws of the several states" to mean only statutes and local law. On questions of general commercial law, federal courts exercised independent judgment and could disregard state decisions.
That is the post-Erie rule. Under Swift, state court decisions on general law did not bind federal courts.
Certification is a modern device, and under Swift the federal court had no obligation to follow the state court's answer on general law.
Diversity jurisdiction covered commercial disputes. The question was which law to apply, not whether the court could hear the case.
topic: Wk 7 · From Swift to Erie — The Swift regime

q: In the 1920s, a Kentucky taxi company held an exclusive contract with a railroad for the station in a Kentucky town. Kentucky courts consistently held such contracts void. To get into federal court, the company's owners dissolved it, reincorporated it in Tennessee, re-signed the contract, and sued a rival Kentucky company in federal court to enforce it. The federal court enforced the contract under general law. Which defect of the Swift regime does this case most clearly illustrate?
o: It let a party manufacture diversity to escape state law that a state court would apply.
It forced federal courts to apply state statutes they believed were unconstitutional.
It prevented federal courts from hearing contract disputes between corporations.
It required federal courts to follow state court decisions on questions of general law.
oe: Black & White Taxicab is the classic example of Swift's abuses. A litigant who could reach federal court could avoid state law, which encouraged forum shopping and unequal treatment. Holmes's dissent became Erie's reasoning.
The problem was the opposite: federal courts ignored state decisional law.
The federal court heard the case. The problem was the law it applied.
Swift freed federal courts from state decisions on general law. That freedom produced the abuse.
topic: Wk 7 · From Swift to Erie — Manufactured diversity under Swift

q: Under the Swift regime, an Ohio citizen injured in Ohio by a Kentucky company could sue in federal court and obtain the benefit of federal general law, while an Ohio citizen injured in the same way by an Ohio company was limited to Ohio courts and Ohio law. Which concern identified in Erie does this example best illustrate?
o: The inequitable administration of the laws.
The lack of federal judicial expertise in Ohio tort law.
The need for federal courts to create uniform national tort rules.
The burden on federal courts from an increasing diversity docket.
oe: Erie criticized Swift for producing unequal treatment: the noncitizen's ability to choose federal court let outcomes turn on citizenship rather than on the law of the place.
Expertise was not the concern. Erie objected that federal courts were not applying Ohio law at all.
Swift's goal was uniformity, but Erie found it failed, because state courts did not follow federal general law.
Erie's reasoning rested on statutory, policy, and constitutional grounds, not docket pressure.
topic: Wk 7 · From Swift to Erie — Erie's twin aims and unequal treatment

q: Which statement best describes the constitutional basis the Supreme Court gave in Erie for overruling Swift?
o: Federal courts have no constitutional power to declare substantive common law for the states.
The Seventh Amendment requires federal juries to apply state law.
Article III forbids federal courts from hearing cases governed by state law.
The Full Faith and Credit Clause requires federal courts to follow state judgments.
oe: Beyond its statutory reading of the Rules of Decision Act and its policy concerns, Erie held that Congress has no power to declare substantive rules of common law applicable in a state, and neither do the federal courts.
The Seventh Amendment preserves the right to jury trial. It says nothing about which law governs.
Article III expressly extends to diversity cases, which are usually governed by state law.
That clause concerns the effect of judgments and acts, not the source of rules of decision.
topic: Wk 7 · From Swift to Erie — Erie's constitutional ground

q: A New York company sued a Delaware company in federal court in Delaware on the basis of diversity, for breach of a contract made and performed in New York. The plaintiff won and asked for prejudgment interest under a New York statute. Delaware's courts would apply Delaware's choice-of-law rules, which do not select New York's interest statute. The court of appeals applied New York law because it thought that the better conflict-of-laws rule. Was that correct?
o: No, because the court had to apply Delaware's choice-of-law rules.
Yes, because choice of law is procedural and governed by federal common law.
Yes, because New York law governs a contract made and performed in New York.
No, because prejudgment interest is governed by the law of the forum state.
oe: Klaxon: a federal court sitting in diversity applies the forum state's conflict-of-laws rules. Otherwise federal and state courts in the same state could choose different governing law, recreating the forum shopping Erie forbids.
Choice-of-law rules are treated as substantive for Erie purposes.
Which state's law governs is decided by Delaware's choice-of-law rules, not the federal court's independent judgment.
Right result, wrong reason. Delaware's choice-of-law rules, not a categorical forum-law rule, decide the question.
topic: Wk 7 · From Swift to Erie — Forum state's choice-of-law rules

q: An employee sued his employer in federal court under a federal employment statute and added a related state-law claim for breach of an implied employment contract. The parties are citizens of the same state. On the state claim, the federal judge proposes to apply what she considers the better general-law rule on implied contracts rather than the rule followed by the state's highest court. Is that proper?
o: No, because Erie governs every state-law claim in federal court.
Yes, because Erie applies only when jurisdiction rests on diversity of citizenship.
Yes, because the federal claim gives the court power to develop federal common law for related claims.
No, because federal courts may not hear state-law claims in federal-question cases.
oe: Erie governs any state-law claim in federal court, including supplemental claims in federal-question cases, not just diversity cases. Forgetting this is one of the classic Erie traps.
Erie applies whenever a federal court decides a state-law claim.
Supplemental jurisdiction gives the court power to hear the claim, not to change the law governing it.
Federal courts hear related state claims under § 1367. The issue is which law governs them.
topic: Wk 7 · From Swift to Erie — Erie and supplemental state claims

q: A truck owned by an oil company injured a soldier. The United States paid his hospital bills and his salary while he was disabled, then sued the oil company in federal court to recover those costs. No federal statute creates such a claim, and the state where the accident occurred would allow it. Which statement best describes how the federal court should approach the case?
o: Federal law governs, but the court should hesitate to create a new federal right of recovery.
State law governs because Erie abolished all federal common law.
State law governs because the accident and injury occurred within that state's borders.
Federal law governs and supplies a recovery equal to what state law would provide.
oe: In Standard Oil, the Court held that federal law, not state law, governs the government's relationship with its soldiers, an area of uniquely federal interest. But it declined to create a new federal cause of action, leaving that fiscal-policy choice to Congress.
Erie abolished federal general common law. Specialized federal common law survives in areas of uniquely federal interest.
The place of the accident does not control when the claim concerns the federal government's own fiscal relationship with its soldiers.
Federal law governed, but the Court declined to create a federal right of recovery at all.
topic: Wk 7 · From Swift to Erie — Federal common law after Erie

q: A federal court in a diversity case must decide whether a state recognizes a claim for negligent infliction of emotional distress by a bystander who did not witness the accident. The state's highest court has never decided the question. Two of the state's intermediate appellate courts have reached opposite conclusions. The state permits its highest court to answer certified questions from federal courts. What should the federal court do?
o: Predict how the state's highest court would rule, or certify the question to it.
Apply the general common law, because state law on the question is unsettled.
Follow whichever intermediate appellate court sits closest to the federal courthouse.
Dismiss the claim, because a federal court may not decide an unsettled state-law question.
oe: When the state's highest court has not ruled, a federal court predicts how it would rule, considering intermediate decisions, dicta, other states, and treatises, or certifies the question where state law allows.
Unsettled state law does not license a federal court to apply its own general law. That was Swift.
Intermediate decisions are evidence of state law, but geography does not decide which one controls.
Federal courts decide unsettled state-law questions regularly by predicting the state high court's ruling.
topic: Wk 7 · From Swift to Erie — Finding state law

q: An Ohio citizen sued the Massachusetts executor of a driver's estate in federal court in Massachusetts on the basis of diversity, over an accident in South Carolina. The process server left the summons and complaint with the executor's wife at his home, as Rule 4(e)(2)(B) permits. A Massachusetts statute requires in-hand delivery to an executor within one year, and that year has passed, so the claim would be barred in state court. The executor moved for summary judgment, arguing that Erie requires the state rule. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because a valid Federal Rule directly covers the question.
Grant the motion, because applying the federal rule would change the outcome of the case.
Grant the motion, because statutes governing suits against estates are substantive.
Deny the motion, because the defendant actually received the papers.
oe: Hanna v. Plumer: when a Federal Rule is sufficiently broad to answer the question in dispute, the court applies it if it is valid under the Rules Enabling Act. Rule 4 really regulates procedure, so it governs, and York's outcome test does not apply at this step.
Outcome determination is the test for the unguided Erie choice, not for deciding whether a valid Federal Rule applies.
The Massachusetts statute may serve substantive purposes, but a valid Federal Rule that covers the point controls in federal court.
Right result, wrong reason. Receipt alone would not validate service. Service was valid because it complied with Rule 4(e)(2)(B), which governs.
topic: Wk 8 · The modern Erie analysis — Federal Rule on point: service

q: Noteholders sued a trustee in federal court on the basis of diversity, seeking equitable relief for breach of trust. The state's statute of limitations would bar the claim in state court, but under federal equity practice the claim would be timely because the delay was reasonable. No federal statute or Federal Rule addresses the question. Should the federal court apply the state limitations period?
o: Yes, because applying the federal practice would make the outcome depend on the choice of forum.
No, because the plaintiff sought equitable relief, which federal courts govern by their own principles.
No, because statutes of limitations are procedural rules.
Yes, because Rule 3 incorporates state limitations periods.
oe: Guaranty Trust v. York: in diversity cases the outcome in federal court should be substantially the same as in a state court a block away. A limitations rule that bars a claim in one court but not the other would encourage forum shopping.
York rejected that distinction. Equitable claims in diversity are subject to Erie like legal ones.
Labels do not control. For Erie purposes, limitations periods are treated as substantive because they decide whether a claim can be pursued at all.
Right result, wrong reason. Rule 3 says nothing about limitations. State law governs through the unguided Erie analysis.
topic: Wk 8 · The modern Erie analysis — Statutes of limitations

q: A plaintiff filed a diversity suit in federal court one week before the state's two-year limitations period expired and served the defendant 60 days later. Under state law, an action is not "commenced" for limitations purposes until the defendant is served. Rule 3 provides that a civil action is commenced by filing a complaint. The defendant moved to dismiss as time-barred. How should the court rule?
o: Grant the motion, because state law decides when the action was commenced for limitations.
Deny the motion, because Rule 3 directly conflicts with the state rule and controls.
Deny the motion, because the plaintiff served within the 90 days allowed by Rule 4(m).
Deny the motion, because federal tolling rules govern claims heard in federal court.
oe: Walker v. Armco: Rule 3 governs the date from which the Federal Rules' timing requirements run. It is not sufficiently broad to control state tolling, so there is no direct collision. Under the unguided Erie choice, the state rule applies, and the claim is barred.
There is no direct collision. Rule 3 was not intended to toll state limitations periods.
Rule 4(m) sets a deadline for service but does not affect when a state claim is commenced for limitations purposes.
In diversity cases, state tolling rules are substantive for Erie purposes, as Walker held.
topic: Wk 8 · The modern Erie analysis — When a Rule is not sufficiently broad

q: A lineman injured while building power lines sued an electric cooperative in federal court on the basis of diversity. The cooperative argued that it was the lineman's statutory employer under the state's workers' compensation law and therefore immune from tort liability. In state court, a judge, not a jury, would decide the disputed factual question of statutory-employer status. The state practice is not tied to the definition of the workers' compensation rights themselves. In the federal case, who should decide the disputed fact question?
o: The jury, because the federal interest in jury fact-finding outweighs the state's allocation to the judge.
The judge, because applying a different procedure in federal court could change the outcome.
The judge, because workers' compensation immunity is a matter of state substantive law.
The jury, because Rule 38 expressly allocates all factual disputes in diversity cases to juries.
oe: Byrd v. Blue Ridge: when a state rule is not bound up with state-created rights and obligations, the strong federal policy favoring jury fact-finding, informed by the Seventh Amendment, can outweigh an uncertain effect on outcome.
Outcome determination is not the end of the analysis. Byrd added a balancing of countervailing federal interests.
The immunity is substantive, but who decides the fact question is a matter of federal court procedure that implicates strong federal interests.
Right result, wrong reason. No Federal Rule decided this allocation. Byrd resolved it through the unguided Erie analysis and balancing.
topic: Wk 8 · The modern Erie analysis — Judge-jury allocation

q: A medical practice brought a class action in federal court, under the Class Action Fairness Act's diversity provisions, against an insurer to recover statutory interest that state law imposes on overdue insurance payments. A state procedural statute bars class actions to recover statutory penalties unless the statute imposing the penalty authorizes class recovery, and this one does not. Rule 23 sets out when a class action may be maintained. Should the federal court allow the class action?
o: Yes, because Rule 23 directly answers whether a class action may be maintained and is valid.
No, because applying Rule 23 would allow recoveries unavailable in state court and encourage forum shopping.
No, because the state statute is part of the state's definition of the statutory-interest remedy.
Yes, because the Class Action Fairness Act expressly preempts all state class-action rules.
oe: Shady Grove: Rule 23 answers the same question as the state statute, so they directly collide, and Rule 23 really regulates procedure. Justice Stevens's controlling concurrence would not apply a Rule that displaces a state rule defining the scope of a state right, but found the state statute was not such a rule.
Forum shopping is the concern of the unguided Erie choice. When a valid Rule is on point, the Rules Enabling Act analysis governs instead.
That was the dissent's view. The controlling opinions concluded that the statute was a procedural rule that applied to all claims, including federal ones.
Right result, wrong reason. CAFA provides jurisdiction. It was Rule 23 that governed the availability of the class action.
topic: Wk 8 · The modern Erie analysis — Class actions and a state bar

q: A federal court in a diversity case must decide whether to apply a Federal Rule of Civil Procedure or a conflicting state rule. The judge begins by asking whether applying the Federal Rule would encourage forum shopping. What is wrong with that approach?
o: It skips the question whether the Rule covers the issue and is valid.
The first question is whether the state rule is labeled procedural or substantive by the state legislature.
The court should ask only whether applying the Federal Rule would change the outcome.
Nothing, because forum shopping is the first consideration in an Erie analysis.
oe: When a Federal Rule is on point, Hanna directs the court to the Rules Enabling Act analysis. The twin-aims and outcome tests apply only to the unguided choice when no federal statute or Rule is on point. Applying York to a Rule on point is the classic trap.
State labels do not control the federal analysis.
That is York's outcome test, which Hanna held does not govern when a valid Rule is on point.
Forum shopping is considered only at the second step, after concluding no federal statute or Rule is on point.
topic: Wk 8 · The modern Erie analysis — The classic trap

q: A state statute requires a shareholder who brings a derivative suit to post a bond securing the corporation's expenses if the suit fails. A shareholder brought a derivative suit in federal court on the basis of diversity. No federal statute or Federal Rule addresses security for expenses, and the federal courts' own practice requires no bond. Should the federal court require the bond?
o: Yes, because ignoring it would encourage plaintiffs to file in federal court to avoid the bond.
No, because bonds are procedural and federal courts follow their own procedures.
No, because Rule 23.1 governs derivative suits and does not require a bond.
Yes, because state statutes control over federal practice in diversity cases.
oe: With no federal statute or Rule on point, the court makes the unguided Erie choice. Judged from the plaintiff's position when choosing a forum, a federal practice that lets a plaintiff avoid a significant cost would encourage forum shopping, so state law applies (as in Cohen v. Beneficial).
Labels do not decide the unguided Erie choice. The twin aims do.
Rule 23.1 addresses pleading requirements in derivative suits, not security for expenses. It is not sufficiently broad to collide with the state statute.
Right result, wrong reason. State law prevails only when the twin aims or Byrd balancing point that way. A valid Federal Rule or statute would prevail over state law.
topic: Wk 8 · The modern Erie analysis — Judge-made practice and twin aims

q: A dealer sued a manufacturer in federal court in Alabama on the basis of diversity. Their contract had a clause selecting the courts of New York. Alabama courts refuse to enforce forum-selection clauses. The manufacturer moved to transfer the case to the Southern District of New York under § 1404(a). Does Alabama's policy control?
o: No, because a valid federal statute that covers the question governs.
Yes, because the enforceability of contract clauses is a question of state substantive law.
Yes, because applying federal law would encourage forum shopping by manufacturers.
No, because Alabama's policy violates the Full Faith and Credit Clause.
oe: Stewart Organization v. Ricoh: § 1404(a) is sufficiently broad to control the decision to transfer, including the weight given a forum-selection clause. A federal statute on point applies if it is constitutional, and § 1404(a) is.
Enforceability might be state law in other contexts, but the federal transfer statute governs whether to transfer.
The twin-aims test applies only when no federal statute or Rule is on point.
Right result, wrong reason. The federal statute governs. Nothing turns on full faith and credit.
topic: Wk 8 · The modern Erie analysis — Federal statute on point

q: A state statute directs courts to order a new trial when a jury's damages award "deviates materially from what would be reasonable compensation," a more searching standard than the federal "shocks the conscience" test. In a diversity case, the jury awarded $450,000. Which standard should the federal district court apply to the defendant's motion for a new trial on the ground that the award is excessive?
o: The state's deviates-materially standard.
The federal shocks-the-conscience standard, because new-trial motions are procedural.
Neither, because the Seventh Amendment bars any review of a jury's damages award.
The federal standard, because Rule 59 directly conflicts with the state statute.
oe: In Gasperini v. Center for Humanities, the Court held that the state standard for reviewing excessive verdicts is substantive for Erie purposes and must be applied by the district court, in a way consistent with the Seventh Amendment.
Gasperini held that the state's limit on damages, implemented through its review standard, is substantive.
Trial judges may grant new trials on excessive damages. The Seventh Amendment limits re-examination by appellate courts, not trial-court review.
Gasperini found no direct collision with Rule 59, which does not set the standard for excessiveness.
topic: Wk 8 · The modern Erie analysis — Reviewing excessive verdicts

q: In a diversity negligence case, state law places on the defendant the burden of proving the plaintiff's contributory negligence. The federal judge believes it would be more efficient to require the plaintiff to prove her own freedom from fault. No Federal Rule addresses the issue. Who bears the burden of proof on contributory negligence?
o: The defendant, because the burden of proof on an element or defense is governed by state law.
The plaintiff, because federal judges control the allocation of proof in their own courtrooms.
The defendant, but only if the state burden is codified in a statute.
The plaintiff, because Rule 8(c) requires plaintiffs to negate affirmative defenses.
oe: Burdens of proof are treated as substantive for Erie purposes. Shifting the burden could change outcomes and invite forum shopping, and no Federal Rule is on point.
Judges control the order of proof, but not the burden on a state-law element or defense.
State decisional law is state law. Codification is irrelevant after Erie.
Rule 8(c) requires defendants to plead affirmative defenses. It does not allocate burdens to plaintiffs.
topic: Wk 8 · The modern Erie analysis — Burdens of proof

q: In applying the unguided Erie analysis to a judge-made federal practice that differs from state law, a court notes that the difference would affect the outcome of this particular case, because the defendant waited until the end of the case to raise it. From what perspective should the court assess whether the difference would encourage forum shopping?
o: From the plaintiff's position at the time of choosing the forum.
From the defendant's position when it raised the issue.
From the court's position at the end of the case.
From the state legislature's position when it enacted the rule.
oe: Hanna said the outcome-determination test must be read through the twin aims, judged when the plaintiff chooses a forum. Almost any rule can be outcome-determinative after the fact, so hindsight is not the test.
The question is whether the difference would lead plaintiffs to choose federal court, which is assessed when the forum is chosen.
Hindsight makes almost every rule outcome-determinative. Hanna rejected that approach.
Legislative purpose bears on whether a rule is bound up with state rights under Byrd, but not on the forum-shopping inquiry.
topic: Wk 8 · The modern Erie analysis — Twin aims judged at the forum choice

q: A state statute caps noneconomic damages in medical-malpractice actions at $500,000. A patient sued a doctor in federal court on the basis of diversity, and the jury awarded $1,200,000 in noneconomic damages. No Federal Rule or federal statute addresses damages caps. What should the court do?
o: Reduce the award to $500,000, because the cap is substantive state law.
Enter judgment for $1,200,000, because the Seventh Amendment protects the jury's assessment of damages.
Order a new trial, because the jury was not instructed about the cap.
Enter judgment for $1,200,000, because federal courts set their own measure of damages.
oe: A cap on damages defines the extent of the state-created right. Ignoring it in federal court would encourage forum shopping and inequitable administration of the laws.
A legislative cap on recoverable damages does not violate the jury right in federal diversity cases; it defines the remedy the state allows.
The cap is applied by the court after the verdict. No new trial is needed.
There is no federal general law of damages for state claims.
topic: Wk 8 · The modern Erie analysis — Damages caps

q: A defendant in a diversity case argues that Rule 35, which allows a court to order a party's medical examination, is invalid as applied because the state where the court sits forbids compelled medical examinations of plaintiffs. Which statement best describes the test for the Rule's validity?
o: The Rule is valid if it really regulates procedure.
The Rule is invalid if applying it would change the outcome of the case.
The Rule is invalid whenever it conflicts with a state rule, because Erie requires state law in diversity cases.
The Rule is valid only if the forum state's legislature or high court has approved it.
oe: The Rules Enabling Act forbids Rules that abridge, enlarge, or modify substantive rights. The Court asks whether a Rule really regulates procedure, the judicial process for enforcing rights. Rule 35 was upheld in Sibbach, and no Rule has ever been held invalid.
Outcome determination is not the test of a Rule's validity.
A valid Federal Rule on point applies in diversity cases notwithstanding a conflicting state rule.
The Federal Rules are promulgated under the Rules Enabling Act by the Supreme Court and Congress. States play no role.
topic: Wk 8 · The modern Erie analysis — Validity under the Rules Enabling Act

q: Subscribers sued the four largest regional internet providers under § 1 of the Sherman Act, which prohibits agreements in restraint of trade. The complaint alleged that none of the providers entered the others' territories even though doing so would have been profitable, and that "upon information and belief, defendants entered into a contract, combination, or conspiracy to divide markets." It alleged no meetings, communications, or other facts suggesting an actual agreement. The providers moved to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6). How should the court rule?
o: Grant the motion, because the facts alleged are just as consistent with independent business decisions.
Deny the motion, because the court must accept as true the allegation that the defendants conspired.
Deny the motion, because the plaintiffs might prove some set of facts showing an agreement.
Grant the motion, because antitrust conspiracies must be pleaded with particularity under Rule 9(b).
oe: Twombly: the bare allegation of a conspiracy is a legal conclusion. Parallel conduct is merely consistent with an agreement and has an obvious alternative explanation, independent decisions to avoid costly expansion, so the claim is not plausible.
Only well-pleaded factual allegations are assumed true. A conclusory allegation of agreement is not entitled to that assumption.
Twombly retired Conley's "no set of facts" language.
Right result, wrong reason. Rule 9(b) applies to fraud and mistake. The standard here is ordinary plausibility under Rule 8(a)(2).
topic: Wk 9 · Pleading & Rule 11 — Parallel conduct without more

q: A detainee sued two senior federal officials, alleging that they "knew of, condoned, and willfully and maliciously agreed" to subject him to harsh conditions "solely on account of his religion and national origin," and that one of them was the "principal architect" of the policy. The complaint's only other factual allegation was that thousands of men of the detainee's religion and national origin were detained after a terrorist attack by men of the same background. The officials moved to dismiss. How should the court rule?
o: Grant the motion, because the complaint does not plausibly allege discriminatory purpose.
Deny the motion, because Rule 9(b) allows malice and intent to be alleged generally.
Deny the motion, because the plausibility standard applies only in antitrust cases.
Grant the motion, because the plaintiff did not attach evidence supporting his allegations.
oe: Iqbal's first step sets aside the bare assertions of discriminatory intent. At the second step, the detentions are more likely explained by a legitimate policy of holding people with possible links to the attacks, so purposeful discrimination is not plausible.
"Generally" in Rule 9(b) relieves the pleader of particularity. It does not permit conclusory allegations that fall short of plausibility.
Iqbal held that Twombly's standard governs all civil actions.
Right result, wrong reason. A plaintiff need not plead or attach evidence. The problem is the absence of factual allegations making discrimination plausible.
topic: Wk 9 · Pleading & Rule 11 — Conclusory allegations of intent

q: In 1957, Black railroad employees sued their union, alleging that the railroad abolished 45 jobs held by Black workers and that the union, their exclusive bargaining agent, refused to protect them because of their race. The union moved to dismiss, arguing that the complaint did not set out specific facts supporting the general allegation of discrimination. Under the standard announced at that time, how should the court have ruled?
o: Deny the motion, because the complaint gave fair notice of the claim and the grounds on which it rested.
Grant the motion, because the complaint did not plead facts making discrimination probable.
Grant the motion, because discrimination claims must be pleaded with particularity.
Deny the motion, because a court may not rule on the sufficiency of a complaint before discovery.
oe: Conley v. Gibson adopted notice pleading: a short and plain statement giving fair notice suffices, and dismissal is proper only if the plaintiff can prove no set of facts entitling him to relief. Twombly later retired the "no set of facts" language.
No pleading standard, then or now, requires facts showing that liability is probable.
Rule 9(b) applies only to fraud and mistake, and courts may not add categories on their own.
Right result, wrong reason. Courts decide Rule 12(b)(6) motions before discovery. This complaint simply satisfied the standard.
topic: Wk 9 · Pleading & Rule 11 — Notice pleading era

q: A tenant sued a landlord for breach of the warranty of habitability, alleging that for three winters the heat in her apartment failed for weeks at a time, that she reported the failures in writing at least six times, and that the landlord made no repairs. The landlord moved to dismiss, submitting an affidavit from its superintendent stating that the heat always worked, and arguing that the tenant is unlikely to win. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because the factual allegations must be taken as true and plausibly show a breach.
Grant the motion, because the superintendent's affidavit contradicts the complaint.
Grant the motion, because plausibility requires a showing that the plaintiff is likely to prevail.
Deny the motion, because a 12(b)(6) motion may not be filed in a landlord-tenant case.
oe: On a Rule 12(b)(6) motion the court takes well-pleaded facts as true, draws reasonable inferences for the plaintiff, and does not weigh credibility or the likelihood of success. These specific allegations make a breach plausible.
The court does not resolve factual disputes on a 12(b)(6) motion. If it considers the affidavit, it must convert the motion to one for summary judgment under Rule 12(d).
Plausible means more than a sheer possibility, but it does not mean probable.
Rule 12(b)(6) applies in all civil actions.
topic: Wk 9 · Pleading & Rule 11 — What remains true after Iqbal

q: A court granted a Rule 12(b)(6) motion because the plaintiff's negligence complaint alleged in conclusory terms that the defendant "failed to use reasonable care," without any facts about what the defendant did. Nothing suggests that the plaintiff acted in bad faith or that amendment would be futile. The plaintiff has not amended before. What is the most likely disposition?
o: Dismissal with leave to amend.
Dismissal with prejudice, because a complaint that fails to state a claim may not be refiled.
Conversion to a motion for summary judgment.
Dismissal without prejudice to refiling in state court only.
oe: Dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6) for insufficient factual allegations is usually with leave to amend, because Rule 15(a)(2) directs that leave be freely given when justice so requires.
Dismissal with prejudice is reserved for cases where amendment would be futile or the plaintiff has repeatedly failed to cure.
Conversion is required only when the court considers matters outside the pleadings, which it did not.
A Rule 12(b)(6) ruling concerns the complaint's sufficiency, not which court system may hear the claim.
topic: Wk 9 · Pleading & Rule 11 — Leave to amend after dismissal

q: A buyer sued a seller, alleging that the seller "made numerous false statements about the condition of the property to induce the sale, knowing they were false." The complaint did not identify what statements were made, by whom, or when. The seller moved to dismiss. How should the court rule?
o: Grant the motion, because the circumstances of the alleged fraud were not stated with particularity.
Deny the motion, because knowledge and intent may be alleged generally under Rule 9(b).
Deny the motion, because the plausibility standard does not apply to fraud claims.
Grant the motion, because fraud claims must be proved by clear and convincing evidence.
oe: Rule 9(b) requires a party alleging fraud to state the circumstances constituting it with particularity: who said what, when, where, and how. Knowledge may be alleged generally, but the false statements themselves may not.
That is true of conditions of mind, but the circumstances of the fraud must still be particular.
Plausibility applies to all claims. Fraud claims must also meet Rule 9(b)'s particularity requirement.
That may be the burden of proof at trial, but it has nothing to do with the sufficiency of the pleading.
topic: Wk 9 · Pleading & Rule 11 — Pleading fraud with particularity

q: A contractor sued a homeowner for the unpaid contract price, alleging that "all conditions precedent to payment have been performed or have occurred." The homeowner's answer stated: "Defendant denies that all conditions precedent have occurred." The contract required an architect's certificate before final payment, and none was issued. The contractor moved to strike the denial as insufficient. How should the court rule?
o: Grant the motion, because a denial of conditions precedent must be made with particularity.
Deny the motion, because a general denial is sufficient to put conditions precedent in issue.
Grant the motion, because the contractor's general allegation of conditions precedent was insufficient.
Deny the motion, because conditions precedent are affirmative defenses that need not be pleaded.
oe: Rule 9(c) allows a party to allege generally that conditions precedent have occurred, but a denial must be made with particularity. The homeowner should have identified the missing architect's certificate.
Rule 9(c) requires particularity for denials of conditions precedent, even though allegations may be general.
Rule 9(c) expressly permits conditions precedent to be alleged generally.
The point is how to deny a pleaded condition. Rule 9(c) requires particularity.
topic: Wk 9 · Pleading & Rule 11 — Conditions precedent and special damages

q: A federal district court adopted a rule requiring that civil-rights complaints against municipalities plead specific facts showing a municipal policy with particularity, beyond what Rule 8(a) requires. A plaintiff's complaint against a city satisfied Rule 8(a) and plausibility but not the court's heightened standard. Should the court dismiss?
o: No, because only the Federal Rules or a statute may impose heightened pleading requirements.
Yes, because district courts may adopt local rules governing pleading.
Yes, because claims against government entities deserve extra protection from discovery.
No, because municipal liability claims may be alleged generally under Rule 9(b).
oe: Leatherman held that courts may not impose heightened pleading for categories of claims not listed in Rule 9(b). Changes must come through rulemaking or legislation.
Local rules must be consistent with the Federal Rules (Rule 83). A heightened standard contradicts Rule 8(a).
That policy concern supported the heightened standard, but Leatherman held courts lack the power to adopt it.
Right result, wrong reason. Rule 9(b) does not address municipal liability. The claim is governed by Rule 8(a).
topic: Wk 9 · Pleading & Rule 11 — Courts may not add heightened pleading

q: A passenger injured in a two-car collision sued both drivers. Count I alleged that the first driver's negligence caused the accident. Count II alleged that the second driver's negligence caused it. Count III alleged that the first driver acted intentionally. The defendants moved to dismiss because the counts are inconsistent. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because a party may plead alternative and inconsistent claims.
Grant the motion, because a pleader certifies under Rule 11 that its allegations are true.
Grant the motion as to Count III, because negligence and intent cannot be alleged against the same driver.
Deny the motion, but require the plaintiff to elect one theory before discovery.
oe: Rule 8(d)(2)-(3) lets a party set out claims alternatively or hypothetically and state as many claims as it has, regardless of consistency. The plaintiff need not choose a theory before discovery.
Rule 11 requires evidentiary support or a reasonable likelihood of it, not certainty. Alternative pleading is expressly allowed when the pleader does not know which version is true.
Rule 8(d) permits inconsistent theories against the same defendant.
No election is required at the pleading stage.
topic: Wk 9 · Pleading & Rule 11 — Alternative and inconsistent pleading

q: A plaintiff's complaint was a single unbroken page of narrative with no paragraph numbers, no caption identifying the court, and claims for breach of contract and for an unrelated assault run together. It attached the contract as an exhibit. Which statement about the complaint is correct?
o: It violates Rule 10, but the attached contract is part of the pleading for all purposes.
It is proper, because Rule 8 requires only a short and plain statement of the claim.
It violates Rule 10, and the attached contract must be disregarded on a motion to dismiss.
It must be dismissed with prejudice, because defects of form cannot be cured.
oe: Rule 10 requires a caption, numbered paragraphs, and separate counts for claims founded on separate transactions where that promotes clarity. Under Rule 10(c), a written instrument attached as an exhibit is part of the pleading.
Rule 8 sets the content standard. Rule 10 separately prescribes form.
An exhibit attached to a pleading is part of it and may be considered without converting the motion.
Form defects are curable by amendment.
topic: Wk 9 · Pleading & Rule 11 — Form of pleadings

q: Before filing a complaint alleging that a manufacturer's ladder had a design defect, the plaintiff's lawyer spoke only to the plaintiff, who said the ladder "just collapsed." The lawyer did not inspect the ladder, which was available, or consult anyone. The lawyer sincerely believed the claim was valid. The complaint did not state that any allegation would likely have support after discovery. Which is the strongest basis for sanctions?
o: The lawyer's factual inquiry was not reasonable under the circumstances.
The lawyer filed the complaint to harass the manufacturer and drive up its costs.
The lawyer's legal theory, design defect, is not recognized by existing law.
The lawyer subjectively believed the claim was valid, which Rule 11 does not permit.
oe: Rule 11(b) certifies that factual contentions have evidentiary support, formed after a reasonable inquiry. The standard is objective, so the lawyer's sincere belief is no defense when an available ladder went uninspected.
Nothing suggests an improper purpose. The defect is the lack of a reasonable factual inquiry.
Design-defect claims are well recognized. The problem is factual, not legal.
Subjective belief is not prohibited. It simply does not excuse an objectively unreasonable inquiry.
topic: Wk 9 · Pleading & Rule 11 — Rule 11 factual certification

q: A defendant believed that one count of the complaint was legally frivolous. On May 1, it served the plaintiff with a separate Rule 11 motion for sanctions but did not file it. On May 15, the plaintiff withdrew the challenged count. On May 25, the defendant filed the motion anyway. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because the plaintiff withdrew the count within 21 days after service.
Grant the motion, because the count was frivolous when it was filed.
Grant the motion, because the defendant served the motion before filing it.
Deny the motion, because Rule 11 motions must be included in the answer.
oe: Rule 11(c)(2)'s safe harbor requires that a sanctions motion be served 21 days before filing, and the motion may not be filed if the challenged paper is withdrawn or corrected within that time.
The safe harbor protects a party that withdraws the offending paper within 21 days, even if it was frivolous when filed.
Serving first is necessary, but the motion may not be filed if the paper is withdrawn within the 21 days.
