A Rule 11 motion must be made separately from any other motion or pleading.
topic: Wk 9 · Pleading & Rule 11 — Safe harbor

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the defendant never served a motion. Instead, on May 1 the court on its own issued an order directing the plaintiff's lawyer to show cause why the count does not violate Rule 11. The plaintiff withdrew the count on May 10. May the court still impose a sanction?
o: Yes, because the safe harbor does not protect against a show-cause order.
No, because the plaintiff withdrew the count within 21 days of the order.
No, because only a party may initiate Rule 11 proceedings.
Yes, and the court may order the plaintiff to pay the defendant's attorney's fees.
oe: The 21-day safe harbor applies only to motions by parties. A court acting by show-cause order under Rule 11(c)(3) may still sanction, though monetary sanctions are limited.
Withdrawal within 21 days protects only against a party's motion.
Rule 11(c)(3) expressly allows the court to act on its own initiative.
On the court's initiative, fees to the opposing party are not available. They may be awarded only on motion.
topic: Wk 9 · Pleading & Rule 11 — Court's own initiative
pre: A defendant believed that one count of the complaint was legally frivolous. On May 1, it served the plaintiff with a separate Rule 11 motion for sanctions but did not file it. On May 15, the plaintiff withdrew the challenged count. On May 25, the defendant filed the motion anyway. How should the court rule?

q: A court found that a complaint's legal contention was frivolous in violation of Rule 11(b)(2). The plaintiff, who is represented by counsel, relied entirely on the lawyer's legal advice. Which sanction is not permitted?
o: A monetary sanction against the represented plaintiff herself.
A monetary penalty paid into court by the plaintiff's lawyer.
A sanction imposed jointly on the law firm that employs the lawyer.
A nonmonetary directive requiring the lawyer to attend training.
oe: Rule 11(c)(5)(A) bars monetary sanctions against a represented party for violating Rule 11(b)(2). Legal contentions are the lawyer's responsibility.
Monetary penalties paid into court are an authorized sanction against the lawyer.
Absent exceptional circumstances, the law firm must be held jointly responsible for its lawyer's violation.
Nonmonetary directives are expressly authorized, so long as they are limited to what suffices to deter repetition.
topic: Wk 9 · Pleading & Rule 11 — Limits on monetary sanctions

q: During discovery, a party served interrogatory answers that were evasive and had no factual basis. The opposing party moved for sanctions under Rule 11. How should the court rule on the Rule 11 motion?
o: Deny it, because Rule 11 does not apply to discovery responses.
Grant it, because papers served in a case must comply with Rule 11.
Grant it, because evasive answers are presented for an improper purpose.
Deny it, because the movant did not wait 21 days after service.
oe: Rule 11(d) provides that Rule 11 does not apply to disclosures and discovery requests, responses, objections, and motions under Rules 26 through 37. Those rules have their own certification and sanction provisions.
Discovery papers are expressly excluded from Rule 11.
Evasive answers may be sanctionable, but under the discovery rules, not Rule 11.
Right result, wrong reason. The safe harbor is irrelevant because Rule 11 does not reach discovery at all.
topic: Wk 9 · Pleading & Rule 11 — Rule 11 and discovery

q: A plaintiff suing her former employer for age discrimination believes, based on comments from co-workers, that her supervisor replaced her with a much younger worker, but she lacks documentation. Which way of pleading the allegation best complies with Rule 11(b)(3)?
o: Allege the replacement, identifying it as likely to have support after discovery.
Allege the replacement as an established fact without qualification.
Omit the allegation until she obtains documentation through discovery.
Allege the replacement and attach the co-workers' unsworn statements as exhibits.
oe: Rule 11(b)(3) permits factual contentions that, if specifically so identified, will likely have evidentiary support after a reasonable opportunity for investigation or discovery.
Without supporting evidence or a specific identification, an unqualified allegation risks violating Rule 11(b)(3).
She may plead it now if she identifies it as likely to have support after discovery. Omitting an element could make the complaint deficient.
Attaching statements is not required and does not substitute for the certification Rule 11 requires.
topic: Wk 9 · Pleading & Rule 11 — Factual contentions likely to have support

q: A legislator proposes amending the Federal Rules to restore Conley's notice-pleading standard. Which argument best supports the proposal?
o: Plausibility pleading burdens plaintiffs who lack access to facts the defendants hold.
Plausibility pleading increases the cost of discovery in antitrust cases.
Plausibility pleading requires plaintiffs to plead their legal theories.
Plausibility pleading applies only in federal-question cases, not in diversity cases.
oe: Critics argue that plausibility forces plaintiffs to plead facts they can learn only through discovery, especially in civil-rights and antitrust cases, and that the judicial-experience-and-common-sense test invites subjectivity.
The opposite: Twombly adopted plausibility partly to screen out weak claims before costly discovery.
Neither standard requires pleading legal theories.
Plausibility applies in all civil actions in federal court.
topic: Wk 9 · Pleading & Rule 11 — Plausibility debate

q: A defendant served with a federal complaint filed a pre-answer motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim. The court denied it. The defendant then answered, raising lack of personal jurisdiction and failure to state a claim. Shortly before trial, it moved to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. Which of these defenses remain available?
o: Failure to state a claim and lack of subject-matter jurisdiction only.
All three, because each was raised before trial began.
Only lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, because the court already rejected failure to state a claim.
Lack of personal jurisdiction and failure to state a claim, but not subject-matter jurisdiction.
oe: Personal jurisdiction was waived because it was left out of the first Rule 12 motion (Rule 12(g)(2), (h)(1)). Failure to state a claim is preserved through trial (Rule 12(h)(2)), and subject-matter jurisdiction may be raised at any time (Rule 12(h)(3)).
Personal jurisdiction must be raised in the first Rule 12 motion if one is made. Raising it in the later answer was too late.
Failure to state a claim may be raised again in a Rule 12(c) motion or at trial.
Subject-matter jurisdiction can never be waived. Personal jurisdiction can.
topic: Wk 9 · Responding to the complaint — The classic waiver sequence

q: A defendant was served on March 1 and filed a Rule 12(b)(6) motion on March 15. The court denied the motion on May 1. When is the defendant's answer due?
o: May 15, 14 days after notice of the court's denial.
March 22, 21 days after service, because the motion did not suspend the answer deadline.
May 22, 21 days after the court's denial.
May 31, 30 days after the court's denial.
oe: Rule 12(a)(4)(A) provides that a Rule 12 motion alters the time to serve a responsive pleading. If the court denies the motion, the answer is due 14 days after notice of the court's action.
Serving a Rule 12 motion suspends the time to answer.
After denial, the defendant gets 14 days, not a fresh 21.
No 30-day period applies. The deadline is 14 days after notice of the denial.
topic: Wk 9 · Responding to the complaint — Time to answer after a motion

q: Which defendant's answer is due latest, measured from the triggering event described?
o: A defendant in Germany who waived service, 90 days after the request was sent.
A defendant in Ohio who was personally served, 21 days after service.
A federal agency, 60 days after service on the United States attorney.
A defendant in Ohio who waived service, 60 days after the request was sent.
oe: Rule 12(a)(1)(A)(ii) gives a defendant who timely waived service 60 days after the request was sent, or 90 days if the defendant was addressed outside the United States.
Personally served defendants get 21 days.
The United States and its agencies get 60 days, which is less than 90.
Domestic waiving defendants get 60 days. Foreign ones get 90.
topic: Wk 9 · Responding to the complaint — Initial response times

q: A defendant filed a pre-answer motion to dismiss for insufficient service of process, which the court denied. Before answering, the defendant filed a second pre-answer motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim. The plaintiff argued that the second motion was improper. Which is correct?
o: The second motion is improper, but the defense is not waived.
The second motion is proper, because failure to state a claim is not waived.
The defense of failure to state a claim is waived for the rest of the case.
The second motion is proper, because the first motion raised only a service defense.
oe: Rule 12(g)(2) bars a second Rule 12 motion raising a defense available when the first was made. Failure to state a claim is not waived, though; Rule 12(h)(2) preserves it for a pleading, a 12(c) motion, or trial.
The defense is not waived, but it may not be raised in a second pre-answer motion.
Rule 12(h)(2) preserves it, even though it may not be raised by a successive pre-answer motion.
The rule bars successive motions on any defense that was available when the first motion was made.
topic: Wk 9 · Responding to the complaint — Second pre-answer motion

q: In a single pre-answer motion, a defendant argued that the court lacked personal jurisdiction, that venue was improper, and that the complaint failed to state a claim. The plaintiff argued that by including merits arguments, the defendant submitted to the court's jurisdiction and waived its objections. Is the plaintiff correct?
o: No, because no defense is waived by joining it with other defenses in one motion.
Yes, because arguing the merits is a general appearance that waives personal jurisdiction.
Yes, as to venue only, because venue must be raised in a separate motion.
No, because personal jurisdiction is not a waivable defense.
oe: Rule 12(b) provides that no defense or objection is waived by joining it with one or more other defenses or objections in a responsive pleading or motion.
The Federal Rules abolished the special-appearance trap. Joining defenses in one motion waives none of them.
All Rule 12(b) defenses may be raised in a single motion.
Right result, wrong reason. Personal jurisdiction can be waived, but not by joining it with other defenses.
topic: Wk 9 · Responding to the complaint — Joining defenses waives none

q: A defendant moved to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), attaching a deposition from an earlier lawsuit that it argued disproved the plaintiff's allegations. The court considered the deposition and granted the motion without giving the plaintiff a chance to respond with her own evidence. Was this proper?
o: No, because the motion had to be treated as one for summary judgment.
Yes, because a court may consider any sworn testimony on a motion to dismiss.
Yes, because the deposition was taken under oath in an earlier case.
No, because a court may consider only the complaint itself on a motion to dismiss.
oe: Rule 12(d): if matters outside the pleadings are presented and not excluded on a 12(b)(6) or 12(c) motion, the motion must be treated as one for summary judgment under Rule 56, and all parties must have a reasonable opportunity to present pertinent material.
Sworn testimony outside the pleadings converts the motion. The court must then follow Rule 56 procedures.
Its reliability does not change the rule. It is still a matter outside the pleadings.
Courts may consider exhibits attached to the complaint, or may consider outside matters if they convert the motion.
topic: Wk 9 · Responding to the complaint — Matters outside the pleadings

q: After the pleadings closed in a contract case, the defendant realized that the complaint, taken as true, failed to allege any consideration for the promise sued on. The defendant had not raised this in its answer. What is the defendant's best procedural vehicle?
o: A motion for judgment on the pleadings under Rule 12(c).
A pre-answer motion under Rule 12(b)(6).
A motion for a more definite statement under Rule 12(e).
None, because the defense was waived when it was omitted from the answer.
oe: Rule 12(c) allows a motion for judgment on the pleadings after the pleadings close, and Rule 12(h)(2) expressly permits raising failure to state a claim that way.
A Rule 12(b) motion must be made before a responsive pleading. The defendant has already answered.
Rule 12(e) is for pleadings too vague to answer, and it must be made before responding.
Failure to state a claim is preserved through trial under Rule 12(h)(2).
topic: Wk 9 · Responding to the complaint — Judgment on the pleadings

q: A complaint against a company alleged, in a single paragraph, that "Defendant did wrong things to Plaintiff at various times and Plaintiff wants damages," and also included several paragraphs accusing the company's CEO of personal misconduct unrelated to the claim. Before answering, the company wants to respond. Which motions are appropriate?
o: A motion for a more definite statement and a motion to strike.
A motion for judgment on the pleadings and a motion for Rule 11 sanctions.
A Rule 12(b)(1) motion, because a vague complaint deprives the court of jurisdiction.
A motion for default, because the complaint fails to plead a claim.
oe: Rule 12(e) applies when a pleading is so vague or ambiguous that the party cannot reasonably prepare a response. Rule 12(f) allows striking redundant, immaterial, impertinent, or scandalous matter.
Rule 12(c) is available only after the pleadings are closed, and the company has not answered.
Vagueness is a pleading defect, not a jurisdictional one.
Default is entered against a defending party that fails to plead, not against a plaintiff whose complaint is deficient.
topic: Wk 9 · Responding to the complaint — More definite statement and striking matter

q: A worker was injured when a forklift driven by an employee struck him on a pier. His complaint alleged that the forklift was "owned, operated, and controlled" by Company A. In fact, Company A owned the forklift, but the driver worked for Company B, to which Company A had transferred its operations. Company A's answer generally denied the whole paragraph. By the time the truth emerged, the limitations period had run against Company B. What is the most likely consequence?
o: Company A will be treated as having admitted that the driver was its agent.
Company A's denial is effective, because the paragraph contained at least one false allegation.
The worker may now sue Company B, because the limitations period is tolled by any misleading pleading.
The worker's claim must be dismissed, because he sued the wrong defendant.
oe: Zielinski v. Philadelphia Piers: a general denial of a partly true paragraph did not fairly respond to its substance. Rule 8(b)(4) requires admitting the part that is true and denying the rest. The court treated the agency allegation as admitted and estopped Company A from denying it.
Partial falsity does not permit a blanket denial. The true parts must be admitted.
The court did not toll the period against Company B. It held Company A to an admission.
The court protected the worker from the consequences of Company A's misleading denial.
topic: Wk 9 · Responding to the complaint — Denial must fairly respond

q: A defendant's answer stated: "Defendant denies each and every allegation of the complaint." The complaint's first paragraph correctly alleged the defendant's state of incorporation and principal place of business, which the defendant knew to be accurate. Was the general denial proper?
o: No, because the defendant did not intend in good faith to deny every allegation.
Yes, because a defendant is entitled to put the plaintiff to its proof.
Yes, because allegations about jurisdiction need not be admitted or denied.
No, because general denials were abolished when the Federal Rules took effect.
oe: Rule 8(b)(3) permits a general denial only when the party intends in good faith to deny all the allegations, including the jurisdictional grounds. Otherwise it must deny specific paragraphs or deny all except those specifically admitted.
The Rules require denials to fairly respond to the substance of the allegations.
Rule 8(b)(3) expressly includes the grounds for jurisdiction among the allegations a general denial reaches.
Right result, wrong reason. General denials are still allowed when made in good faith.
topic: Wk 9 · Responding to the complaint — General denials

q: A complaint alleged that the defendant's delivery driver was on duty at the time of an accident. The defendant's answer stated that it "lacks knowledge or information sufficient to form a belief" about the allegation. The driver's time records are in the defendant's own files. How is the response likely to be treated?
o: As an admission, because the information is within the defendant's own knowledge or control.
As a denial, because Rule 8(b)(5) gives a lack-of-knowledge statement the effect of a denial.
As a motion for a more definite statement.
As an affirmative defense that the defendant must prove at trial.
oe: Rule 8(b)(5) treats a statement of insufficient knowledge as a denial, but courts reject it when the information is within the party's own knowledge or control, as the driver's time records are.
That is the general rule, but it does not apply when the party can easily learn the truth from its own records.
A lack-of-knowledge response is part of an answer, not a Rule 12(e) motion.
It is a response to an allegation, not an affirmative defense.
topic: Wk 9 · Responding to the complaint — Lack of knowledge

q: A complaint alleged that the defendant ran a red light and that the plaintiff suffered $80,000 in damages. The defendant's answer responded to every other paragraph but said nothing about these two allegations. At trial, what is the effect of the omission?
o: The red-light allegation is admitted, but the damages allegation is not.
Both allegations are admitted.
Neither allegation is admitted, because the plaintiff must prove every element at trial.
The defendant is in default as to both allegations.
oe: Rule 8(b)(6) treats an allegation, other than one relating to the amount of damages, as admitted if a responsive pleading is required and the allegation is not denied.
Allegations about the amount of damages are excepted from Rule 8(b)(6).
Unanswered allegations other than damages are admitted and need not be proved.
Default applies to a party that fails to plead or otherwise defend. This defendant answered.
topic: Wk 9 · Responding to the complaint — Failure to deny

q: A defendant answered a complaint and asserted the affirmative defense of release. Without any court order, the plaintiff filed a "reply to affirmative defenses" denying the release. Is the reply a permitted pleading?
o: No, because a reply to an answer is allowed only if the court orders one.
Yes, because a plaintiff must respond to an affirmative defense in a reply.
Yes, because a reply to an answer is permitted as of right.
No, because only defendants may file responsive pleadings.
oe: Rule 7(a) lists the only allowed pleadings: complaint, answer, answer to a counterclaim or crossclaim, third-party complaint, answer to a third-party complaint, and a reply to an answer if the court orders one.
Affirmative defenses in an answer are treated as denied or avoided without a reply (Rule 8(b)(6)).
Only a court-ordered reply is permitted.
Plaintiffs file responsive pleadings to counterclaims, and replies when ordered.
topic: Wk 9 · Responding to the complaint — Permitted pleadings

q: A borrower sued a lender for breach of a loan agreement. The lender's answer denied the allegations but did not mention that the borrower had signed a general release of all claims. At trial, the lender offered the release into evidence. The borrower objected. What is the most likely ruling?
o: The release is excluded, because release is an affirmative defense that the lender failed to plead.
The release is admitted, because a defendant may prove any fact that defeats the claim.
The release is admitted, because the borrower bears the burden of disproving release.
The release is excluded, because releases are void as against public policy.
oe: Rule 8(c) requires a party to affirmatively state release in its responsive pleading. An unpleaded affirmative defense is generally waived, subject to amendment under Rule 15.
An affirmative defense defeats the claim even if the allegations are true, and it must be pleaded to give notice.
The defendant usually bears the burden of proving an affirmative defense.
Releases are generally enforceable. The problem is the failure to plead it.
topic: Wk 9 · Responding to the complaint — Unpleaded affirmative defense

q: In a negligence action, which of the following must the defendant plead as an affirmative defense?
o: That the plaintiff's own negligence contributed to her injury.
That the defendant did not breach the duty of care.
That the defendant's conduct did not cause the plaintiff's injury.
That the plaintiff's damages are less than the amount claimed.
oe: Contributory negligence is listed in Rule 8(c)(1). An affirmative defense is an independent reason the defendant should win even if the plaintiff's allegations are true.
Denying breach contests an element of the plaintiff's claim. It is a denial, not an affirmative defense.
Causation is an element the plaintiff must prove. Denying it is a denial.
Disputing damages is a denial. Allegations of the amount of damages are not even deemed admitted if unanswered.
topic: Wk 9 · Responding to the complaint — Identifying an affirmative defense

q: A lender sued a borrower for $42,350 due on a promissory note, plus contractual interest computable from the note. The borrower, an adult, was properly served and never appeared or responded. The clerk entered the borrower's default. The lender submitted an affidavit of the amount due. Who may enter a default judgment?
o: The clerk, because the claim is for a sum certain against a defendant who has not appeared.
Only the court, because a default judgment requires a hearing.
The clerk, but only after giving the borrower 7 days' written notice.
No one, because a default judgment requires that the borrower first be personally served with the default.
oe: Rule 55(b)(1) lets the clerk enter judgment on the plaintiff's request, with an affidavit of the amount due, when the claim is for a sum certain or one that can be made certain by computation, against a defendant who has not appeared and is neither a minor nor incompetent.
A hearing is needed only when the court must determine damages or establish facts. The clerk may act on a sum certain.
The 7-day notice requirement applies to a party that has appeared, in proceedings under Rule 55(b)(2).
No further service is required on a party that has not appeared.
topic: Wk 9 · Responding to the complaint — Clerk's default judgment

q: Variation: Same facts, except that the lender's claim is for unliquidated damages for fraud, and the borrower's lawyer sent the lender's lawyer a letter acknowledging the suit and asking for more time, though no answer was ever filed. Which statement is correct?
o: Only the court may enter judgment, after giving the borrower 7 days' written notice.
The clerk may enter judgment, because the borrower never filed an answer.
The court must enter judgment for the full amount demanded, because a default admits all allegations.
No default judgment may be entered, because the borrower has appeared.
oe: Rule 55(b)(2) governs all cases not covered by (b)(1). Unliquidated damages require the court, and a party that has appeared, which courts often find from informal contacts like this, must be served with written notice at least 7 days before the hearing.
The clerk may act only for a sum certain against a non-appearing defendant.
A default admits well-pleaded facts, but the court must determine unliquidated damages, often by hearing.
An appearance entitles the party to notice; it does not prevent a default judgment.
topic: Wk 9 · Responding to the complaint — Unliquidated damages and an appearance
pre: A lender sued a borrower for $42,350 due on a promissory note, plus contractual interest computable from the note. The borrower, an adult, was properly served and never appeared or responded. The clerk entered the borrower's default. The lender submitted an affidavit of the amount due. Who may enter a default judgment?

q: Record companies sued an individual for copyright infringement, alleging that she downloaded and distributed eight identified songs. She was properly served by leaving papers with her adult son at her home, never responded, and the clerk entered her default. The plaintiffs moved for a default judgment for the minimum statutory damages of $750 per work. What must the court do before entering judgment?
o: Confirm that the well-pleaded allegations state a claim for relief.
Hold an evidentiary hearing to establish that infringement occurred.
Require the plaintiffs to re-serve the defendant personally.
Nothing, because a default requires judgment for whatever the plaintiff requests.
oe: A default admits the well-pleaded factual allegations, but the court must still confirm that they state a claim (Virgin Records). Because the minimum statutory damages were fixed by law, no evidentiary hearing on damages was needed.
The well-pleaded facts are admitted by default. A hearing is needed only when damages or facts must be established.
Abode service under Rule 4(e)(2)(B) was valid. No further service is required.
The court must confirm a claim is stated, and Rule 54(c) limits the judgment to what the pleadings demand.
topic: Wk 9 · Responding to the complaint — Default admits facts, not law

q: A clerk entered a defendant's default after it failed to answer because its in-house lawyer was hospitalized. Ten days later, before any judgment, the defendant moved to set aside the default and attached an answer raising a substantial defense. What standard governs?
o: Good cause, which courts apply liberally because defaults are disfavored.
The standards of Rule 60(b), because the default has been entered.
The defendant must show that the plaintiff consented to setting aside the default.
An entry of default cannot be set aside once entered by the clerk.
oe: Rule 55(c) allows the court to set aside an entry of default for good cause. Courts prefer decisions on the merits, and a prompt motion with a meritorious defense and an excusable reason usually succeeds.
Rule 60(b) governs setting aside a default judgment. An entry of default is set aside for good cause.
No consent is required. The court decides under the good-cause standard.
Rule 55(c) expressly permits setting it aside.
topic: Wk 9 · Responding to the complaint — Setting aside default

q: An Oregon homeowner sued a Florida roofing manufacturer in an Oregon state court for $300,000, alleging that its shingles failed. The manufacturer sells only in the Southeast and has no Oregon contacts; the homeowner bought the shingles while living in Florida and took leftover bundles with him when he moved. The manufacturer timely removed to federal court and, five days later, moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction. The homeowner argued that by removing, the manufacturer submitted to the federal court's jurisdiction. How should the court rule?
o: Grant the motion, because removal waived nothing and Oregon lacks jurisdiction.
Deny the motion, because a defendant who invokes federal jurisdiction consents to personal jurisdiction.
Deny the motion, because the manufacturer did not raise personal jurisdiction in the state court.
Remand the case, because a court lacking personal jurisdiction must return the case to state court.
oe: Removal changes the court, not the defendant's right to contest personal jurisdiction. The objection was raised in the defendant's first Rule 12 response, within Rule 81(c)'s time. On the merits, the shingles reached Oregon only through the plaintiff's unilateral move.
Invoking federal subject-matter jurisdiction by removal is not consent to personal jurisdiction.
It had no obligation to respond in state court before removing. Its first Rule 12 response came in federal court.
Lack of personal jurisdiction leads to dismissal, not remand. Remand is for defects in removal or lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.
topic: Wks 1–9 · Integrated problems — Removal does not waive personal jurisdiction

q: A Texas resident sued a Louisiana individual in federal court in the District of Colorado for $500,000, alleging fraud in a land sale that took place entirely in Louisiana. The Louisiana defendant was personally served while skiing in Colorado for a week. In his first Rule 12 motion, he moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction and improper venue. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the personal-jurisdiction challenge but grant the venue challenge or transfer the case.
Deny both challenges, because personal service in Colorado establishes both jurisdiction and venue.
Grant both challenges, because the claim has no connection to Colorado.
Grant the personal-jurisdiction challenge only, because tag jurisdiction applies only in state courts.
oe: In-state service on a voluntarily present individual gives personal jurisdiction (Burnham). Venue is separate: the defendant resides only where he is domiciled, and no events occurred in Colorado, so venue is improper and the court must dismiss or transfer under § 1406(a).
Venue residence for individuals is domicile. Being served in a district does not make it a proper venue.
Tag jurisdiction does not require that the claim relate to the forum.
Rule 4(k)(1)(A) lets a federal court exercise whatever jurisdiction a state court there could, including tag jurisdiction.
topic: Wks 1–9 · Integrated problems — Tag jurisdiction does not fix venue

q: A Nevada company sued a Maine individual in a Nevada state court. The individual believed he had no contacts with Nevada and ignored the suit entirely. The Nevada court entered a default judgment for $90,000. The company then sued on the judgment in a Maine court. In Maine, the individual argued that the Nevada court lacked personal jurisdiction over him. May the Maine court consider that argument?
o: Yes, because a defendant who never appeared may attack jurisdiction collaterally.
No, because the individual waived the defense by failing to appear in Nevada.
No, because full faith and credit requires Maine to enforce the Nevada judgment.
Yes, and he may also relitigate the merits of the company's underlying claim.
oe: A judgment entered without personal jurisdiction is void and is not entitled to full faith and credit (Pennoyer). A defendant who stays out of the case may raise jurisdiction when enforcement is sought, but if the rendering court had jurisdiction, he will have lost his chance to contest the merits.
Waiver by omission applies to a defendant who appears and fails to raise the defense. A defendant who never appears preserves a collateral jurisdictional attack.
Full faith and credit does not extend to judgments rendered without jurisdiction.
The collateral attack is limited to jurisdiction. If the Nevada court had jurisdiction, its default judgment is enforceable on the merits.
topic: Wks 1–9 · Integrated problems — Default judgment and collateral attack

q: A Utah plaintiff sued a Wyoming defendant in federal court in Utah. The court dismissed the action for lack of personal jurisdiction. The plaintiff then filed the same claim against the same defendant in federal court in Wyoming. The defendant argued that the Utah judgment bars the new suit. How should the Wyoming court rule?
o: The new suit may proceed, because a dismissal for lack of jurisdiction is not a judgment on the merits.
The new suit is barred by claim preclusion, because the same claim was already dismissed.
The new suit is barred because the plaintiff should have sought a transfer instead of refiling.
The new suit may proceed only if the plaintiff first obtains leave from the Utah court.
oe: Claim preclusion requires a judgment on the merits. A dismissal for lack of personal jurisdiction decides only that the first court could not hear the case. It would preclude relitigating the Utah jurisdiction issue, but not the claim in Wyoming.
Only a judgment on the merits has claim-preclusive effect.
Transfer was an option, but refiling in a proper forum is permitted.
No leave is required. The plaintiff may file in any court with jurisdiction.
topic: Wks 1–9 · Integrated problems — Dismissal for lack of jurisdiction and preclusion

q: A plaintiff sued in federal court under a federal statute and added a related state-law claim. The court applied the state's highest court's precedent on the state claim, then dismissed the federal claim on summary judgment and declined supplemental jurisdiction over the state claim. The state limitations period had expired while the case was pending. Twenty days later, the plaintiff refiled the state claim in state court. Which statement is correct?
o: The court correctly applied state law, could decline jurisdiction, and the refiled claim is timely.
The court should have applied federal common law to the state claim, because jurisdiction rested on § 1331.
The court was required to keep the state claim, because it had already invested time in the case.
The refiled claim is time-barred, because the limitations period expired during the federal case.
oe: Erie governs state-law supplemental claims. Section 1367(c)(3) permits declining jurisdiction after the federal claims are dismissed, and § 1367(d) tolls the limitations period while the claim was pending and for 30 days after dismissal.
Erie applies to every state-law claim, whatever the source of jurisdiction.
Judicial economy is a factor, but § 1367(c) gives the court discretion to decline.
Section 1367(d) tolled the period during the federal case and for 30 days after dismissal.
topic: Wks 1–9 · Integrated problems — Supplemental claim, Erie, and tolling

q: A Delaware company sued a Korean electronics maker with no United States offices in federal court in Ohio under the federal Lanham Act. The maker sells infringing products online to customers throughout the United States but is not subject to jurisdiction in any single state's courts. The court authorized service by email under Rule 4(f)(3). The maker moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction and improper venue. How should the court rule?
o: Deny both motions.
Grant both motions, because the maker has no contacts with Ohio.
Deny the jurisdiction motion but grant the venue motion, because no events occurred in Ohio.
Grant the jurisdiction motion only, because email service cannot support personal jurisdiction.
oe: Rule 4(k)(2) supplies jurisdiction over a federal claim against a defendant not subject to any state's jurisdiction, based on contacts with the nation as a whole. Venue is proper because a defendant not resident in the United States may be sued in any district (§ 1391(c)(3)). Court-ordered email service is valid under Rule 4(f)(3).
Ohio contacts are unnecessary under Rule 4(k)(2), and venue is proper anywhere for a non-U.S. defendant.
The events test is unnecessary when the defendant is not a United States resident.
Service and jurisdiction are separate. Email service was valid, and jurisdiction rests on Rule 4(k)(2).
topic: Wks 1–9 · Integrated problems — Federal claim, foreign defendant, and venue

q: On January 5, a Georgia plaintiff sued a Georgia defendant and an Alabama defendant in a Georgia state court for $400,000. On February 1, the Georgia defendant moved to Alabama and changed its domicile there. On February 20, the Alabama defendant, which had been served on February 10, removed the case with the Georgia-turned-Alabama defendant's consent. The plaintiff moved to remand within 30 days. How should the court rule?
o: Grant the motion, because diversity was lacking when the action was commenced.
Deny the motion, because complete diversity existed when the notice of removal was filed.
Deny the motion, because the removal was timely and unanimous.
Grant the motion, because the formerly Georgian defendant is a forum defendant.
oe: In a removed case, complete diversity must exist both when the action was filed and when it was removed. On January 5, the plaintiff and one defendant were both Georgia citizens, and a later change of domicile cannot create jurisdiction.
Diversity at removal is necessary but not sufficient. It must also have existed when the action was commenced.
Timeliness and unanimity do not cure a lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.
Right result, wrong reason. By the time of removal it was not a Georgia citizen. The problem is the absence of diversity at filing.
topic: Wks 1–9 · Integrated problems — Diversity, removal, and the time-of-filing rule

q: A defendant removed a state-law case to federal court and, within the time allowed by Rule 81(c), filed an answer that denied liability but raised no defenses. Two months later, it concluded that the complaint fails to state a claim under the governing state law. What should it do?
o: Move for judgment on the pleadings under Rule 12(c).
Move to dismiss under Rule 12(b)(6), because the motion is not waived.
Move to remand, because a federal court may not decide a state-law pleading question.
Nothing, because the defense was waived by answering without raising it.
oe: Failure to state a claim is preserved through trial under Rule 12(h)(2). Once the pleadings are closed, the proper vehicle is a Rule 12(c) motion, decided by the same standard as a 12(b)(6) motion.
The defense is not waived, but a Rule 12(b) motion must be made before a responsive pleading. After answering, Rule 12(c) is the vehicle.
Federal courts decide state-law claims in diversity cases. Nothing about this warrants remand.
Failure to state a claim is not among the defenses waived by omission. It is preserved through trial.
topic: Wks 1–9 · Integrated problems — Removed case: answer, then failure to state a claim

q: A plaintiff sued in federal court on the basis of diversity. State law requires that an action against a physician be served by a sheriff, and service by anyone else is void. The plaintiff used a private process server, an adult nonparty, who handed the papers to the physician personally within 30 days of filing. The physician moved to dismiss for insufficient service, relying on the state law. How should the court rule?
o: Deny the motion, because Rule 4 governs who may serve and was satisfied.
Grant the motion, because applying Rule 4 would let plaintiffs avoid state service requirements by filing in federal court.
Grant the motion, because state law governs service in diversity cases.
Deny the motion, because the physician received the papers within the 90 days allowed by Rule 4(m).
oe: Rule 4(c)(2) allows any nonparty adult to serve, and Rule 4(e)(2)(A) authorizes personal delivery. Under Hanna, a valid Federal Rule that covers the question applies in federal court despite a conflicting state rule.
Forum-shopping concerns belong to the unguided Erie analysis. When a valid Rule is on point, it controls.
Rule 4(e)(1) permits state methods, but Rule 4(e)(2) independently authorizes personal delivery, and Rule 4(c) governs who may serve.
Right result, wrong reason. Timeliness does not validate the manner of service; compliance with Rule 4(c) and 4(e) does.
topic: Wks 1–9 · Integrated problems — Erie, a Federal Rule, and service

q: A contract between a Texas supplier and a Virginia buyer required suit in the Eastern District of Virginia. The supplier sued in federal court in Texas on the basis of diversity, hoping to benefit from Texas choice-of-law rules that would apply Texas law. The court enforced the clause by transferring the case to Virginia under § 1404(a). Which state's choice-of-law rules will the Virginia court apply?
o: Virginia's, because the transfer enforced a forum-selection clause.
Texas's, because the transferor state's law follows a § 1404(a) transfer.
Neither, because the federal court applies federal choice-of-law rules in a transferred case.
Texas's, because the supplier filed there before the clause was enforced.
oe: Ordinarily a § 1404(a) transfer carries the transferor's law (Van Dusen). Atlantic Marine created an exception: when transfer enforces a forum-selection clause, the transferee court applies its own state's choice-of-law rules (Klaxon).
That is the Van Dusen rule, but Atlantic Marine made an exception for transfers enforcing forum-selection clauses.
Under Klaxon, a federal court in diversity applies a state's choice-of-law rules, not federal ones.
Filing first in the wrong forum does not let the plaintiff keep its preferred law under Atlantic Marine.
topic: Wks 1–9 · Integrated problems — Forum-selection clause and choice of law
